A small, closed pocketknife was later reported found in his pocket, which is often cited as a nuance but does not contradict that he was not holding or using a weapon during the confrontation.

claim: "Oregon school districts are directing 24 percent of their food budgets to purchase local foods. That’s the highest percentage in the country."
rationale: I cannot find corroborating national data that Oregon school districts direct 24% of their food budgets to local foods or that this is the highest rate in the country. National Farm to School and USDA reports use varied metrics (share of districts buying any local food, number of local purchases, or percent of budget), and reported budget shares are typically much lower or not comparable across states. The claim appears to conflate different measures or omit a source/year.

claim: Says Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Tammy Baldwin ranks "as the most liberal member of the House."
rationale: The claim asserts Tammy Baldwin was "the most liberal member of the House" but that absolute statement is not supported consistently across ideological metrics. Different rankings (DW-NOMINATE, GovTrack, National Journal, ADA) sometimes listed her among the most liberal members, but none uniformly identify her as the single most liberal representative across years and scoring systems.

claim: The people who want President Barack Obama impeached "are all white, they're all older, and guess what, they're in the far right wing of the Republican Party."
rationale: The statement is an overbroad generalization. While calls to impeach Obama were concentrated among conservative and Tea Party-aligned Republicans (often older and disproportionately white), it is not true that everyone who supported impeachment was white, older, and in the far right; the claim wrongly universalizes a heterogeneous set of activists and commentators.

claim: Says David Perdue wants to abolish the U.S. Department of Education, which would cost Georgia schools $1 billion a year and eliminate millions in student loans.
rationale: While David Perdue has at times supported eliminating the U.S. Department of Education, the specific claim that doing so "would cost Georgia schools $1 billion a year and eliminate millions in student loans" is unsupported. Federal K–12 and higher-education funding levels are set by Congress and many programs could be reallocated or continue under other agencies, so a $1 billion annual loss to Georgia is not an automatic or documented consequence. Likewise, federal student loans are legal obligations backed by the federal government and would not simply be wiped out by abolishing the Department — administration could shift but debts would remain unless canceled by law.

claim: "As of today, no one has the right to film or photograph Mr. Biden as he climbs the flight of stairs. New White House spokesman orders!!?"
rationale: There is no credible evidence of a new blanket order from the White House forbidding anyone from filming or photographing President Biden while boarding or descending stairs. The press and bystanders retain First Amendment protections subject to normal security and access controls (e.g., Secret Service, restricted tarmac or secure areas), and official communications would be required for any change to press pool arrangements.

claim: The Department of Homeland Security’s database of legal immigrants has "never" been "bounced against a state’s voter rolls."
rationale: The absolute claim that DHS immigration databases have "never" been compared to state voter rolls is incorrect. Public reporting and records show that some states and election officials have queried DHS/USCIS verification systems or matched voter lists against federal immigration records in specific checks to identify potential noncitizen registrants.

claim: "Since 2004, more than 2,000 suspected terrorists have legally purchased weapons in the United States."
rationale: No authoritative public data supports the claim that over 2,000 suspected terrorists have legally purchased firearms since 2004. Figures cited in circulation stem from misinterpretations of initial name-matches in background-check or watchlist systems and include false positives or unresolved matches, not confirmed completed purchases by known terrorists. Multiple fact-checks and descriptions of NICS/watchlist procedures show the claim conflates different datasets and meanings.

claim: "As a 27 year old staff attorney for the House Judiciary Committee during the Watergate investigation, Hillary Rodham was fired by her supervisor, lifelong Democrat Jerry Zeifman. When asked why Hillary Rodham was fired, Zeifman said in an interview, ‘Because she was a liar. She was an unethical, dishonest lawyer, she conspired to violate the Constitution, the rules of the House, the rules of the Committee, and the rules of confidentiality.’"
rationale: While former committee staffer Jerry Zeifman did publicly criticize Hillary Rodham in later interviews and is quoted using harsh language and saying he dismissed her, the historical record is contested: other witnesses and Clinton-era accounts say she resigned from the Judiciary Committee staff in 1974. Fact-checking of this episode shows Zeifman’s claim that he 'fired' her and his quoted characterization are disputed and not established as an uncontested factual record.

claim: "There is a growing body of evidence that radiation in excess of what the government says are the minimum amounts you should be exposed to are actually good for you and reduce cases of cancer."
rationale: The claim overstates the evidence: the mainstream scientific and public-health consensus is that increased ionizing radiation generally raises cancer risk and regulatory limits are set on a precautionary basis (commonly using the linear no-threshold model). While a few limited and contested studies propose low-dose radiation hormesis, the evidence is neither strong nor widely accepted and does not support the claim that exposures above recommended limits are beneficial or reduce cancer.

claim: Says health insurance premiums will rise under Obamacare.
rationale: The Affordable Care Act’s impact on premiums was mixed: many individual-market premiums rose in some states and years, particularly for unsubsidized buyers, but federal subsidies offset costs for many enrollees and employer-plan premiums did not uniformly increase because of the law. Therefore the blanket statement that “health insurance premiums will rise under Obamacare” is inaccurate without specifying market segment, time frame, and whether net cost after subsidies is meant.

claim: "Since President (Donald Trump’s) election, 36,000 jobs have been created in WI."
rationale: The claim gives a single cumulative number without specifying the end date or whether it refers to payroll, private-sector, or seasonally adjusted jobs. Official state and BLS employment series for Wisconsin show different job-change totals depending on the chosen start and end months, and there is no unambiguous BLS figure that exactly matches 36,000 'since President Trump's election' without additional context. Because the statement omits timeframe and metric, it cannot be verified as stated.

claim: Says Mitt Romney "paid only 14 percent in taxes — probably less than you."
rationale: The claim compresses nuance into a misleading statement. Romney’s publicly released returns showed an effective federal tax rate in the mid‑teens in some years (roughly around 13–15% depending on the year and which taxes are counted), so the precise ‘‘14 percent’’ figure is an approximation, and the follow‑on ‘‘probably less than you’’ is speculative and misleading because it depends on which taxes, which year, and the taxpayer being compared.

claim: Donald Trump would "engage in a risky scheme to privatize Social Security."
rationale: The claim is predictive and not supported by public evidence: Trump and his campaigns have repeatedly pledged not to cut or privatize Social Security, and his administrations did not advance a concrete plan to privatize the program. Privatizing Social Security would require major legislation and has been politically unpopular, so characterizing it as something he 'would engage' in is speculative rather than a documented fact.

claim: "Fox News went from 97% reporting to 94% in Virginia. The fraud is so blatant it's not funny anymore."
rationale: The claim provides no date, race, or source and mixes changing reported percentages with an unsubstantiated allegation of fraud. Reported percentages on live election pages routinely shift (for example as late-counted absentee or provisional ballots are added) and a drop from 97% to 94% reporting is consistent with normal updates, not by itself proof of fraud.

claim: "U.S. military at the White House arresting Congress."
rationale: There are no credible reports that the U.S. military is at the White House arresting members of Congress; such an event would be unprecedented and immediately widely reported. Domestic use of the military to detain elected officials would conflict with constitutional norms and legal restrictions on military law enforcement.

claim: "When I become the nominee, the Democratic nominee, I will be the only pro-choice candidate on the ballot."
rationale: A person who becomes the Democratic nominee cannot ensure they are the only pro-choice candidate on the general-election ballot. Third-party or independent candidates (and occasionally candidates from other major parties) can also run and hold pro-choice positions, and ballot access varies by state.

claim: The last three days of early voting "happen to be the most populated days of voting that we have in early voting."
rationale: The claim is an overgeneralization. While many jurisdictions do see a surge in turnout in the final days of early voting, patterns vary by state, county, election type, and year, so it is not universally true that the last three days are the most populated.

claim: "For four years, we balanced the budget and paid off $405 billion in debt."
rationale: The U.S. did experience consecutive budget surpluses in the late 1990s/2000–often described as four years of balanced or surplus budgets—but the specific claim of paying off $405 billion is misleading. Official Treasury measures of federal debt depend on definitions (debt held by the public vs. gross public debt) and the commonly cited reductions in public debt over that period do not cleanly match a $405 billion payoff as stated.

claim: The COVID-19 vaccine "will make the common cold/flu extremely lethal."
rationale: There is no evidence that COVID-19 vaccines make unrelated respiratory viruses such as the common cold or seasonal influenza "extremely lethal." COVID-19 vaccines induce immune responses targeted to SARS‑CoV‑2 and have been subject to large-scale safety monitoring; studies and surveillance have not shown an increase in severity or mortality from other common respiratory viruses after vaccination.

claim: A photo shows three men on crosses who "feel like they’re being crucified by being required to stay at home."
rationale: There is no reliable evidence that the photo depicts people literally crucified as punishment or that they actually said they ‘feel like they’re being crucified by being required to stay at home.’ Images of people on crosses are typically staged protests or performance art and are often reposted out of context with misleading captions. Claim conflates a metaphorical complaint about lockdowns with a literal interpretation of the photo, which is unsupported.

claim: About 750,000 people die in China each year from auto emissions.
rationale: While China does have very high deaths from air pollution (on the order of about one million premature deaths annually), mainstream studies attribute only a portion of those to road-transport emissions. Most peer-reviewed estimates put deaths directly linked to motor-vehicle emissions in China far below 750,000 per year, so the specific figure of ~750,000 deaths from auto emissions alone is inconsistent with the literature.

claim: Says Joe Biden said, "This country is doomed, not just because of African Americans, but because by 2040 this country is going to be minority white European."
rationale: There is no reliable record or credible reporting that Joe Biden ever said this sentence; fact-checkers have found the quote is fabricated or misattributed. Publicly available transcripts and videos of Biden’s speeches and interviews do not contain this wording, and the claim appears to be a manufactured quotation circulated on social media.

claim: The planned expansion of Savannah’s port is a "jobs creating project."
rationale: Infrastructure expansions like Savannah’s port typically create jobs both during construction and through increased long‑term operations, and the port authority’s planning documents commonly forecast job gains from the project. That said, exact numbers and the balance of temporary (construction) versus permanent jobs are estimates and can be disputed. Overall, calling it a "jobs creating project" aligns with standard economic effects and official project claims.

claim: A Georgia law has not "criminalized giving people bottles of water." It pertains to political organizations.
rationale: Reporting and reviews of Georgia's recent election law (SB 202) show the controversial provision limits distribution of food, drink or gifts near polling places when done as part of organized, political activity or to influence voters, rather than broadly criminalizing a private person handing someone a bottle of water. Fact-checkers concluded the restriction targets organized political actors and campaign-style distribution in designated buffer zones.

claim: "The fundraising numbers are in, and our grassroots support is unmatched!"
rationale: The claim combines an asserted release of fundraising figures with an unqualified comparative statement that grassroots support is 'unmatched,' but no specific numbers, timeframe, or comparison group are provided. Without verifiable campaign finance filings, independent fundraising tallies, or metrics comparing supporter engagement across organizations, the claim cannot be substantiated and is treated as false.

claim: "More businesses are closing than opening in Virginia today."
rationale: The claim asserts a real-time net decrease in Virginia businesses for "today," which cannot be confirmed without up-to-date official data. Openings and closures are reported with a time lag (typically monthly or quarterly) and vary by industry and locality, so the blanket, same-day statement is unsubstantiated.

claim: A state report’s "projection is that approximately half of public employees" would live outside municipal boundaries in a decade if the state bans local residency requirements.
rationale: The claim names no specific state or identifiable report, and I find no widely reported, verifiable state analysis that projects 'approximately half of public employees' would move outside municipal boundaries within a decade if local residency requirements were banned. Such a projection would depend heavily on local labor markets, housing availability, and modeling assumptions, so the statement cannot be confirmed as presented. Without a cited report or state, the claim is unverified and thus judged false.

claim: "Much more than 50 percent of parents out there are spankers."
rationale: The statement is too broad and unsupported: prevalence of parents who spank varies widely by country, culture, child age and survey year, and is not uniformly "much more than 50%." In many high-income countries recent surveys show rates at or below 50% and trends of decline, while some other contexts report higher rates, so the blanket claim is not justified.

claim: "This is the first time since Roe was decided in 1973 that a court has granted personhood status to the preborn."
rationale: This is incorrect: since Roe (1973) many courts have recognized the unborn as legal persons for specific purposes, such as fetal homicide statutes, wrongful-death claims, and related criminal and civil protections. Those decisions and state laws have routinely treated fetuses as legal victims long before recent cases.

claim: "If we keep the minimum wage at the current level, then single-parent families earning the minimum wage at a full-time job will live in poverty in New Jersey."
rationale: The statement is too categorical: whether a single-parent family working full-time at the minimum wage lives in poverty depends on the exact wage, number of children, hours worked, taxes, and public benefits. With New Jersey's recent minimum-wage levels (around $13–$15/hr by 2023–2024) a single parent with one child working full time may be near or above the federal poverty threshold, while parents with multiple children can still fall below it. State and federal tax credits and assistance programs also change whether families end up below official poverty lines.

claim: "The Obama-Clinton war on coal has cost Michigan over 50,000 jobs."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Michigan lost over 50,000 coal-related jobs specifically because of an "Obama-Clinton war on coal." Michigan historically had very few coal mining jobs, and most employment declines in coal-fired generation were driven by market factors (cheap natural gas, plant retirements, automation) rather than a targeted policy that eliminated tens of thousands of jobs in that state. Independent fact-checkers and state employment data do not support the 50,000 figure or the causal attribution to Obama/Clinton policies.

claim: Says North Carolina’s "Democratic Secretary of State" controls the state's elections.
rationale: North Carolina’s Secretary of State does not control the state’s elections. Elections in North Carolina are administered by the North Carolina State Board of Elections and county boards; the Secretary of State primarily handles business registrations and related filings, not election administration.

claim: "Our children do not spend any time in school learning about our own U.S. Constitution."
rationale: The claim is inaccurate as a general statement: U.S. K–12 curricula commonly include U.S. history, civics, and government courses that cover the Constitution, and most states have standards requiring civics or history instruction. Time spent and depth vary by grade, district, and school type, but it is incorrect to assert that children spend no time learning about the Constitution at all.

claim: Voters in Maricopa County, Ariz., were forced to vote using Sharpie pens that aren’t read by voting machines.
rationale: Maricopa County officials provided Sharpie markers at some polling locations but did not force voters to use them, and county and state election authorities — backed by multiple fact-checks — reported that Sharpie ink is readable by the county’s optical-scan tabulators and that no votes were lost due to Sharpie use. Claims that machines couldn’t read Sharpie-marked ballots were investigated and debunked by election officials and independent reporting.

claim: Says the state’s budget shortfall is "not that much different" than it was in 2003.
rationale: The claim is unverifiable as stated because it gives no state or specific figures; state budget shortfalls vary widely and must be compared using the same accounting rules and inflation-adjusted dollars. In most cases a nominal comparison to 2003 would be misleading, and without those details the assertion that the shortfall is "not that much different" is not supportable.

claim: During Lyndon B. Johnson’s first 20 years in Congress, "he opposed every civil rights measure that came up for a vote."
rationale: Johnson did oppose some early civil-rights proposals (for example he opposed certain anti-lynching and FEPC measures), but he did not oppose every civil-rights measure during his first two decades in Congress. By the 1950s his record had become mixed and he supported and helped pass measures such as the 1957 Civil Rights Act, so the blanket claim is inaccurate.

claim: "This is the only state in the country that bypassed the General Assembly to authorize [in-state tuition for undocumented immigrants]."
rationale: The statement asserts a unique nationwide occurrence but is implausible: several states have authorized in‑state tuition for undocumented students through means other than their full legislatures (for example via governors' actions, university/regent boards, or court rulings). Because multiple jurisdictions have used non‑legislative routes, the claim of being the only state to bypass the General Assembly is incorrect without specific context or timeframe.

claim: Georgia is the second-fastest growing state for international tourists.
rationale: The claim is unspecified by timeframe or source and is not supported by commonly cited data on international arrivals, which typically show states like California, New York, Florida and Texas leading international visitation. Rankings of growth rates vary by year and data source, and there is no consistent evidence that Georgia (U.S. state) is broadly the second-fastest growing destination for international tourists. Without a specific period or dataset, the blanket statement is unreliable.

claim: "The labor participation rate is at an all-time low."
rationale: The claim is unverifiable as written because it fails to specify a country or time period; labor force participation rates vary by country and over time. In many cases (for example the United States), participation dropped sharply during the 2020 pandemic but has since recovered and is not currently at a documented all-time low. Without specific jurisdiction and date, the blanket statement is false.

claim: When Honduran children came into this country, "Secretary Clinton said send them back."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Hillary Clinton ever said “send them back” about Honduran children; media and fact-checkers found no recording or contemporaneous report of that quote. Clinton left the State Department in early 2013 and was not in office during the 2014 surge of unaccompanied Central American children, and searches of her public statements do not turn up this phrase.

claim: "For the first time in history, Wisconsin has more government jobs than manufacturing jobs."
rationale: The claim is implausible without a specific year or data source; historically Wisconsin’s workforce has been dominated by manufacturing and while government employment has grown relative to manufacturing in recent years, authoritative labor-series (BLS/CES and Wisconsin DWD) are needed to confirm any first-time crossing. Available public data show declines in manufacturing jobs and relatively stable government employment, but do not unambiguously support the blanket statement that this is the first time in history statewide.

claim: "Senator Obama has, in fact, never had a serious Republican challenger."
rationale: As a U.S. Senate candidate in 2004 Barack Obama did face Republican opponents: Jack Ryan was the original Republican nominee (seen as a potentially credible challenger) before withdrawing amid scandal, and Alan Keyes replaced him in the general election. Because Obama did have Republican challengers and a potentially serious contender briefly existed, the absolute claim that he 'never had a serious Republican challenger' is inaccurate.

claim: "In 2005, Dan Branch tried to expand third-trimester abortions in Texas."
rationale: Dan Branch is a Republican Texas legislator known for a pro-life record; in 2005 he did not seek to expand third‑trimester abortions but instead backed measures that restricted abortion access. Contemporary accounts and his legislative history show he sponsored and supported restrictions rather than expansions of late‑term abortion. Therefore the claim is incorrect.

claim: In Europe, "church attendance rates (are) in the single digits" because churches are supported by taxes.
rationale: The claim overgeneralizes. Weekly church attendance in Europe varies widely — some countries (e.g., Czech Republic, Estonia) have single-digit weekly attendance, but others (e.g., Poland, Romania, parts of Ireland and Italy) have much higher rates. Moreover, while several European states have church-tax or state-support arrangements, tax support is not universal and does not reliably explain cross-country attendance differences, which are driven more by culture, history, and levels of religiosity.

claim: Refugees are throwing rocks and trying "to kill you."
rationale: This is a sweeping, unqualified allegation about refugees as a group that lacks supporting evidence. While isolated incidents of violence involving individuals who are refugees or migrants have occurred in specific places and times, there is no basis to assert that refugees generally are throwing rocks and trying to kill people.

claim: Says Virginia Republican "Scott Taylor has been convicted in at least four different courts across the country, at times failing to even appear, and having a warrant issued for his arrest."
rationale: Available reporting on former Virginia congressman Scott Taylor documents a handful of local legal incidents and at least one warrant-related episode, but does not support a claim that he was convicted in at least four different courts across the country. The statement appears to conflate separate local charges and procedural actions and exaggerates the number and geographic scope of convictions.

claim: "Instagram has been limiting our posts so that no more than 7% of our friends see our posts."
rationale: There is no evidence that Instagram universally limits post visibility to a fixed 7% of friends/followers. Instagram uses an algorithmic ranking that shows content to varying fractions of an account's audience based on factors like engagement, recency, and relevance, so reach fluctuates by account and post rather than being a single fixed percentage.

claim: "No member of the American public has ever been killed by commercial nuclear power — a record unmatched by other fuels."
rationale: There are no documented cases of members of the American public being directly killed by releases from commercial nuclear power plants in the United States; major U.S. commercial incidents such as Three Mile Island (1979) produced no immediate public fatalities. Fatal reactor incidents in U.S. history (e.g., SL‑1) involved military or research reactors and workers, not commercial civilian plants, while other fuels (coal, oil, natural gas, hydro) have a record of causing public deaths from mine and dam disasters, pipeline explosions and air‑pollution effects.

claim: Dozens of artists, including Justin Timberlake, Jay Z and Rihanna, are canceling Florida shows like Stevie Wonder in protest of  "stand your ground."
rationale: There is no evidence that dozens of major artists cancelled Florida shows in protest of 'stand your ground.' While a small number of performers (notably Stevie Wonder) publicly pulled shows or voiced opposition after the Zimmerman verdict, high-profile acts like Justin Timberlake, Jay‑Z and Rihanna did not cancel Florida dates as part of a broad coordinated boycott. The claim overstates both the number of cancellations and the participation of the named artists.

claim: The Buffalo Billion is "still breaking every job promise"
rationale: Saying the Buffalo Billion is "still breaking every job promise" is inaccurate because the program’s results have been mixed: state audits and press investigations found multiple projects failed to meet pledged job targets and there were corruption probes, but other investments did create jobs and met or partially met goals. The absolute word "every" is contradicted by documented cases of jobs being created under the program.

claim: "From 2000 to 2016, every major drug that was introduced came out of" National Institutes of Health funding.
rationale: The statement is an overgeneralization. While NIH-funded basic research contributed to the discovery or development of many important drugs between 2000 and 2016, not every major drug introduced in that period was the direct product of NIH funding—many were discovered and developed primarily within private pharmaceutical or biotech companies without direct NIH support.

claim: "We’re the seventh highest taxed state in America. And that’s not just state, it’s local as well."
rationale: The statement as presented is unverifiable and likely misleading because it omits which state and which tax metric (per-capita tax burden, share of income, effective tax rate, or a particular year) is being used. Tax rankings for states vary substantially by metric and year—a state could be 7th by one measure and far from it by others—so the blanket claim cannot be accepted as true. Without a specified state and data source, the assertion that 'we' are the seventh-highest taxed state (including local taxes) is not supported.

claim: "Scott Walker gave Wisconsin job creation money to his cronies: corporate friends who contributed to his campaigns" and got $570 million in job-development incentives
rationale: While Wisconsin under Gov. Scott Walker awarded hundreds of millions in economic development incentives through the WEDC and some recipient companies had donated to or had ties with Walker or allies, reliable public audits and reporting do not substantiate the specific claim that he 'gave job creation money to his cronies' as a proven pay‑for‑play scheme or that exactly $570 million was paid specifically to campaign contributors. Investigations documented poor oversight and conflicts of interest concerns, but direct causal wrongdoing and the precise $570 million figure are not clearly supported by the public record.

claim: "I went to the Olympics that was out of balance, and we got it on balance."
rationale: The claim is a vague, first-person statement about attending an unspecified Olympics and an ambiguous outcome ('we got it on balance') with no verifiable details. Without identification of who spoke, which Games, or independent evidence (records, reporting, photos), the assertion cannot be confirmed and is treated as unsupported.

claim: "The spillover violence (from Mexico) in Texas is real and it is escalating."
rationale: Cross‑border incidents and isolated episodes of violence along the Texas–Mexico border have occurred, so some spillover is real; however available reporting and official data do not support a clear, sustained statewide escalation of spillover violence. Experts and law enforcement describe these events as localized and episodic rather than a broadly escalating trend across Texas.

claim: A 13-year-old girl "is now in critical care in the hospital here in Halifax because her heart stopped right after she had a vaccine."
rationale: I could not find independent, verifiable evidence that a 13-year-old in Halifax is in critical care after her heart stopped immediately following vaccination; the claim appears anecdotal and lacks corroboration from hospitals or public health authorities. Even if an event occurred, temporal proximity alone does not establish that the vaccine caused the heart to stop.

claim: "The CBO says (the Build Back Better Act) is $3 trillion of deficit spending."
rationale: The CBO did not state that the Build Back Better Act was $3 trillion of deficit spending. CBO and JCT scores for various BBB versions showed substantially lower net deficit increases after offsets (commonly in the roughly $1–2 trillion range depending on the version), and the $3 trillion (or $3.5 trillion) figures typically refer to gross proposal totals, not CBO’s net deficit estimate.

claim: "70 percent of the people who voted" on June 5, 2012, "just didn’t feel comfortable with the recall of the governor," weakening any idea that Wisconsin is "fully behind this Walker agenda."
rationale: There is no evidence that 70% of people who voted on June 5, 2012 said they were uncomfortable with the recall. The June 5, 2012 Wisconsin recall election resulted in Scott Walker winning re‑election by roughly 53% to 46%, and contemporaneous polls did not show a 70% majority opposing the recall itself. The 70% figure is unsupported and likely conflates different measures (turnout, vote share, or a specific poll) with a broad claim about voter sentiment.

claim: Says "President Trump makes English the official language of the United States!"
rationale: No federal law was passed making English the official language of the United States during President Trump's tenure, and a president cannot unilaterally change statutory law to designate an official language. While administrations can issue orders or guidance affecting federal agencies' use of language, that does not create a nationwide official-language law.

claim: "There's been a 1,700 percent increase in asylum claims over the last 10 years."
rationale: The claim is presented without any country, time window specification, or data source and is implausibly large as a general statement. Asylum claim trends vary widely by country and year; while some countries have experienced large percentage increases over short periods, there is no consistent evidence of a 1,700% increase in asylum claims globally or across most major destination countries over the past decade.

claim: "The collective net worth of Americans has taken a $5.5 trillion hit ... mainly due to plummeting home values."
rationale: The claim gives no date or source for the $5.5 trillion figure and attribution, so it cannot be verified as stated. Changes in U.S. household net worth are tracked by the Federal Reserve and BEA and can be driven by both housing values and equity markets; without a specific timeframe and source the assertion that the loss was $5.5 trillion and was driven mainly by plummeting home values is unsubstantiated.

claim: "The higher the education level, the more likely they are to vote Democratic."
rationale: The claim is an overbroad generalization. In recent U.S. elections higher education (especially postgraduate degrees) has correlated with greater Democratic support, but this pattern varies strongly by race, region, and over time and historically college-educated voters sometimes leaned Republican; other countries show different relationships between education and party preference.

claim: "In the 18th Congressional District, 100% of electric generation comes from coal."
rationale: No congressional district in the U.S. is served solely by coal generation; electricity supply is provided by regional grids with diverse mixes (coal, natural gas, nuclear, hydro, wind, solar and imports). Public generation and grid data for any specific '18th Congressional District' show a combination of sources rather than 100% coal. The claim is implausible without a specific state or date and contradicts typical grid operations.

claim: "Over 73% of all donations raised (from the ALS Ice Bucket Challenge) are going to fundraising, overhead, executive salaries, and external donations."
rationale: Independent reporting and the ALS Association’s financial statements from the Ice Bucket Challenge period indicate a large share of funds were used for research grants, patient services, and program expenses rather than being consumed by fundraising, overhead, or executive pay. The specific claim that over 73% of donations went to fundraising, overhead, executive salaries, and external donations contradicts audited expense breakdowns and charity watchdog analyses from that time.

claim: Huckabee "was one of the highest taxing governors that we had in this country and rivaling Bill Clinton in terms of the Cato ratings."
rationale: Cato’s Fiscal Policy Report Card consistently gave Mike Huckabee poor scores for tax and spending policy, marking him among governors who raised taxes or expanded government; those low grades put him near other historically low-scoring governors such as Bill Clinton in his gubernatorial record. Saying Huckabee was “one of the highest taxing governors” and “rivaling Bill Clinton in terms of the Cato ratings” reflects those Cato assessments.

claim: "Due to the recent downturn in steel production, more than 13,600 Americans have been laid off and the steel industry is facing billions in losses."
rationale: The specific claim ties a recent downturn to an exact figure of "more than 13,600" U.S. layoffs and "billions in losses" without a cited timeframe or source. Public reporting and industry data typically specify periods and company-level losses; I found no widely reported, verifiable aggregate figure that matches this claim as stated. The statement is therefore unverified and likely inaccurate as presented.

claim: While in Congress, Nathan Deal was a leader when it came to protecting our borders.
rationale: The statement is vague and unsubstantiated: Nathan Deal did generally vote for stricter immigration enforcement and supported border-security measures, but there is no clear evidence he was widely recognized as a national congressional leader on border protection (e.g., chairing major border/security committees or authoring signature federal border-security legislation). Calling him a 'leader' overstates his documented role in Congress.

claim: Clean energy employs "more than half a million Californians. That’s nearly ten times more the number of coal mining jobs that exist in the entire nation."
rationale: State and industry tallies in recent years put California’s clean-energy workforce at roughly half a million or more, while U.S. coal mining employment has been on the order of about 40,000–60,000 workers. That makes California’s clean-energy employment roughly ten times the size of the entire nation’s coal-mining workforce, within the usual margins of reporting variation.

claim: "Florida’s high school graduation rate falls well below the national average."
rationale: Recent U.S. data show Florida's four-year high school graduation rate has been at or slightly above the national average in multiple recent cohorts, so the characterization that it "falls well below" the national average is inaccurate. While rates vary by year and subgroup, Florida is not broadly trailing the national rate by a large margin.

claim: Says Gerald Daugherty advocated lowering the penalty for crimes like strangulation in domestic violence cases because "they just ‘throw more people into the’" jail "‘system."
rationale: There is no reliable, corroborated reporting or primary-source quote attributing this statement or advocacy to a person named Gerald Daugherty. Without verifiable evidence tying him to that policy position and the quoted language, the claim appears unsubstantiated and is likely false.

claim: Athletes are collapsing with heart-related issues due to the COVID-19 vaccines
rationale: There is no reliable evidence that COVID-19 vaccines are causing widespread collapses of athletes from heart problems. While rare cases of myocarditis have been observed after mRNA vaccination (mostly mild and in young males), public-health surveillance and studies show these events are uncommon and that SARS-CoV-2 infection itself carries a higher risk of cardiac complications; investigations of athlete collapses have not supported a broad causal link to vaccination.

claim: "Our economy created over 6.5 million new jobs just last year, more jobs in one year than ever before in the history of the United States of America."
rationale: Official Bureau of Labor Statistics payroll data show the US added roughly 6.3–6.6 million payroll jobs in 2021 depending on the exact month range, commonly reported as about 6.4 million — slightly below the claim of "over 6.5 million." It is correct that the 2021 annual increase was the largest year-over-year gain on record in the BLS series, so the second part (largest single-year gain) is true but the precise count in the claim is overstated.

claim: Says his plan to end the toll on Ga. 400 fulfills his campaign promise to commuters.
rationale: The claim reports that someone 'says his plan to end the toll on Ga. 400 fulfills his campaign promise,' but it provides no named speaker, date, or source. Without attribution or independent reporting confirming the statement, the assertion cannot be verified as true. Therefore I must mark it false given the missing evidence.

claim: Says Pope Francis "was arrested Saturday in connection with an 80-count indictment of charges including possession of child pornography, human trafficking, incest, possession of drug paraphernalia and felony fraud."
rationale: No credible news organizations or Vatican authorities reported that Pope Francis was arrested on any such indictment; the story matches widely circulated social-media hoaxes and fabrications. An arrest of the Pope on eighty felony counts would be globally reported and confirmed, which has not occurred.

claim: Says Adam Schiff used taxpayer money to "reach a sexual harassment settlement with a 19-year-old male."
rationale: There is no credible evidence or public record showing Rep. Adam Schiff used taxpayer funds to settle a sexual‑harassment claim with a 19‑year‑old male; major news outlets and fact‑checkers found no substantiation and Schiff’s office has denied such payments. Additionally, House rules and recent reforms bar using congressional funds for such settlements, making the specific claim unlikely without clear documentation.

claim: Says Hillary Clinton dressed up in blackface.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Hillary Clinton dressed in blackface. Viral images and claims alleging she did have been investigated and debunked by multiple independent fact-checkers as manipulated or false.

claim: Says Republican Gov. Phil Scott "just voted to impeach President Trump."
rationale: Governors do not cast votes in federal impeachment proceedings — the U.S. House of Representatives votes to impeach and the Senate conducts the trial. There is no record of Vermont Gov. Phil Scott voting in Congress; at most he could publicly support or oppose impeachment, but he could not have 'voted to impeach' as governor.

claim: New and proposed state laws on voting mean "if you are going to be standing in that line for all those hours, you can’t have any water or any food."
rationale: This statement is an overgeneralization. While some new or proposed state laws create buffer zones that restrict electioneering and the distribution of materials (and in some cases food or drink) near polling places, they typically do not impose a blanket ban on voters carrying or consuming personal water or food while standing in line; provisions and exceptions vary by state.

claim: Says a New York physician and his wife jumped to their deaths because they "can’t afford" Obamacare.
rationale: Multiple fact-checkers and contemporaneous news reports found no evidence that a New York physician and his wife jumped to their deaths because they ‘couldn’t afford’ the Affordable Care Act. Law enforcement and credible reporting did not attribute the deaths to Obamacare, and the social-media claim appears to be an unfounded attribution circulated after the tragedy.

claim: "Dr. Oz releases COPD gummies that help quit smoking, detox lungs and stop COPD."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that any gummy product — including ones promoted by Dr. Oz — can cure or stop COPD, "detox" lungs, or reliably make people quit smoking. COPD is a chronic, largely irreversible lung disease managed with prescribed medications, oxygen therapy, and smoking cessation programs; claims of a simple gummy cure are unsupported by medical research.

claim: "The committee that advises @GovEvers and his department tasked with leading during this pandemic is recommending allowing prisoners to receive the vaccine before 65 year old grandma?"
rationale: State and federal vaccine advisory guidance during the COVID-19 rollout prioritized healthcare workers and residents of long-term care, then older adults (often 65+) before broader groups in congregate settings. Wisconsin’s advisory bodies did not recommend statewide that incarcerated people be vaccinated ahead of all 65+ adults, though some local jurisdictions made different operational choices.

claim: Tapping the Strategic Petroleum Reserve would immediately lower gasoline prices
rationale: Releasing oil from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve can increase crude supply and may put downward pressure on oil prices, but it does not reliably produce an immediate drop in retail gasoline prices. Gasoline prices depend on crude prices, refinery runs and capacity, regional distribution, fuel blends, and taxes, so changes typically take time and can be offset by market expectations or limited refinery throughput.

claim: Photos show Kamala Harris, Joe Biden, Gretchen Whitmer and Cory Booker violating COVID-19 safety precautions.
rationale: The claim is stated too broadly and lacks necessary context. While individual photos have circulated showing Harris, Biden, Whitmer or Booker unmasked or in close proximity at various times, whether those images show violations depends on timing, location, and prevailing public-health guidance (for example outdoor settings, vaccination status, or local rules). I cannot verify a single body of photos that definitively proves all four were unlawfully or unjustifiably violating COVID-19 precautions.

claim: Says Gov. Rick Scott's approval ratings are up.
rationale: The claim lacks any timeframe or source and approval ratings for Rick Scott have varied across different polls and periods. Without a specific date, poll, or comparator it's impossible to verify a general statement that his approval ratings are "up," so the claim cannot be confirmed as presented.

claim: Says Georgia ranks "near the bottom in per capita transportation spending."
rationale: The statement is too categorical without specifying a year or which spending measure is used. Federal and state comparisons show Georgia is often below the national average on some state-only per-capita transportation spending metrics but is not consistently ranked 'near the bottom' across years and when federal and local spending or large highway projects are included. Therefore the blanket claim is not reliably supported.

claim: "Two million more people just dropped out of Obamacare. It is in a death spiral."
rationale: There is no authoritative evidence of a sudden additional two million people 'dropping out' of the ACA marketplaces recently; official enrollment reports and nonpartisan analyses have shown stable or rising marketplace enrollment in recent years. The claim's 'death spiral' characterization is a political shorthand that is not supported by observed enrollment trends, federal subsidies that stabilize premiums, and insurer participation data.

claim: "Nobody suffered any lasting injuries" from the CIA interrogation program.
rationale: Extensive investigations, medical assessments, and legal findings document that multiple detainees subjected to the CIA detention and 'enhanced interrogation' program suffered lasting physical and psychological injuries (including PTSD, long-term health problems, and at least one death). The U.S. Senate Intelligence Committee's 2014 report, Red Cross and human-rights reports, and subsequent legal cases corroborate enduring harm from the program's techniques.

claim: "The average person who gets the minimum wage in America is 35 years old."
rationale: Published labor statistics and research show that workers paid at or near the minimum wage skew younger than age 35; the typical (median or mean) age is lower and varies by year, state, and definition. Claims that the average minimum-wage worker is exactly 35 are common political talking points but do not match standard BLS analyses.

claim: "There was never a single shred of evidence presented to anyone" that the attacks in Benghazi, Libya, were "spontaneous, and in fact, the CIA themselves understood that early on."
rationale: The claim that there was "never a single shred of evidence" that the Benghazi attacks were spontaneous is inaccurate: in the immediate aftermath U.S. officials and intelligence reports cited local demonstrations and a nearby protest tied to an anti‑Islam video, and those accounts were reflected in early public talking points. At the same time, CIA and other intelligence assessments evolved over days and weeks, with some analysts early on noting indicators of a coordinated militant attack and later assessments concluding it was a terrorist operation; the record therefore does not support the absolute statement in the claim.

claim: Dan McCready backed state legislation that raised consumers "$149 million a year in higher energy costs."
rationale: There is no clear public record that Dan McCready sponsored or voted for state legislation that directly raised consumer energy costs by $149 million a year. McCready was a congressional candidate and not a member of the North Carolina General Assembly, and the $149 million figure appears to originate from opponent analyses or ads attributing projected costs to other bills rather than a documented action by McCready.

claim: Says Trump ties are made "in China, not Colorado. Trump suits in Mexico, not Michigan. Trump furniture in Turkey, not Ohio. Trump picture frames in India, not Wisconsin."
rationale: The claim rigidly assigns single foreign countries as the manufacturing origin for several Trump-branded product categories, which is an overgeneralization. While many Trump-branded or licensed goods have indeed been produced overseas (including in China, Mexico, Turkey, India and elsewhere), manufacturing sources vary by product line, licensee and time period, so the categorical statement is not strictly accurate.

claim: Multnomah County has faced "11 straight years" of cuts
rationale: The statement that Multnomah County has faced "11 straight years" of cuts is not verifiable as an uncomplicated fact. County budgets typically fluctuate year-to-year, and public budget records show periods of both reductions and increases depending on the fund and time period; there is no clear, universally applied metric showing eleven consecutive years of cuts to Multnomah County as a whole. Without a specific timeframe and definition of "cuts" (which budget, adjusted for inflation, personnel vs. capital, etc.), the claim is unsupported.

claim: Illegal immigration on the U.S.-Mexico border is "the lowest in 17 years."
rationale: The statement is too specific and, without a clear timeframe or metric, is not supported by publicly available U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) and Department of Homeland Security data. In recent years (especially since 2021) encounters at the U.S.–Mexico border have been higher than many prior years, and official counts vary by measure (apprehensions, encounters, estimated illegal entries), so claiming it is the "lowest in 17 years" is misleading and not verifiable as stated.

claim: "There was a raid on the Biden residence yesterday by the military!"
rationale: There is no credible evidence or wide media reporting that the U.S. military conducted a raid on the Biden residence yesterday. An operation of that magnitude would be nationally significant and almost certainly accompanied by official statements and extensive mainstream coverage; absent such corroboration, the claim appears false. Additionally, domestic raids on private residences are ordinarily carried out by civilian law enforcement (e.g., the FBI), not the military, except under extraordinary legal authority.

claim: Says the fluoride Austin is putting in its drinking water is "toxic waste."
rationale: The fluoride compounds used in municipal water systems (commonly hydrofluorosilicic acid, sodium fluoride, or sodium fluorosilicate) are added at low, regulated concentrations and are not treated or classified as 'toxic waste' in the context of water fluoridation. Although some fluoridation chemicals originate as byproducts of phosphate fertilizer production, that manufacturing origin does not make the diluted, regulated additives legally or scientifically 'toxic waste.'

claim: "How is a misogynist bigot of epic proportions (like U.S. Rep. Steven Smith) allowed to serve?"
rationale: The statement asserts a value judgment about a specific individual ('U.S. Rep. Steven Smith') without presenting verifiable examples. There is no clear, verifiable record of a current U.S. Representative by that exact name widely recognized in national Congress as of my last update, and labeling someone a 'misogynist bigot of epic proportions' requires documented statements or conduct that are not supplied here.

claim: Says Brett Kavanaugh "refused to uphold key patient protections in the past."
rationale: The statement is a broad, unsourced assertion and cannot be confirmed as a general fact without specifying which "key patient protections" and which actions are meant. While Brett Kavanaugh's D.C. Circuit opinions were criticized by some for rulings in cases involving the Affordable Care Act, insurers, and regulatory deference, critics point to particular decisions rather than a single, categorical refusal to uphold patient protections across the board. Because the claim is vague and lacks concrete examples, it is not verifiably true as stated.

claim: State "school funding per pupil is down 16 percent compared to 2009, after adjusting for inflation."
rationale: The claim is unverifiable as stated because it does not identify which state or what funding sources are included. National and many state-level datasets show that inflation-adjusted per-pupil spending fell in some states after the 2008–09 recession but recovered and in many places rose by the mid-2010s; a blanket 16% decline since 2009 is not supported as a general fact. Without a specified state, year of comparison method, and data source, the statement cannot be confirmed.

claim: The mobilization of the military in response to the storms in Puerto Rico and the U.S. Virgin Islands "is the largest ever mobilization of our military in a naval and marine operation" and an Air Force carrier there "was the first-ever as well."
rationale: The claim is incorrect: far larger naval and marine mobilizations have occurred in history (for example major World War II amphibious operations and large Cold War/war-era deployments), and significant domestic disaster responses (e.g., Hurricane Katrina) involved massive military assets. Additionally, the statement refers to an "Air Force carrier," which is a category error—aircraft carriers are operated by the Navy, not the Air Force.

claim: "I campaigned on (the proposals in the budget repair bill for Wisconsin) all throughout the election. Anybody who says they are shocked on this has been asleep for the past two years."
rationale: The claim asserts the speaker campaigned on the specific proposals in Wisconsin’s 2011 budget-repair bill ‘all throughout the election.’ Contemporary reporting and campaign materials show the campaign emphasized fiscal restraint and broad reform themes, but the detailed provisions of the 2011 budget-repair bill (including major limits on public-sector collective bargaining) were developed and announced after the election and were not presented as explicit, fully formed campaign promises throughout the campaign.

claim: "Americans not vaccinated before 2022 will be put in camps"
rationale: There is no evidence that U.S. federal or state governments planned or implemented rounding up unvaccinated Americans into camps before or after 2022. Public-health responses included vaccination campaigns, workplace mandates in some sectors, and limited quarantine/isolation for contagious individuals, but mass internment would violate constitutional protections and would have produced widespread official documentation and legal challenges. Claims about 'vaccine camps' trace to conspiracy theories and misinformation rather than documented policy.

claim: "The current (agriculture) commissioner allowed tainted beef to be sent to school cafeterias."
rationale: The claim is unsubstantiated as written: it names no specific agriculture commissioner, jurisdiction, timeframe, or evidence that contaminated beef was knowingly allowed into school cafeterias. Publicly reported incidents of contaminated meat typically involve recalls, inspections, and agency actions rather than deliberate allowance, and I find no corroborating, verifiable reports matching this broad assertion. Without specific, credible sourcing, the claim cannot be confirmed.

claim: Barack Obama's church gave a lifetime achievement award to Louis Farrakhan.
rationale: Trinity United Church of Christ in Chicago, the church Barack Obama attended for many years, honored Nation of Islam leader Louis Farrakhan with a lifetime achievement award when Farrakhan spoke there in 2005; this was reported by multiple news organizations. The award was given by the church, not personally by Obama.

claim: Under the Iran nuclear deal, "we give them $150 billion, we get nothing."
rationale: This claim is misleading and inaccurate: the United States did not hand Iran a $150 billion lump-sum payment. The 2015 JCPOA led to the phased lifting of certain sanctions and the release or unfreezing of some Iranian assets held overseas (estimates vary and are commonly much lower than $150B), and in return Iran accepted significant nuclear restrictions, monitoring and verification by the IAEA. It is therefore incorrect to say 'we give them $150 billion, we get nothing.'

claim: "We have one of the lowest mortality rates in the world" from COVID-19.
rationale: The claim as written is not verifiable: it omits which country or population 'we' refers to and which mortality measure and time period are meant. COVID-19 mortality varies greatly by metric (deaths per capita, case fatality rate, infection fatality rate), testing, demographics, and reporting practices, so a blanket assertion that 'we have one of the lowest' cannot be supported without specific data.

claim: Quotes show Democrats supported riots "when BLM was BURNING down cities and killing people in the streets!"
rationale: The claim that quotes show Democrats supported riots while 'BLM was burning down cities and killing people' is misleading and not supported by the record. Many Democratic leaders condemned violence while defending the right to protest, and the Black Lives Matter movement and most 2020 protests were peaceful; incidents of arson, looting, and deaths were carried out by a variety of actors and not uniformly endorsed by Democrats. Broadly attributing endorsement of violence to 'Democrats' based on selected quotes is inaccurate.

claim: "$575 billion cut from Medicare in Trump’s proposed 2020 budget."
rationale: The 2020 presidential budget proposal included several changes affecting Medicare spending, but it did not unambiguously specify a single $575 billion ‘cut’ to Medicare as stated. Different official and independent estimates reported varying savings or reductions over different timeframes and definitions (reductions in projected growth, program changes, or reallocations), so the $575 billion figure is a misleading simplification without context.

claim: Gov. McDonnell's proposed budget "is cutting" public education.
rationale: The claim is unspecific and therefore not reliably verifiable as stated. Gov. McDonnell (commonly Bob McDonnell of Virginia) proposed multiple budgets during his term with varying impacts on different parts of education—some proposals reduced spending in certain areas while others restored or reallocated funds. Without a specific year, state, and line-item detail, the blanket statement that his proposed budget "is cutting" public education is unsupported.

claim: Water rates in Manila, Philippines, "were raised up to 845 percent" when a subsidiary of the World Bank became a partial owner.
rationale: While Manila’s water concession process did involve investors from the World Bank Group (notably the IFC) and water tariffs rose substantially over the concession period, the claim that rates were "raised up to 845 percent" at the moment a World Bank subsidiary became a partial owner is misleading. Tariff changes were phased, regulated by MWSS, and the 845% figure appears to be an exaggerated or out-of-context cumulative or category-specific number used by critics rather than an immediate, contract-triggered hike tied to a single investment event.

claim: "I've got five years of experience as a national security staffer in the U.S. Congress."
rationale: There is no independent evidence provided here to confirm the speaker’s claimed five years as a national security staffer in the U.S. Congress. Employment in congressional staff roles is verifiable through official staff directories, payroll/HR records, press releases, or reputable third-party profiles; absent such documentation the claim cannot be substantiated and is treated as false under uncertainty.

claim: Medicare insurance premiums will be rising to "$120.20 per month in 2013 and $247.00 per month in 2014."
rationale: This claim is false. The standard Medicare Part B premium was about $104.90 per month for 2013 and remained approximately $104.90 for most beneficiaries in 2014; the cited figures $120.20 and $247.00 do not match CMS-published standard premium amounts (though higher-income enrollees can pay additional income-related surcharges).

claim: "I'm also the only lieutenant governor to not take a security detail."
rationale: The claim asserts a unique status but provides no name, jurisdiction, or timeframe; uniqueness claims require comprehensive evidence across all lieutenant governors. Security details for lieutenant governors vary widely by state and era, so without specific supporting records this statement is unsubstantiated.

claim: There are fewer wars, there are fewer people dying in wars "now than there have been in quite some time."
rationale: Long-term data show global battle deaths and large-scale interstate wars peaked during the first half of the 20th century (World Wars) and have been lower on average in the post‑1945 era; datasets and scholarly reviews report a general decline in war deaths and fewer major interstate wars. That said there are still many ongoing conflicts and recent spikes (e.g., Syria, Afghanistan, Russia–Ukraine) that raise fatalities in particular years, but overall levels are lower than the high points of the 20th century.

claim: "We have 41,000 people right now on the waitlist for financial-based assistance for our tech colleges and universities," most of them for tech schools.
rationale: The claim gives a precise number but provides no jurisdiction, time frame, or source, and there are no widely reported, verifiable datasets that corroborate a current 41,000-person waitlist specifically for financial aid at 'tech colleges and universities.' Because the statement is unverifiable as presented and lacks the necessary context, it cannot be accepted as fact.

claim: The wife of the Ferguson, Mo., police chief said African-Americans in Ferguson "are feral and violent."
rationale: Contemporaneous fact-checks and reporting found no reliable evidence that the Ferguson police chief’s wife made that statement; the inflammatory Facebook posts circulating after the 2014 events were misattributed or came from different individuals/accounts. Major fact-check organizations concluded the specific quote was wrongly linked to the chief’s spouse.

claim: Between 2000 and 2006,  "health insurance company profits quadrupled."
rationale: The claim is an overgeneralization. While some U.S. health insurers saw large profit increases in the early 2000s, whether profits 'quadrupled' depends on which companies, which profit metric (net income, pre-tax income, per-share earnings), and whether figures are inflation-adjusted; no clear, widely accepted source shows industry-wide profits exactly quadrupled from 2000 to 2006.

claim: The Wisconsin Economic Development Corp. "cannot account for creating one single job."
rationale: This absolute claim is inaccurate: while audits and news reports have documented serious record-keeping and verification problems at the Wisconsin Economic Development Corporation (WEDC), WEDC has reported creating and retaining thousands of jobs and some projects do have supporting documentation. State auditors found WEDC could not always substantiate many specific job claims, but that is not the same as being unable to account for a single job.

claim: Because of omicron, "the Biden administration has decided to leave the U.S. southern border completely open."
rationale: The Biden administration did not announce a decision to leave the U.S. southern border "completely open" because of Omicron. Throughout the pandemic the administration used public-health measures (like Title 42 expulsions) and routine immigration enforcement and has made policy adjustments rather than abandoning border control entirely.

claim: "We’re losing almost 6,000 state jobs."
rationale: The claim lacks essential context (which state and what time period) and therefore cannot be verified as stated. State job counts and reported losses vary by state and over time; confirming a figure of "almost 6,000" would require a specific source such as a state's payroll records, labor department statistics, or official layoff announcements. Without that specificity the assertion is unsubstantiated.

claim: "If you look at the jobs lost in the private sector as opposed to the job gains in the public sector, it's out of whack. The government's growing and the private economy's shrinking."
rationale: The claim is a sweeping, context-free assertion that government employment is growing while the private economy is shrinking; without a specified timeframe or country it cannot be verified. In the U.S. and many other economies the private sector comprises the vast majority of jobs and, over most multi-year periods, produces larger absolute job gains and losses than government, while government employment typically changes more slowly. Therefore the blanket statement is misleading and not supported as a general fact.

claim: U.S. Rep. Connie Mack "voted to raise his own pay several times."
rationale: There is no clear, well-documented record showing that Rep. Connie Mack repeatedly voted to raise his own pay several times. Congressional pay changes are uncommon and often occur via automatic COLA adjustments or as parts of broader legislation, and claims of multiple direct pay-raise votes require specific roll-call evidence that is not present here.

claim: Says Ron Johnson said Americans should go back to work, because "death is an unavoidable part of life."
rationale: In April 2020 Senator Ron Johnson publicly urged reopening and was widely quoted saying that "death is an unavoidable part of life" while arguing Americans should get back to work amid the COVID-19 shutdowns. Multiple contemporary news reports and transcripts captured him using that phrasing as part of his case for resuming economic activity. Wording in coverage varies slightly, but the substance of the claim matches recorded remarks.

claim: "Both Cruz and Rubio are missing the vast majority of their votes."
rationale: The statement is vague and misleading: it gives no timeframe or context, and it is not true as a general claim. Public roll-call and attendance records show both Ted Cruz and Marco Rubio have missed some votes at times, but neither has missed the vast majority of votes during their Senate careers.

claim: "Boy passes Joe Biden a vial of fresh blood to drink on his way back to the White House"
rationale: There is no credible evidence, reputable reporting, or official footage showing President Biden being handed and drinking a vial of fresh blood. The allegation matches patterns of manipulated or fabricated political content and viral hoaxes rather than documented fact.

claim: "It’s been proven over and over again Medicaid has the worst outcomes in the industrialized world as far as the quality of health care."
rationale: The assertion is overly broad and unsupported: there is no consistent, peer-reviewed evidence showing that Medicaid produces the worst health outcomes across the industrialized world. While some studies find Medicaid enrollees have worse outcomes than privately insured patients for certain measures, results vary by metric, state, and population, and international comparisons typically evaluate whole national systems not a single insurance program.

claim: Says former President Barack Obama’s Supreme Court nominations "required 60 votes."
rationale: Supreme Court nominees are confirmed by a simple majority in the Senate under the Constitution. Historically the Senate's filibuster/cloture practice meant 60 votes were often needed to end debate on nominations, but that was a Senate rule/practice, not a constitutional requirement; Obama nominees Sotomayor and Kagan did receive cloture votes above 60, while Merrick Garland received no floor vote.

claim: "Some people are going to die from the vaccine directly. But a large number of people are going to start getting horribly sick and get all kinds of autoimmune diseases."
rationale: The claim predicts many direct vaccine deaths and a large wave of autoimmune illnesses; while vaccines can very rarely cause serious adverse events (including occasional deaths in causal or temporal association), large-scale death or widespread new autoimmune disease caused by vaccination is not supported by evidence. Extensive safety monitoring and epidemiological studies have found only rare, specific adverse events (e.g., anaphylaxis, very rare clotting syndromes, or myocarditis in some groups) and no signal of mass autoimmune disease outbreaks attributable to vaccines. Overall, benefits of approved vaccines greatly outweigh the small, well-characterized risks.

claim: "If we ban the practice of earmarks, we could save the American taxpayer anywhere between $15 (billion) to $20 billion dollars a year in pork-barrel spending."
rationale: This claim is misleading. Earmark totals have varied by year and often were below $20 billion, and even if earmarks were banned not all of that money would necessarily be 'saved' because projects can be funded through other programs or reclassified. Historical experience after the 2011 earmark moratorium shows overall federal spending did not fall by a clear $15–20 billion tied solely to eliminating earmarks.

claim: "The reality is when you look at the Biden plan, it reads an awful lot like what President Trump and I and our task force have been doing every step of the way."
rationale: This is a subjective, overbroad claim that is not supported by the record: while there are some overlapping areas (e.g., emphasis on vaccines and economic relief), Biden’s published plans and policies differ in emphasis, scope, and federal coordination from actions taken by President Trump and his task force. Saying Biden’s plan “reads an awful lot like” what Trump and the task force did “every step of the way” is an exaggeration rather than a verifiable factual statement.

claim: "The president early on called on NATO member countries to step up their contributions ... and as a result of that countries have stepped up contributions toward their own defense."
rationale: U.S. presidents in recent administrations publicly pressured NATO members early in their terms to increase defense spending, and NATO-wide defense spending and the number of countries meeting the 2% of GDP guideline have risen since those calls. While multiple factors contributed, the timing and public diplomatic pressure are widely credited with prompting many allies to boost their budgets.

claim: Bill Gunter would "drain millions from local public schools, and give our tax dollars to private, for-profit schools run by out-of-state corporations."
rationale: The claim asserts a specific policy outcome (draining millions from public schools to private, for‑profit, out‑of‑state operators) that would be documented in bills, budgets, voting records, or explicit campaign proposals. I found no verifiable, specific public record attributing such a plan to Bill Gunter, so the allegation is unsubstantiated as presented.

claim: "Illegal immigrants currently occupy 8 million jobs."
rationale: Reliable estimates from sources that measure unauthorized/undocumented workers put the number of employed unauthorized immigrants in the United States closer to the mid-single millions (often estimated around 4–6 million in recent years), not 8 million. Figures vary by year and methodology, but 8 million is higher than most reputable estimates and appears to overstate the count of jobs held by undocumented workers.

claim: "There's no court session between now and the end of this election."
rationale: The claim asserts an absolute absence of any court sessions until the end of an unspecified election, which is implausible and cannot be verified. Courts at various levels sit year-round and election-related litigation frequently occurs before, during, and after elections; without a specific jurisdiction and timeframe the statement is unprovable and very likely false.

claim: "Records suggest more than 100 batches of absentee ballots in Fulton County could be missing."
rationale: Investigations and official explanations found that apparent gaps in Fulton County’s batch numbering do not indicate missing absentee ballots. County election officials and independent fact-checkers reported that numbering gaps resulted from administrative practices (consolidation, renumbering, or unused batch slots) and that audits and chain-of-custody records account for all ballots.

claim: "Of all the 62 counties in New York state, all of them, unemployment is going up except for the five counties of New York City."
rationale: The claim is an absolute, time‑dependent statement but offers no timeframe or data source. Unemployment rates vary by county and over time, and it is extremely unlikely (and not supported by typical labor statistics) that all 57 non‑NYC counties simultaneously experienced rising unemployment while the five NYC counties did not. Without a specific date range, the blanket assertion is misleading and almost certainly false.

claim: Says Sen. Sherrod Brown voted to keep "an extreme, job-killing Internal Revenue Service paperwork mandate."
rationale: The claim is imprecise and misleading: the phrase refers to a contested proposed 1099-K reporting change (the $600 threshold) that drew partisan attacks, but that proposal originated in House reconciliation text and was later altered and never enacted in that form in final law. There is no clear, single Senate vote where Sen. Sherrod Brown 'voted to keep' an 'extreme, job‑killing' IRS paperwork mandate as described, so the blanket statement is false without more specific context.

claim: "We have 76% of Americans living paycheck to paycheck, meaning they are one paycheck away from poverty."
rationale: The specific 76% figure is not a consistently supported, authoritative statistic — different reputable surveys report a wide range (commonly around 50–70%), and survey methods/timeframes vary. Moreover, being 'paycheck to paycheck' typically means limited savings or cash-flow fragility, but does not uniformly equate to being literally one missed paycheck from falling into poverty for all respondents.

claim: "Estimates say individuals who escaped these high tax states have taken with them around $2 trillion in adjusted gross income."
rationale: The statement is unverified as written: while some analyses of IRS migration and state tax data show substantial adjusted gross income shifting between states, there is no widely accepted, specific estimate that 'individuals who escaped these high tax states' have taken precisely about $2 trillion in AGI. Such figures vary greatly by time period, which states are included, and the methodology used, so the blanket $2 trillion claim is not reliably supported without more context.

claim: Says Republican U.S. Senate candidate Ted Cruz "opposes the DREAM Act, which is supported by 85% of Latinos."
rationale: Ted Cruz has publicly opposed the DREAM Act and similar legislative paths to legal status for undocumented immigrants brought to the U.S. as children. Multiple national polls of Hispanic/Latino adults (e.g., Pew and other surveys) have found roughly mid‑80% support for DREAM‑Act‑style relief, so the 85% figure is consistent with many surveys though it varies by poll.

claim: "We have an 80 percent graduation rate in high school after spending more per student than any country in the world other than Liechtenstein, I think, or Luxembourg and a couple other small countries."
rationale: The U.S. four‑year high school graduation rate in recent pre‑pandemic years was around the mid‑80s percent, not precisely 80%, and pandemic-era figures varied. While the U.S. is among the highest spenders per student internationally, exact rankings depend on year, age group, and how spending is measured, and several countries (including Luxembourg, some small jurisdictions, and others like Switzerland or Norway in some datasets) can exceed or match U.S. spending—so the speaker’s specific phrasing is imprecise and misleading.

claim: The media has "a lower approval rate than Congress."
rationale: The statement is too general and not universally true: public-opinion polls show both the news media and Congress often have low approval ratings, but which one is lower varies by poll, time, and country. Therefore it’s incorrect to assert as a blanket fact that the media has a lower approval rate than Congress.

claim: Says that during his eight years as Florida governor, "we created 1.3 million net new jobs -- more jobs created than Texas."
rationale: While Florida did add roughly on the order of 1.2–1.3 million jobs over an eight‑year span under that governor, statewide BLS employment data and contemporary fact‑checks show Texas added more net jobs over the same period. Multiple analyses comparing nonfarm payroll gains during the governor’s eight years found Texas outpaced Florida.

claim: "Biden impeachment in progress."
rationale: The claim is ambiguous and I lack up-to-date information past June 2024. As of my last update, Republicans had announced or pursued an impeachment inquiry into President Biden in 2023, but there was no widely reported completed impeachment and Senate trial in progress. Without current confirmation that formal impeachment proceedings or a Senate trial are actively underway, the statement cannot be verified as true.

claim: Says that "along the southern border of the U.S.," the government apprehends "seven individuals a day who are either known or suspected terrorists."
rationale: There is no reliable evidence that U.S. authorities apprehend an average of seven known or suspected terrorists per day along the southern border. Public data and reporting from DHS/CBP and independent fact-checkers show far smaller totals and very different timeframes, and officials have not documented a sustained daily rate of seven. The claim conflates different categories (e.g., watchlist encounters, referrals, investigations) and is therefore misleading.

claim: This video shows "Russian war in Ukraine."
rationale: No video or supporting contextual evidence was provided, so the claim cannot be verified. Without footage, metadata, geolocation, timestamps, or independent corroboration, it is not possible to confirm that the content depicts the Russian war in Ukraine.

claim: "The forest fires were so grotesque last year that we had the worst air in the world in Washington."
