The nuclear-codes wording has been used by other politicians and commentators and appears to be an unverified or misattributed claim when tied to Rubio.

claim: Says a CNN headline said, "In And Out is the fast food of white supremacists."
rationale: There is no credible record of CNN publishing a headline that reads "In And Out is the fast food of white supremacists." Claims like this have circulated as manipulated screenshots or misattributions on social media, but mainstream archives and fact-checkers do not show such a CNN headline. It is more consistent with a doctored image or satirical content than an actual CNN publication.

claim: "The number of SWAT raids have gone up by 1,400 percent since the 1980s."
rationale: SWAT deployments and paramilitary policing have increased substantially since the 1980s, but the precise figure '1,400 percent' is not a consistently verified, universally reported number. Estimates vary widely (from several hundred percent to roughly 1,500% in some accounts) depending on the data source, the end year chosen, and whether one counts raids, deployments, or number of teams, so the claim as stated is misleading without context.

claim: Says a leader of the Blackfeet Nation tribe designed the current Washington Redskins logo and once said it "made us all proud to have an Indian on a big-time team."
rationale: There is no reliable evidence that a leader of the Blackfeet Nation designed the current Washington Redskins logo, nor any verifiable record of the quoted praise. Historical accounts and contemporary reporting attribute the team's logo changes to team-commissioned designers and artists, and fact-checkers have not found a sourced attribution or statement matching that quote. The claim appears to be a repeated unverified story rather than a documented fact.

claim: "There's been no conclusive or specific report to say" Russia was trying to muddy the election.
rationale: Multiple U.S. government assessments and investigations concluded that Russian actors carried out coordinated influence and disinformation operations aimed at interfering in and sowing discord during the 2016 U.S. election. The 2017 U.S. intelligence community assessment, the Special Counsel (Mueller) report, bipartisan Senate Intelligence Committee reports, and several criminal indictments document specific actions and intent.

claim: Says "taxes were raised 115 times in the eight years before I became governor" and those increases were part of a "path that led to wealth and jobs and people leaving our state."
rationale: The claim cannot be verified as stated because it lacks crucial context (which state, exact eight-year period, and what counts as a "tax increase"). Counts like "115 times" can vary widely depending on whether one includes fee changes, local levies, or repeated legislative votes, and the asserted causal link from those increases to statewide wealth loss, job declines, and outmigration is not established by the statement alone. Without precise sourcing and evidence tying the enumerated tax actions to the economic outcomes, the claim is not reliably supported.

claim: "We could build 30 walls with the $150 billion Obama gave to Iran."
rationale: The claim mischaracterizes the 2015 Iran nuclear agreement. The U.S. did not hand Iran a $150 billion cash payment; sanctions relief allowed Iran access to certain frozen assets and future oil revenue over time, and figures quoted ($50–150B) are estimates and include assets held abroad, not a single transfer from the U.S. government. The "30 walls" comparison also relies on an assumed wall cost and is rhetorical rather than a factual accounting.

claim: Says President Barack Obama's parents were communists.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Barack Obama’s parents were communists. Biographies and Obama’s own memoirs describe his father as a Kenyan economist who worked for the Kenyan government and international institutions and his mother as an American anthropologist and development worker; neither is documented as a member of any communist party.

claim: Estimated annual COVID-19 deaths in the U.S. totals 27,530, after you subtract those who died "with, not from" COVID-19, not in nursing homes and who didn't have four or more comorbidities.
rationale: The 27,530 figure is not supported by official mortality data or standard cause-of-death practices; U.S. annual COVID-19 deaths (even in recent lower years) have generally been much higher than that. The claim depends on arbitrarily excluding deaths classified as 'with, not from' COVID-19, all nursing-home deaths, and anyone with fewer than four comorbidities—criteria that are not consistent with how medical certifiers determine the underlying cause of death and would substantially undercount deaths where COVID-19 was a contributing or underlying cause. Therefore the specific trimmed estimate is misleading and unsupported.

claim: "Three years ago, a newly elected President Obama told America that if Congress approved his plan to borrow nearly a trillion dollars, he would hold unemployment below 8 percent."
rationale: There is no record that newly elected President Obama made a categorical promise to keep unemployment below 8% if Congress approved a nearly trillion-dollar plan. The 2009 stimulus (ARRA) was about $787 billion (often cited as roughly $800B), and Obama framed it as saving/creating jobs and reducing unemployment versus a worse baseline rather than guaranteeing a sub-8% rate. Unemployment nonetheless rose to about 10% in late 2009.

claim: "By the word religion in the First Amendment, the founders meant Christianity."
rationale: The First Amendment's Religion Clauses were drafted to prohibit Congress from establishing a national religion and to protect free exercise generally, not to define 'religion' as only Christianity. Founding-era writings (Jefferson, Madison), early federal actions, and later Supreme Court interpretation treat the clause as religiously neutral rather than limited to Christianity.

claim: Says he can be on the ballot for Congress while serving time in jail.
rationale: The U.S. Constitution sets only age, citizenship, and inhabitancy as qualifications for the House and Senate, and does not bar incarcerated persons or most felons from appearing on the ballot. Historical precedent exists of candidates running for federal office while imprisoned. Practical obstacles (filing, signature collection) and narrow legal exceptions can complicate specific cases.

claim: Says Bill O’Reilly spoke 40 percent of the words in an interview with President Barack Obama.
rationale: There is no reliable, publicly validated transcript analysis showing Bill O’Reilly spoke exactly 40% of the words in a widely reported interview with President Obama. The claim appears to be an unsupported numeric assertion and media/transcript checks do not corroborate that precise percentage.

claim: Video shows that Sûreté du Québec officers "removed their identifying names and badge numbers from their uniforms in Ottawa."
rationale: Multiple news reports and official statements documented video footage from the 2022 Ottawa protests that showed some Sûreté du Québec officers removing or obscuring identifying nameplates and badge numbers while deployed in Ottawa. The images prompted public criticism and internal reviews by Quebec authorities and oversight bodies.

claim: Says Sen. Thad Cochran "voted to spend hundreds of millions of dollars on ... the Bridge to Nowhere in Alaska instead of shifting the money to repair a bridge damaged by Hurricane Katrina."
rationale: The claim frames a single clear vote by Sen. Thad Cochran to send 'hundreds of millions' to the Alaska 'Bridge to Nowhere' rather than to Katrina bridge repairs, but the record does not show a single direct vote that made that explicit trade. The Gravina Island earmark (roughly $223 million) was driven primarily by Alaska senators and was part of larger transportation appropriations; votes Cochran cast were on omnibus transportation/appropriations bills containing many earmarks, not a single binary choice to deny Katrina bridge repairs and fund the Alaska bridge.

claim: "[Hillary Clinton]'s not trusted -- virtually at all."
rationale: The claim is an overbroad absolute that Hillary Clinton is 'not trusted -- virtually at all.' Public-opinion data and election results show substantial portions of the electorate do trust or have supported her; trust ratings are mixed and vary greatly by party and over time, but they are far from zero.

claim: A congressional laundry closed due to the partial government shutdown.
rationale: There is no broadly reported evidence that a "congressional laundry" (a legislative branch laundry service) was shut down by a recent partial federal government shutdown. Many congressional support services are funded through member fees or separate branch appropriations and were generally not closed during past partial shutdowns, and claims about a specific laundry closure lack corroborating reporting.

claim: Says recent studies indicate that nationally, only 8 percent of white voting-age citizens but 25 percent of African-American voting-age citizens lack government-issued photo IDs.
rationale: Multiple analyses — most notably a Brennan Center survey of adult citizens — reported national estimates similar to these: roughly 8% of white adults and about 25% of African-American adults lacked a government-issued photo ID. The claim accurately reflects widely cited national estimates from those studies.

claim: Claims that Obama said, "For those who oppose our policies, you should just shut up and go away."
rationale: There is no credible record, transcript, or reliable news reporting showing Barack Obama saying, “For those who oppose our policies, you should just shut up and go away.” Fact-checking outlets and public speech archives do not support this attribution, and the line appears to be a fabricated or misattributed quote circulated online.

claim: Says actor Dwayne "The Rock" Johnson wore a T-shirt stating: "We Stand for the flag, we kneel for the fallen."
rationale: I cannot verify that Dwayne "The Rock" Johnson wore a T‑shirt bearing the exact phrase "We Stand for the flag, we kneel for the fallen." While similar slogans have been used on shirts by others, I have no reliable memory or confirmed report of Johnson specifically wearing that exact shirt or posting a photo of it.

claim: "We've got 7.2 percent unemployment (in Ohio), but when you include the folks who have stopped looking for work, it's actually over 10 percent."
rationale: The claim gives specific percentages but provides no date; unemployment rates fluctuate and whether Ohio's official U-3 rate of 7.2% and a broader measure including discouraged/marginally attached workers exceeding 10% are both true depends on the month. Broad measures (U-5/U-6) that add discouraged workers are typically higher than U-3, but they do not always exceed 10% for Ohio. Without a time reference or citation, the specific paired numbers cannot be verified as a general fact.

claim: Says Mitt Romney "just gave a speech a few weeks ago" and said "we should still have troops in Iraq."
rationale: The claim is not verifiable as stated because it gives no date or source for the alleged speech; without a timestamp it's impossible to confirm that Romney 'just gave a speech a few weeks ago' and that he said specifically 'we should still have troops in Iraq.' While Mitt Romney has at times supported a U.S. presence in the Middle East, I cannot confirm this precise recent quote and timing from available context.

claim: "Pasco County has the second highest population of homeless in all of Florida."
rationale: Available homelessness counts (HUD Point-in-Time and Continuum of Care reports) and common county rankings show Miami‑Dade, Broward, and other large counties (e.g., Palm Beach, Orange, Hillsborough) have higher homeless populations than Pasco County. Pasco is not typically listed as second highest in statewide homelessness rankings.

claim: Says "If you compare the Portland Metro area to the CDC’s statewide cavity rates ... the Portland Metro area would actually rank as having the 15th lowest cavity rate in the U.S."
rationale: The statement asserts a specific numeric ranking (15th lowest) based on comparing a Portland Metro estimate to CDC statewide cavity rates, but CDC data are reported at the state level and use different sampling frames and time periods than local metro surveys. Without a transparent, directly comparable calculation (same age groups, years, and measurement methods), the precise rank claim is unverified and likely misleading.

claim: "Kids are less likely to get it (COVID-19). You know, they’re less likely to spread. So I think there’s some pretty good data out there that will help alleviate some of the concerns."
rationale: The statement is an overbroad generalization. Early-pandemic studies showed children were often less susceptible and sometimes less likely to transmit SARS-CoV-2, but later variants (notably Delta and Omicron), changing immunity/vaccination levels, and setting-specific factors made infection and transmission among children much more similar to adults in many contexts.

claim: "If every house in Florida had a solar-heated water tank, that would eliminate consumption by 17 percent."
rationale: The claim is misleading. While water heating typically represents about 15–20% (around 17%) of residential energy use, and solar thermal systems can greatly reduce that portion, installing solar‑heated water tanks in every house would not literally 'eliminate' consumption because systems need backups, have variable performance, and not all homes are suitable. The statement also fails to define what kind of 'consumption' (total energy, electricity, or residential energy) it refers to.

claim: "Criminals don’t go through (gun) background checks. I think it’s like 3% go through a background check."
rationale: The 3% figure is inconsistent with government and research surveys. Studies (e.g., Bureau of Justice Statistics surveys of prisoners and RAND/DoJ reviews) find a substantially larger share of offenders obtained guns from retail or documented channels, with estimates of purchases from dealers or other traced sources commonly in the double digits rather than 3%.

claim: "After 30 years of inaction, we raised fuel standards so that by the middle of the next decade, cars and trucks will go twice as far on a gallon of gas."
rationale: In 2012 the administration and regulators finalized new federal fuel-economy/greenhouse rules that phase in through the mid-2020s and yield a corporate average light‑duty fleet equivalent of about 54.5 mpg by 2025, roughly double the earlier CAFE baseline. The claim’s reference to roughly 30 years of relative CAFE stagnation is also consistent with the long period after the early‑1980s when standards saw little overall tightening. The statement is a concise, slightly simplified but essentially accurate summary of that policy outcome.

claim: In the U.S. Constitution, "there’s a little section in there that talks about life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness."
rationale: The phrase "life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness" is from the Declaration of Independence (1776), not the U.S. Constitution. The Constitution (including its amendments) uses different language about rights—for example, the Fifth and Fourteenth Amendments refer to "life, liberty, or property."

claim: Says that Tim Pawlenty eliminated health insurance for 33,000 to 35,000 people when he was governor of Minnesota.
rationale: This claim overstates and simplifies a complex history. Pawlenty's administration enacted budget cuts and program changes (notably affecting MinnesotaCare and other state-subsidized programs) that led to tens of thousands losing state-subsidized coverage at various times, but it is not accurate to characterize this as a single, direct action that explicitly "eliminated health insurance for 33,000–35,000 people." Estimates and causes vary by program, year, and how loss of coverage is counted.

claim: "Bicycle ownership drops by half while obesity in Rhode Island rises by 154 percent"
rationale: The claim gives precise large changes without a timeframe or source; state and federal health data (BRFSS/CDC) do not show Rhode Island adult obesity rising 154% and transportation surveys do not report a statewide halving of bicycle ownership. Observed obesity increases in U.S. states over recent decades are much smaller, and bicycle ownership/usage changes are typically modest, so the paired assertion is unsupported and implausible as stated.

claim: "Millions have died from COVID injections."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that COVID-19 vaccines have caused millions of deaths. Large-scale safety monitoring by public health agencies and multiple peer-reviewed studies find deaths causally linked to the vaccines are extremely rare, while passive reporting systems that some cite include unverified, temporally associated events. Millions of deaths during the pandemic were caused by COVID-19 illness, not the vaccines.

claim: In 2011, "the average annual compensation for a teacher in the Milwaukee Public Schools system will exceed $100,000."
rationale: Available public-data and historical salary figures show that in 2011 the average teacher salary and total compensation in Milwaukee Public Schools were far below $100,000. Typical teacher salaries in Wisconsin and nationally in that period were roughly in the $40k–$60k range, and even after adding employer-paid benefits would not push the district average above $100k.

claim: The Senate Republican education plan is an unfunded mandate for local school districts.
rationale: The statement is a political characterization that cannot be verified as a factual blanket truth without identifying which Senate Republican education plan is meant and examining its statutory text and funding provisions. Whether a plan constitutes an 'unfunded mandate' depends on whether it requires local districts to carry out new duties without providing sufficient federal funding or offsets. Many Republican proposals vary — some include grants or block grants while others shift responsibilities — so the claim is too general to be established as fact.

claim: If public employees don’t pay more for benefits starting April 1, 2011, "the equivalent" is 1,500 state employee layoffs by June 30, 2011 and 10,000 to 12,000 state and local government employee layoffs in the next two years.
rationale: This claim is a specific conditional projection presented as a certainty but cannot be independently verified. Layoffs at those precise counts would depend on budget choices, bargaining outcomes, legislative actions, and other fiscal measures, so presenting fixed numbers as inevitable is misleading. Without a named jurisdiction and authoritative source showing those calculations, the claim should not be treated as established fact.

claim: "Hurricane Irma could be a Category 6 by the time it hits East Coast."
rationale: There is no official "Category 6" on the Saffir–Simpson Hurricane Wind Scale; the scale only runs from Category 1 to Category 5. A storm cannot be classified as Category 6 by official agencies, although a storm with extremely high winds would simply be designated Category 5 and described by its wind speed and expected impacts.

claim: Bull sharks were released in an Arkansas river.
rationale: There are no credible, verifiable reports that bull sharks were deliberately released into an Arkansas river. While bull sharks can tolerate freshwater and occasionally move upriver, such an intentional release would have been documented by local authorities and news outlets, and no authoritative evidence supports this claim.

claim: Says Harvard scientists say the coronavirus is "spreading so fast that it will infect 70% of humanity this year."
rationale: This exact statement is misleading and not supported by credible Harvard sources. Early pandemic modelling by various groups suggested that without control measures a large share (often cited as 40–70%) of the global population could eventually be infected, but reputable scientists did not assert that Harvard scientists had declared COVID-19 would infect 70% of humanity 'this year'—the timeframe and attribution are incorrect or exaggerated.

claim: Says Melania Trump hired exorcist to "cleanse White House of Obama demons."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Melania Trump formally hired an exorcist to 'cleanse the White House of Obama demons.' The claim appears to originate from sensational tabloid and social-media posts and is not supported by reliable mainstream reporting or documented statements. While members of the first family have on occasion invited clergy for blessings, that is not the same as documented exorcism targeted at a predecessor.

claim: Miami-Dade County is the "No. 1 donor county in the state."
rationale: The claim is unqualified and cannot be verified as universally true. While Miami‑Dade County (presumably in Florida) is the state’s largest county and often a major source of political contributions, rankings depend on the election cycle and the metric (total dollars, per‑capita, party, or candidate), so it is not inherently always the 'No. 1 donor county.'

claim: "The (health care) law does not demand that all of these cancellations go out."
rationale: The statement is too vague to verify because it does not identify which health-care law or which “cancellations” are being referenced. Legal obligations vary widely by statute, regulation, jurisdiction, and time period—some laws require notice or action on cancellations, others do not. Without a specific law and factual context, the claim cannot be reliably established as true.

claim: "Japan says goodbye Moderna, hello ivermectin."
rationale: There is no official Japanese government policy abandoning Moderna nationwide or replacing COVID-19 vaccination with ivermectin. Japan continues to use mRNA vaccines (including Moderna and Pfizer) for COVID-19 vaccination, and ivermectin has not been endorsed by Japanese health authorities as a substitute treatment except within clinical trials.

claim: "Unions don’t have to comply with Obamacare."
rationale: There is no blanket exemption for labor unions from the Affordable Care Act. Employers (including unions that are employers) with 50+ full-time equivalent employees are subject to the employer mandate, and union-sponsored group health plans must follow ACA market reforms (e.g., coverage rules, no preexisting condition exclusions).

claim: Says for otherwise healthy people "experiencing mild to moderate respiratory symptoms with or without a COVID-19 diagnosis … only high temperatures kill a virus, so let your fever run high," but not over 103 or 104 degrees.
rationale: The claim is inaccurate: while fever is part of the immune response, body temperatures that are safe for humans do not reliably ‘kill’ viruses in vivo, and most respiratory viruses can tolerate febrile-range temperatures. There is no clinical evidence that deliberately letting a fever climb to 103–104°F improves outcomes, and intentionally allowing high fevers is risky because fevers at that level can cause dehydration, organ stress, and seizures.

claim: Says unsuccessful Texas abortion legislation "was supported by a majority of" Texans.
rationale: There is no clear, consistent evidence that a single unsuccessful Texas abortion bill was supported by a majority of Texans; public-opinion results vary by poll, question wording, timing, and which provisions are described. Many polls show mixed or conditional support for some restrictions but not for specific legislative packages, so the blanket claim that a majority supported the unsuccessful legislation is not reliably supported.

claim: "Debt has almost doubled in Austin under Gov. Perry."
rationale: The claim is too vague to verify and is therefore unsubstantiated. It fails to specify a timeframe or which debt measure (total debt, bonded debt, per-capita debt, general-obligation debt) is meant; municipal debt levels are set by local officials and bond issuances, not directly by a state governor. Without those specifics and a review of Austin’s audited financial statements across Rick Perry’s tenure, the assertion that debt "almost doubled" cannot be supported.

claim: In the wake of the Republican-backed tax bill, "more than 100,000 American workers have already been laid off in 2018."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that the Republican-backed tax bill directly caused more than 100,000 layoffs in 2018. Public tallies that circulated conflated various announced workforce changes, voluntary buyouts, and unrelated layoffs and many companies did not attribute cuts to the tax law; independent fact-checkers found the large-number causal claim unsupported.

claim: "I've always known this is a real, this is a pandemic. I've felt it was a pandemic long before it was called a pandemic."
rationale: This is a first-person claim about the speaker’s private belief prior to an official designation; internal states like 'I always knew' cannot be independently verified without contemporaneous evidence. Absent dated public statements or records showing the speaker explicitly made that assessment before the pandemic was declared, the claim is unprovable and thus cannot be confirmed as true.

claim: Says there have been no cases of wolves killing people in Rocky Mountain states.
rationale: The claim is unlikely to be strictly true: while wolf attacks on people in the Rocky Mountain states are extremely rare in modern times, historical records and wildlife reports indicate at least some incidents and ambiguous cases have occurred. Absence of frequent attacks does not mean there have been none ever, and records vary by state and era.

claim: "Washington State Legislature votes to change its name because George Washington owned Slaves."
rationale: The Washington State Legislature has not voted to change the state's name. While activists and some lawmakers have proposed or discussed renaming the state because George Washington owned enslaved people, no formal legislative action to rename Washington State has passed; renaming a state would also require additional constitutional/ballot steps.

claim: The typical elementary school teacher pays $7,239 in federal income taxes, and firefighters pay $5,328, while Donald Trump paid $750.
rationale: The statement mixes a narrowly reported figure about Donald Trump (reportedly $750 in federal income tax for 2016) with unverified, context‑dependent ‘‘typical’’ tax amounts for teachers and firefighters. Federal tax paid by teachers or firefighters varies by year, location, pay scale and whether averages or medians are used, so the rounded figures quoted are not universally verifiable and the comparison is misleading.

claim: Says Hillary Clinton "shows up in Broward County" and had a private meeting with elections supervisor Brenda Snipes.
rationale: There is no credible evidence, contemporaneous reporting, or entries in Hillary Clinton’s public schedules showing she traveled to Broward County for a private meeting with elections supervisor Brenda Snipes. The allegation appears to originate from unverified social-media rumors and has not been substantiated by reputable news outlets or official records.

claim: "Too many dead people voted" in Michigan
rationale: Multiple official reviews, audits, and statements by Michigan election officials found no evidence of widespread voting by deceased people; investigations identified only a very small number of isolated cases (often explained by ballots cast before a voter's death, clerical errors, or family members submitting ballots) compared with millions of votes. There is no support for the claim that 'too many' dead people voted in Michigan as a systemic or large-scale problem.

claim: "A Cornell University research study concludes that ethanol generates a 29 percent energy loss, meaning it takes more than a gallon of gasoline to produce a gallon of ethanol."
rationale: A Cornell analysis by David Pimentel reported an energy output/input ratio of about 0.71, which the authors described as a ~29% energy loss (i.e., more fossil energy consumed in production than the energy contained in the ethanol). The claim accurately summarizes that Cornell study’s conclusion, though the wording about 'gallons of gasoline' conflates volume and energy units and simplifies a contested debate.

claim: "Violent crime is up since the last year of Sharpe James’ administration. This year it’s higher. … The unemployment rate is almost 15 percent. The high school dropout rate is over 50 percent."
rationale: The statement bundles several specific statistical claims but gives no place or exact year, making them unverifiable as stated. Sharpe James was Newark’s mayor through 2006; violent-crime, unemployment and dropout trends since then have varied and require precise yearly/local data, but widely available city and state sources do not support blanket figures like ~15% unemployment and >50% high-school dropouts for recent years—those numbers are implausibly high and appear exaggerated.

claim: "Most young Americans right now, they’re not covered" by health insurance.
rationale: Available data show that a majority of young Americans have health coverage; uninsured rates for typical 'young' age groups (late teens through 30s) have generally been well below 50% in recent years. Many young people are covered through employers, parental plans up to age 26, Medicaid, or the ACA marketplaces, so the claim that most are uninsured is incorrect.

claim: Quotes Kamala Harris as saying: "After we impeach, we round up the Trump supporters."
rationale: There is no credible video, transcript, or contemporaneous reporting showing Vice President Kamala Harris saying this; major fact-checking organizations have determined the quote is fabricated or misattributed. The line appears in manipulated images and social posts rather than any verifiable speech or interview.

claim: Imitation dairy products often differ nutritionally from those they mimic, and labeling them "milk" or "cheese" or "yogurt" is "against the law."
rationale: It is true that many imitation dairy products differ nutritionally from the animal-derived products they mimic (differences in protein, fat, micronutrients and fortification are common). However, the claim that labeling them "milk", "cheese" or "yogurt" is universally "against the law" is false: rules vary by jurisdiction, and many jurisdictions permit qualified labeling (e.g., "soy milk", "almond milk") or have specific legal exceptions while others restrict or reserve certain dairy terms.

claim: "Thirty-four of the last 44 (debt ceiling increases) have been for less than a year. So, this notion that short-term is somehow the exception, it's actually the rule."
rationale: The specific numeric claim is not reliably supported: counts of “the last 44” debt-ceiling actions depend on how one defines an “increase” (statutory raise vs. temporary measure or suspension) and the starting point, and independent fact-checks have found the speaker’s math to be misleading. While many recent debt-ceiling actions have been short-term, the asserted figure (34 of 44 under one year) cannot be confirmed as accurate without a precise, consistent definition and dataset.

claim: "Nationwide tuition at public universities is up almost 300 percent ... in the last 20 years."
rationale: U.S. national data (e.g., College Board trends) show published tuition and fees at public four‑year in‑state institutions rose substantially over the past two decades but well below a 300% increase — more typically on the order of roughly 100–200% nominal depending on the exact period and measure, and much smaller when adjusted for inflation. Even when including room and board or out‑of‑state rates, aggregate increases nationwide do not approach a near‑300% rise.

claim: "Kasich’s budget raised taxes by billions, hitting businesses hard and the middle class even harder."
rationale: The claim overstates and simplifies a mixed record. As Ohio governor John Kasich signed budgets that included some revenue-raising measures (broadening the sales tax base and fee increases) but also significant tax cuts (including income-tax rate reductions and business tax changes), independent analyses characterize the net package as a mix of cuts and new revenues rather than a straightforward multibillion-dollar tax increase that hit businesses and the middle class hardest.

claim: Says police unions have it "written into a contract that (officers) are not going to be accountable" for misconduct.
rationale: The claim as stated is an absolute assertion that police unions have contractual language guaranteeing officers will not be held accountable for misconduct. While many collective bargaining agreements include procedural protections (due process, arbitration, timelines, limits on disciplinary records disclosure) that can make accountability harder, they do not universally contain a provision that literally immunizes officers from discipline. Whether particular contracts meaningfully impede accountability varies by jurisdiction and specific contract language.

claim: "Death penalty opponents like Roy Cooper and Josh Stein have imposed a de-facto moratorium on capital punishment."
rationale: While both Roy Cooper and Josh Stein have expressed concerns about the death penalty and supported limiting its use, they did not unilaterally ‘impose’ a statewide moratorium. The lack of executions in some states (including North Carolina) has resulted largely from court rulings, legal challenges to procedures (like lethal-injection protocols), and prosecutorial discretion rather than a formal, sole action by those officials. Governors can grant clemency or announce moratoria, and attorneys general can influence charging decisions, but neither can by themselves permanently ban capital punishment without broader legal or legislative changes.

claim: "Hollywood celebs: We will go on ‘total strike’ if Trump does not resign."
rationale: There is no evidence that Hollywood celebrities collectively pledged a coordinated "total strike" demanding Trump’s resignation. While individual entertainers have publicly criticized Trump or announced boycotts of events, major industry groups and unions did not organize or announce a unified total-strike pledge tied to his resignation. The claim appears to conflate individual statements or social-media posts into a nonexistent coordinated industry-wide action.

claim: Says a military Humvee labeled "COVID-19 quarantine team" was on Interstate 696 in Michigan.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that an officially marked military Humvee reading "COVID-19 quarantine team" was operating on Interstate 696 in Michigan. Such images circulated online were not corroborated by officials or reputable local news/fact-check outlets and are consistent with misattribution or image alteration. U.S. military and National Guard units do not typically label vehicles in that manner for public road operations.

claim: NASCAR eliminated the national anthem at races.
rationale: The claim asserts a blanket elimination of the national anthem at NASCAR races, which is not true: the national anthem remains a customary part of pre-race ceremonies at major NASCAR events and there has been no widely reported official policy removing it across all races. While occasionally anthems may be shortened, omitted at smaller or non-televised events, or presented differently, there is no evidence of a league-wide elimination.

claim: Congressman Scott DesJarlais "is spending his one year anniversary on vacation -- only working 6 days in all of January."
rationale: The claim is unverified and lacks essential context (which year and what counts as “working”); no public evidence is cited here that DesJarlais worked only six days in a given January or spent a one-year anniversary on vacation. Verifying such a precise attendance claim would require specific House calendars, office schedules, or voting records for the named month and year, which are not provided. Absent that evidence, the assertion is unsubstantiated and treated as false.

claim: "Fifty seats have already changed hands from the Republicans to the Democrats since Donald Trump was elected."
rationale: The claim is not supported by congressional election results since Trump’s 2016 victory. In the 2018 midterms Democrats achieved a net gain of about 41 U.S. House seats and picked up a handful of additional seats in special elections, but the total number of Republican-to-Democrat flips in Congress does not equal 50, and Democrats did not achieve comparable gains in the Senate.

claim: "I finished" the controversy about where President Barack Obama was born.
rationale: The claim attributes personally ending the long-running 'birther' controversy to the speaker, but the dispute was publicly resolved when President Obama released his long-form Hawaiian birth certificate in 2011 and Hawaiian officials verified his birth in Honolulu. Absent context showing the speaker was the official who produced or authenticated those records, there is no basis to credit a private individual with 'finishing' the controversy.

claim: "Thanks to President Trump and Republicans over the past year through July, U.S. manufacturing added 327,000 jobs, the most of any 12-month period since April 1995, when the figure added a healthy 345,000 positions."
rationale: This specific numeric claim appears inconsistent with official BLS manufacturing payroll data for the Trump years: a 12‑month gain of 327,000 manufacturing jobs through a July in that period is substantially larger than the reported manufacturing gains in most 12‑month spans then, and the cited 1995 comparator (345,000) is ambiguous. Additionally, the statement’s causal attribution (“Thanks to President Trump and Republicans”) is not supported by the employment series alone; BLS data show trends but do not establish direct political causation.

claim: A defense bill "includes language that would require military hospitals to provide abortions on demand."
rationale: Legislative language in recent U.S. defense bills has expanded or clarified circumstances under which military health facilities or TRICARE can cover or provide abortions (for example in cases of life endangerment, rape, or incest) but has not imposed a blanket requirement that military hospitals provide abortions 'on demand' irrespective of restrictions. Most proposals and enacted provisions include exceptions, limitations, or compliance with applicable law rather than an unlimited mandate.

claim: 40 percent of illegal immigrants "had a visa and then became illegal," mostly because "they changed jobs."
rationale: The broad claim is misleading. While U.S. data sources (DHS/Pew) show a substantial share of unauthorized immigrants are visa overstays in some years, the exact share varies by year and the assertion that they became illegal 'mostly because they changed jobs' is incorrect: overstays usually result from visas expiring or status violations, not primarily job changes, and employment visas typically have transfer procedures that prevent automatic loss of status.

claim: "The Public Employee Retirement System is making more millionaires than the Oregon state lottery."
rationale: The claim is unproven and ambiguous: there is no clear publicly available count comparing how many people became millionaires because of Oregon’s Public Employee Retirement System (by account balance or present value of benefits) versus how many became millionaires from Oregon Lottery prizes. Both programs can create high-net-worth outcomes depending on definitions and timeframes, but I could not find definitive data showing PERS has produced more millionaires than the lottery.

claim: "U.S. government reports record tax haul after Trump tax cuts spur economic growth."
rationale: The claim overstates and misattributes facts. While nominal federal receipts rose in some years after the 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act, overall deficits increased and independent analyses (CBO, Treasury, many economists) conclude the tax cuts reduced revenues and produced only modest growth that did not fully offset the revenue loss. The government did not report that the tax cuts definitively 'spurred' growth leading to a record tax haul; any revenue increases reflect inflation, timing, and the business cycle rather than a proven payoff of the cuts.

claim: "In the past year, Floridians, not government, created almost 135,000 new private sector jobs. We netted more than 120,000 total jobs in the first 11 months of 2011; the third most of any state in the nation."
rationale: The claim combines specific numeric totals with a partisan attribution and cannot be independently verified as stated: official federal and state employment series for 2011 do not unambiguously support the exact phrasing that 'Floridians, not government, created almost 135,000 new private sector jobs' and the ranking depends on the precise time window and data source. Such figures were often reported by Florida officials using a particular state payroll series and a selected 12‑month window, but federal BLS series and broader measures show different totals and rankings, so the statement as presented is misleading.

claim: "Seattle police begin gun confiscations: no laws broken, no warrant, no charges."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Seattle police have initiated a broad program of warrantless, charge-free gun confiscations. U.S. and Washington law generally require a warrant, probable cause, an Extreme Risk Protection Order, or exigent circumstances for law enforcement to seize firearms, and public reporting has described targeted legal processes rather than indiscriminate takings.

claim: "Under Terry McAuliffe (there was a) record investment in education."
rationale: The claim is too vague to be verified as stated. While Terry McAuliffe’s administrations did increase education spending in Virginia, whether those outlays constitute a 'record investment' depends on the metric (nominal dollars vs. inflation-adjusted, total vs. per-pupil, K–12 vs. higher education) and the specific time frame; when adjusted or compared on a per-pupil or inflation-adjusted basis previous budgets can be comparable or larger. Therefore the blanket assertion that there was a record investment is not reliably supported without qualifiers.

claim: "An amendment, pushed by Lyndon Johnson many years ago, threatens religious institutions with a loss of their tax-exempt status if they openly advocate their political views."
rationale: This refers to the 1954 'Johnson Amendment' introduced by Lyndon B. Johnson, which prohibits 501(c)(3) tax-exempt organizations (including churches) from participating in partisan political campaign activity and can jeopardize tax-exempt status for violations. The rule targets endorsements or opposition to candidates, not all expressions of political views on public policy.

claim: Bill McCollum "backed Jim Greer's effort to hide financial irregularities."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Bill McCollum actively 'backed' an effort by Jim Greer to hide financial irregularities. Reporting from the time documents that Jim Greer, former Florida GOP chair, faced allegations and later pleaded guilty to wrongdoing, but McCollum is not shown to have participated in or endorsed any cover-up; at most he had political associations with party leaders. The claim asserts a specific conspiratorial action for which reliable sourcing is lacking.

claim: "You take Pulse nightclub. If you had one person in that room that could carry a gun and knew how to use it, it wouldn’t have happened, or certainly to the extent that it did."
rationale: This is a speculative counterfactual that cannot be established as factual. There is no conclusive evidence that a single armed civilian in the Pulse nightclub would have prevented or substantially reduced the attack; outcomes of armed bystanders in active-shooter events are unpredictable and depend on many variables such as training, positioning, and the shooter's behavior.

claim: Says a WHO proposal "portrays milk and dairy products as an obstacle to a healthy start in life."
rationale: WHO guidance that has attracted criticism focuses on restricting promotion of breast‑milk substitutes and protecting breastfeeding, not on portraying all milk and dairy products broadly as an 'obstacle to a healthy start in life.' The documents aim to limit marketing practices that undermine breastfeeding for infants, rather than declaring dairy in general harmful for early life.

claim: Says presidential candidate Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand said, "Social Security must (be) expanded to illegal immigration, it’s their right."
rationale: There is no credible record or reliable news reporting showing Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand uttered that quote or called to extend Social Security directly to undocumented immigrants. Gillibrand has spoken in favor of immigration reform and pathways to citizenship, but that is not the same as a public statement advocating immediate expansion of Social Security benefits to people in the country unlawfully.

claim: "More than 80% of Republicans think we ought to at least be doing universal background checks."
rationale: Large national polls consistently show strong overall U.S. support for universal background checks, but Republican support in most reputable surveys typically falls below 80%, often in the 60–75% range. While select polls or specific question wordings can sometimes find Republican support near or above 80%, the blanket claim that more than 80% of Republicans support universal checks is not generally supported across major surveys.

claim: "Wisconsin took a break, and when they returned, Biden coincidentally came back ahead by 100k."
rationale: There is no evidence that Wisconsin paused counting and then Biden suddenly returned ahead by 100,000 votes. In the 2020 presidential election Biden’s certified margin in Wisconsin was about 20,682 votes, and while some counties briefly paused processing for procedural reasons, there was not a single 100k swing produced by a single 'break.'

claim: "Breaking: Trump fires deputy attorney general Rod Rosenstein, raising questions over Mueller’s fate."
rationale: This did not happen as stated: Rod Rosenstein was not fired by President Trump. Although media reported Trump at times considered dismissing Rosenstein (which would have raised questions about Special Counsel Mueller), Rosenstein remained in office until he announced his resignation in May 2019 rather than being fired.

claim: Says Michelle Obama said Florida shooting "is clearly our president’s fault."
rationale: There is no reliable evidence that Michelle Obama said the exact line "is clearly our president’s fault" about a Florida shooting. Major news outlets and fact-checkers have not documented her making that direct quote; it appears to be a misattribution or fabricated quote rather than a verifiable statement.

claim: "Tim Kaine doubled down in his support of devastating defense cuts, saying the ‘the deal was the right thing to do.’"
rationale: There is no well-documented, attributable instance in mainstream reporting or public transcripts where Senator Tim Kaine is recorded as 'doubling down' in support of 'devastating defense cuts' with the quoted line 'the deal was the right thing to do.' The claim appears to be editorialized and lacks a specific date, context, or verifiable source tying Kaine to that exact statement or characterization.

claim: Under Scott Walker, Wisconsin "moved from 16th to third in percentage of people with student loan debt."
rationale: There is no clear, consistent data showing Wisconsin moved specifically from 16th to 3rd in the percentage of people with student loan debt during Scott Walker’s tenure. State rankings for student-loan prevalence vary by data source, year, and whether the measure is households, all adults, or a specific age cohort; independent fact-checks found the claim cherry-picks metrics and time periods. While Wisconsin did see increases in student indebtedness, the precise 16th-to-3rd shift as stated is not supported by standard datasets.

claim: "Iowa, for good reason, for constitutional reasons, for reasons related to the Lord, should be the first caucus and primary."
rationale: This statement is a prescriptive opinion, not a factual assertion. There is no constitutional requirement that Iowa must be the first caucus or primary, and timing of primaries/caucuses is set by state law and political party rules; invoking religious justification (‘for reasons related to the Lord’) does not create a constitutional mandate.

claim: Says a "Pro-Stimulus economist admits it is not working … "
rationale: The statement is a vague, unattributed claim and provides no named economist, quote, date, or context to verify. Without a specific source it cannot be confirmed that a self-described pro-stimulus economist publicly 'admitted it is not working' — the claim may be a misquote, taken out of context, or fabricated.

claim: After attacking Emma Gonzalez, U.S. Rep. Steve King is "facing arrest."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Rep. Steve King was facing arrest after criticizing or attacking Emma González; his interactions with González were political/online and prompted public criticism and calls for censure, not criminal charges or announced arrests. Insulting or criticizing a public figure is generally protected speech and would not by itself lead to arrest absent a separate criminal act.

claim: Says Jim Renacci has "consistently voted" for loopholes that "encourage outsourcing of our jobs."
rationale: The statement is a broad, interpretive claim that cannot be verified as a factual pattern without citing specific bills and votes. While Jim Renacci has supported pro-business measures (for example backing the 2017 tax cut and other business-friendly policies), calling that a consistent record of voting for unnamed 'loopholes that encourage outsourcing' is an evaluative assertion rather than a documented factual summary of specific votes. Absent identified legislation demonstrating a clear, repeated intent to create outsourcing incentives, the claim is not verifiable as stated.

claim: Says Mark Kelly wants to "defund the police."
rationale: Senator Mark Kelly has publicly said he does not support "defunding the police" and has instead called for police accountability, reform, and investment in community-based services. Characterizing him as saying he wants to defund the police misrepresents his stated position.

claim: "Recently we have seen our government debt grow by $3.4 trillion during the first 29 months of the Obama administration -- the equivalent of about $4 billion per day."
rationale: Treasury-reported federal debt outstanding rose by roughly $3.3–$3.5 trillion from President Obama's start in January 2009 through about June 2011 (the first 29 months), and spreading ~ $3.4 trillion over that ~870-day span averages to about $3.9–$4.0 billion per day. The claim is a rounded but accurate characterization of aggregate debt growth for that period.

claim: "Hillary replaces Kamala Harris."
rationale: There is no evidence that Hillary Clinton (or any person named Hillary) has replaced Vice President Kamala Harris. Under the U.S. Constitution and the 25th Amendment, a vice president can only be replaced by a presidential nomination confirmed by both houses of Congress, and no such nomination or confirmation has occurred. Contemporary official records and reliable news sources do not report any replacement.

claim: Says Charlie Crist "was pro-life, pro-gun and vehemently anti-tax."
rationale: During his years as a Republican and as Florida governor (mid-2000s), Charlie Crist held positions consistent with being pro-life, supported gun rights, and promoted tax cuts and anti-tax rhetoric. These stances shifted after he left the GOP and later became an independent and then a Democrat, so the claim is accurate for his earlier political record.

claim: "A clear majority of Americans support removing the cost-sharing requirement for prescription contraceptive coverage."
rationale: Multiple national opinion polls over recent years have found that a majority of Americans favor insurance coverage of prescription contraception without cost-sharing. While exact percentages vary by poll and question wording, the consensus from major pollsters has been majority support for removing copays or other cost barriers for contraceptives.

claim: "Fox Sports cancels all NFL broadcasts ‘until players respect the flag.’ "
rationale: There are no credible reports that Fox Sports cancelled all NFL broadcasts; Fox continued to air NFL games throughout the anthem protest period. Fox holds contractual broadcast rights for NFL games and did not unilaterally suspend coverage 'until players respect the flag.'

claim: The Senate immigration bill "has immediate legalization ... and the border security is sometime in the future, and just like in 1986, it's designed never to come into being."
rationale: This characterization overstates and misrepresents the typical text of recent Senate comprehensive immigration bills. Those bills generally did not give unconditional, permanent legalization 'immediately' — they created conditional or provisional legal status with background checks, fees, and phased steps toward permanent residence and citizenship, and they linked later immigration benefits to achieving specified border-security benchmarks rather than leaving security entirely undefined. The assertion that border security was 'designed never to come into being' is a subjective political claim and not a verifiable fact about the bill’s written provisions.

claim: "John Cornyn has voted to increase the debt, raise taxes, bail out Wall Street banks and fund Obamacare."
rationale: The claim bundles four assertions and at least two are incorrect. Cornyn did vote in favor of the 2008 bank bailout (TARP) and has supported votes to raise or extend the federal debt ceiling, but he voted against the Affordable Care Act and has not been a proponent of tax increases characteristic of 'raising taxes.' Therefore the conjunctive claim is false.

claim: "At least 450,000 ballots in the key states ... miraculously only have a mark for Joe Biden on them, and no other candidate."
rationale: There is no credible evidence or official audit showing that 'at least 450,000' ballots in unspecified key states were exclusively marked for Joe Biden and no other candidate. Post‑election tallies, state certifications, and multiple recounts and audits did not substantiate claims of such a large, anomalous block of single‑candidate ballots. The statement appears to be an unverified and likely inflated assertion circulated without supporting data.

claim: Says Common Core is a federal mandate.
rationale: Common Core is not a federal mandate. The standards were developed by state-led groups (NGA and CCSSO) and individual states chose whether to adopt them; the federal government only encouraged adoption through incentives (e.g., Race to the Top grants and waiver conditions) rather than issuing a legal national requirement.

claim: "My opponent, in 2008, had contributions investigated by the federal government."
rationale: The claim as stated is unverifiable because it does not identify who “my opponent” is, which federal agency allegedly investigated, or what specific contributions were under review. Federal investigations and their targets are matters of public record, so without a named individual, agency, or corroborating documentation from 2008 this statement cannot be confirmed.

claim: "Moderna chief medical officer admits: mRNA alters DNA."
rationale: This is false: Moderna's chief medical officer was not admitting that mRNA alters human DNA and viral clips have mischaracterized his remarks. mRNA vaccines work in the cytoplasm to direct protein production and do not integrate into genomic DNA, and there is no credible evidence that vaccine mRNA alters recipients' DNA.

claim: "The average cost of child care in this country is more than what it costs to send a child to college for one year."
rationale: The claim is a categorical statement but lacks a specified country and definitions (type of child care, age, college tuition vs total cost). In many countries (including the U.S.), average annual center-based child care costs are often comparable to or lower than one year of college tuition at private institutions and often less than total college costs once room and board are excluded; costs vary widely by location and institution. Because of this variation, the blanket claim that child care costs are higher than a year of college is not generally true.

claim: An all-female construction company built the Florida bridge that collapsed.
rationale: The claim is false for the widely reported 2018 Florida International University pedestrian bridge collapse: the project was designed and built by established engineering and construction firms (e.g., FIGG Bridge Engineers and Munilla Construction Management), not an all-female construction company, and the construction workforce was not an all-female crew. No credible reporting or the official investigations indicate the bridge was built by an all-female firm.

claim: The Pfizer COVID-19 vaccine contains an "undisclosed ingredient. … How is informed consent possible?"
rationale: The Pfizer–BioNTech COVID-19 vaccine’s ingredients are publicly disclosed in regulatory fact sheets and the product label, which list the mRNA, the lipid nanoparticle components, salts, sugars, and other excipients. Regulatory agencies (FDA, EMA and others) review the full ingredient list and manufacturing/impurity data as part of authorization/approval; there is no credible evidence of a deliberately 'undisclosed ingredient.' Informed consent is based on these disclosed ingredients and the safety/efficacy information provided to patients.

claim: "Over the last two years since President Obama has taken office, the federal government has added 200,000 new federal jobs."
rationale: Official federal employment series from the Bureau of Labor Statistics and Office of Personnel Management do not show an increase of 200,000 federal civilian jobs in the two years after Obama took office; totals were roughly flat or slightly down depending on whether Postal Service employees are included. Therefore the claim that the federal government added 200,000 new federal jobs in that two-year span is inaccurate.

claim: Says when he was governor, "we expanded participation in Virginia in early childhood programs by nearly 40 percent."
rationale: The claim is not verifiable as written because it omits which governor, which early childhood programs, and the exact time period; participation rates differ by program and year and I could not confirm a near‑40% increase without those specifics. Absent a named official and defined datasets (e.g., state pre-K, Head Start slots, subsidized child care), the assertion cannot be substantiated.

claim: "NYT is correcting their lies..Trump paid $1M in 2016 & $3.8M in 2017-18..THEY LIED..AGAIN. INFO ON TWITTER THIS AM."
rationale: The tweet-like claim mixes an accusation that the New York Times 'lied' and gives precise payment figures ($1M in 2016 and $3.8M in 2017–18) that are not supported by NYT’s published reporting. The New York Times’ 2020 reporting on Trump’s taxes reported very low federal income tax payments in some years (commonly cited as $750) and different totals for other years; there is no widely reported NYT correction that changes to the specific amounts cited in this claim. The post provides no primary source or context for the numbers.

claim: Says Tammy Baldwin's record includes "opposing harsher punishments for criminals who commit violent crimes near schools."
rationale: There is no clear, specific evidence that Tammy Baldwin’s public record contains an explicit position described as 'opposing harsher punishments for criminals who commit violent crimes near schools.' While Baldwin has supported criminal justice reform and reductions in certain mandatory sentences, that general stance is not the same as a documented opposition to enhanced penalties for violent crimes committed in school zones without reference to a particular bill or vote.

claim: "Republicans would give seniors a (Medicare) voucher that limits what's covered, costing seniors as much as $6,400 more a year."
rationale: The claim is an overgeneralization. Some Republican proposals (notably premium‑support or voucher plans advanced by particular lawmakers and platforms) could reduce guaranteed benefits and, under certain CBO or private‑model assumptions and future years, result in seniors paying several thousand dollars more annually; however not all Republicans endorse the same voucher plan and the $6,400 number depends on specific plan details, assumptions and timeframe, so the blanket statement is misleading.

claim: "MSNBC announced Trump won 2020 election."
rationale: This claim is false. Major U.S. networks, including MSNBC, did not announce that Donald Trump won the 2020 presidential election; on November 7, 2020 networks projected Joe Biden as the winner after key state results (notably Pennsylvania). MSNBC's on-air coverage and official reporting acknowledged Biden's victory, not a Trump win.

claim: Federal law adopted "under Tommy Thompson's watch" prohibits the government from negotiating for "better prices" on prescription drugs for senior citizens
rationale: The Medicare Prescription Drug, Improvement, and Modernization Act of 2003, enacted while Tommy Thompson was HHS Secretary, included a statutory 'noninterference' clause that barred the HHS Secretary from negotiating drug prices on behalf of Medicare Part D beneficiaries. That language has long been cited as preventing the federal government from directly negotiating lower prescription drug prices for seniors under Part D.

claim: Police are "20.8 times more likely to kill than be killed by a criminal."
rationale: In recent U.S. data, roughly 900–1,100 people are killed by police each year while the number of officers killed by felonious acts is on the order of 40–60 annually; dividing those figures yields a ratio near 20:1 (about 20.8 in some year-by-year comparisons). The exact number depends on the year and definitions used, but the claim matches published tallies comparing annual police-caused deaths of civilians to officers killed by criminals in recent U.S. data.

claim: Says that except for Donald Trump, "every other major party nominee" for the past 40 years has released their tax returns.
rationale: Reviewing the major-party (Democratic and Republican) general-election nominees across roughly the last 40 years, the nominees other than Donald Trump publicly released tax returns (for example, Reagan, Mondale, Dukakis, Bush Sr., Clinton, Dole, Gore, Bush Jr., Kerry, McCain, Obama, Romney, Biden and Clinton in their respective cycles). Trump broke with the modern norm by refusing to release his federal tax returns in 2016 and 2020. This makes the blanket claim largely accurate for the stated period.

claim: When Mitt Romney was governor, Massachusetts lost 40,000 manufacturing jobs, a rate twice the national average, and fell to 47th in job creation, fourth from the bottom.
rationale: The statement mixes selectively chosen time windows and presents misleading conclusions. Massachusetts did lose manufacturing jobs around the early 2000s, but the 40,000 figure, the claim that the loss rate was twice the national average, and the 47th (fourth-from-bottom) job-creation ranking depend on specific short-term snapshots; comprehensive BLS data and contemporary fact-checks show those particular numbers were cherry-picked and do not accurately describe Romney’s full gubernatorial term.

claim: Countries with a higher minimum wage than the United States’ $7.25 an hour include Denmark at $21, Australia at $15.81, Germany at $11 and France at $12.35.
rationale: The claim is inaccurate because Denmark does not have a statutory national minimum wage—wages are set by collective bargaining—so presenting a single USD/hour figure (e.g., $21) is misleading. While Australia, Germany and France do have national or broadly applied minimum wages that often convert to amounts above US$7.25, the exact USD values cited vary by exchange rate and the effective date of the wage.

claim: Says detained immigrant parents separated from their children at the border are being charged "as much as $8 a minute to call their children."
rationale: Multiple major news reports and investigations during the family-separation period documented that some immigration detention facilities and their phone vendors charged very high per-minute rates for calls, including reports of charges up to about $8 per minute for some calls. Those reports referred to specific vendors and facilities rather than a single uniform national rate.

claim: "There's more than 100,000 people working at the Department of Agriculture. That's 1 employee for every 30 farmers."
rationale: While the U.S. Department of Agriculture does employ on the order of 100,000 people, the claimed ratio of 1 employee per 30 farmers is a misleading oversimplification. The USDA Census of Agriculture reports roughly 2.0 million farms (and commonly-cited counts of individual producers are about 3.0–3.5 million), which yields a ratio closer to about 1:20 if comparing to farms or about 1:30–1:35 if comparing to individual producers — so the statement depends on which population and year are used and is not a precise fact as stated.

claim: "The bill also provides full federal funding for abortions…"
rationale: The statement is unverified and likely false as written because it names no specific bill; federal law and longstanding appropriations practice (the Hyde Amendment) generally prohibit use of federal funds for most abortions. For a bill to "provide full federal funding for abortions" it would need explicit statutory language and appropriations repealing those restrictions, which is uncommon and would be widely reported.

claim: "We won Georgia easily. We won it by hundreds of thousands of votes."
rationale: The statement is misleading. In the 2020 U.S. presidential election Georgia’s certified results show Joe Biden won the state by about 11,779 votes after recounts and certification, not by hundreds of thousands. While Donald Trump carried Georgia in 2016 by roughly 211,000 votes, the claim as phrased omits the year and therefore misstates the actual recent result.

claim: "When I became mayor of Los Angeles, we had a 44 percent (high school) graduation rate. I said that was unacceptable. I challenged that notion. I said the mayor needs to be involved with our schools. We need to partner together. As I left, after a number of reforms, we grew our graduation rate from 44 percent to 72."
rationale: The headline numbers (a low mid‑40s rate earlier and a rate in the low 70s later) are similar to widely cited LAUSD figures across the 2000s–2010s, but the claim is misleading because the increase reflects changes in how graduation was measured and many district‑level efforts beyond the mayor’s direct authority. The mayor of Los Angeles does not control LA Unified Schools, and attribution of the entire jump to his actions overstates his role.

claim: Says Mark Zuckerberg invented the word "BFF," and if it doesn’t appear green after you type it in a Facebook comment, your account has been hacked.
rationale: The abbreviation "BFF" (best friends forever) long predates Facebook and was in common use well before Mark Zuckerberg popularized any social platform. The claim that a missing green appearance of "BFF" in a Facebook comment indicates your account has been hacked is a viral hoax; Facebook has not used green text as a signal of account compromise, and visual formatting can vary without implying a security breach.

claim: U.S. tariffs on China are "not hurting anybody" in the United States.
rationale: Tariffs raise the cost of imported goods and inputs, and studies of the U.S.–China tariff episode show those costs were partly passed on to U.S. consumers and firms. Many manufacturers that rely on Chinese components faced higher production costs, and U.S. exporters (notably farmers) were hurt by Chinese retaliatory tariffs, though some protected domestic producers saw benefits.

claim: "We had bipartisan legislation that got through the Senate" that would have prevented bonuses like AIG's "and then somehow mysteriously disappeared."
rationale: There is no evidence a bipartisan bill actually 'got through the Senate' and then vanished. In the AIG bonus episode (2009) the House quickly passed emergency restrictions and Congress debated measures, but the Senate did not enact a final ban before the payments; legal and contractual issues and subsequent negotiations/clawbacks followed. The claim that a Senate-passed bipartisan law existed and then mysteriously disappeared is not supported by legislative records or contemporaneous reporting.

claim: "News report accidentally reveals doctors giving ‘banned’ COVID treatment to the Queen."
rationale: There is no credible evidence or verified footage showing doctors administering a supposedly ‘banned’ COVID treatment to the Queen; the claim appears to have originated on social media and has been debunked by fact-checkers. Official sources and reputable news organizations did not report any accidental reveal, and treatment details for the monarch were not publicly disclosed in that way.

claim: Says Donald Trump "has the second-highest disapproval ratings of anyone running for president."
rationale: The claim is a specific ranking that cannot be confirmed without citing a particular poll, date, and voter sample. Disapproval ratings for Donald Trump and other presidential candidates vary widely across pollsters and over time; while Trump often has among the highest disapproval scores, he is not consistently or unambiguously the "second-highest" in all reputable national polls. Without a precise source, the statement is not verifiable as presented.

claim: "By the way, I'm not raising tolls 50 percent....Jon Corzine did."
rationale: There is no clear evidence that Jon Corzine personally enacted a single, across-the-board 50% toll increase. During Corzine’s term some toll increases and proposals occurred and independent authorities set many rates, but characterizing it as “Jon Corzine did” raise tolls 50% misattributes a specific unilateral 50% hike to him. The actual changes varied by facility and were implemented through authorities or legislation rather than a single governor action.

claim: Says the United States has the "highest corporate tax rate in the world."
rationale: The United States does not currently have the highest corporate tax rate in the world. After the 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act the federal statutory rate was cut to 21% (with state additions bringing typical combined rates into the mid-20s), which is lower than the statutory rates in many other countries; historically the U.S. was among the highest before 2018.

claim: "We were not, I repeat, were not told that waterboarding or any of these other enhanced interrogation methods were used."
rationale: The blanket assertion that 'we were not told' that waterboarding or other enhanced interrogation methods were used cannot be verified and is likely false. Public record — including Department of Justice legal memoranda, reporting, and later investigations such as the Senate Intelligence Committee review — indicates that many senior officials and oversight bodies were briefed about or otherwise became aware of the use of waterboarding and other enhanced interrogation techniques. Without specifying who 'we' refers to or the time period, the denial is implausible as a general statement.

claim: Says his "Act 10 reforms" have "saved the taxpayers some $3 billion."
rationale: The claim that Act 10 "saved the taxpayers some $3 billion" is not supported by a consensus of independent analyses. Estimates of savings from Wisconsin's Act 10 vary widely depending on the time period and what costs are counted, and nonpartisan fiscal analyses and media fact-checkers have found substantially lower or more qualified savings figures than a definitive $3 billion.

claim: "Hundreds of illegal immigrants subject to detainers were released in the last week since the new sanctuary policy was adopted by the Travis County Sheriff's Office."
rationale: There are no verifiable reports from official Travis County jail release logs, the sheriff’s office, or independent local reporting that show 'hundreds' of people subject to ICE detainers were released within a single week after a new sanctuary policy. Coverage of Travis County's policy change has noted reduced cooperation with ICE and disputes with state officials, but concrete numbers cited in reliable reporting do not support the specific claim of hundreds released in one week.

claim: John McCain "voted against the tax cuts of 2001 and 2003, wrongly claiming they helped only the rich."
rationale: The claim is inaccurate on two counts: McCain did not simply cast uniform 'no' votes on both the 2001 and 2003 Bush tax bills, and the assertion that those cuts "helped only the rich" is an overstatement. Detailed roll-call records and contemporary reporting show McCain's votes and positions were more nuanced, and independent analyses (CBO/Tax Policy Center) find the 2001/2003 tax cuts delivered larger absolute dollar benefits to higher-income households but also provided tax reductions to middle- and lower-income taxpayers, so saying they helped "only" the rich is incorrect.

claim: "There's a loophole where you can sell guns without a background check … 40 percent of guns are sold that way" at gun shows and over the Internet.
rationale: It is true that federal law requires licensed dealers to run background checks while purely private sales (including some transactions at gun shows or online) are not federally mandated to use the background-check system, but the claim that 40% of guns are sold that way is misleading. The often-cited "40%" comes from specific surveys of recent purchasers or self-reported transfers and does not represent a verified share of all gun sales; other studies and definitions produce substantially different estimates. Conflating private transfers, gun-show sales, and online sales into a single 40% figure overstates what is established by available data.

claim: Says "we are overcharging students . . . to help pay for the health care law."
rationale: The claim is a broad assertion without any named institution, jurisdiction, timeframe, or evidence. While some colleges and universities have added mandatory health-insurance fees or adjusted charges in response to healthcare law changes, there is no general, verifiable rule that students are being universally or intentionally "overcharged" specifically to "help pay for the health care law." The statement is therefore unsubstantiated as framed.

claim: "Thom Tillis cut almost $500 million from education."
rationale: The claim is misleading and lacks necessary context. While North Carolina budgets in the early 2010s involved expiration of one‑time federal or nonrecurring education funds and legislative choices that changed education financing, it is inaccurate to say Thom Tillis personally “cut almost $500 million from education” as a simple, attributable unilateral cut; fact‑checks have found the figure misstates the timing, scope, and causes of budget changes.

claim: Says Gary Farmer’s claim that he "received an 'A' from the NRA" is "an absolute lie."
rationale: I cannot confirm that Gary Farmer did not receive an 'A' from the NRA; public NRA candidate ratings exist and vary by cycle and by which NRA body (national vs. state) is meant. Calling the statement 'an absolute lie' requires evidence that he in fact received an A, which I do not have available. Because the claim is time- and source-specific and unverified, I default to false pending documentation.

claim: "California lawmakers are planning to push free abortion pills on all students across the state as part of a ‘super progressive’ new policy."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that California lawmakers are planning a statewide program to 'push free abortion pills on all students.' While California has enacted and considered measures to expand and fund abortion access (including medication abortion) and some proposals have addressed student health services, those efforts focus on increasing access and funding for eligible patients, not mandatory or universal distribution to every student.

claim: "I am the only member of Congress that voted for both inquiries -- the Clinton inquiry and now the Trump inquiry."
rationale: The claim of uniqueness is inconsistent with the historical record: many long-serving members of Congress overlapped the 1998 Clinton impeachment era and the 2019 Trump impeachment inquiry, and roll-call votes show more than one member could have voted for both. Without a specific name and roll-call evidence, the assertion that any single member was the only one to do so is very unlikely and not supported by available records.

claim: "Biden says he doesn’t need voters to get elected."
rationale: There is no credible record of President Joe Biden saying he “doesn’t need voters to get elected.” Publicly he has repeatedly solicited votes and campaigned for electoral support; a statement like that would have been widely reported if made. The claim appears to be a misquote, out-of-context clip, or disinformation.

claim: "The only time over the last 25 years when the state’s unemployment rate exceeded the U.S. average was when (Mary) Burke was commerce secretary."
rationale: The claim is implausible and likely incorrect: it names no state but appears to refer to Wisconsin (where Mary Burke served as commerce secretary), yet Wisconsin’s unemployment rate exceeded the U.S. average in multiple periods over the last 25 years (notably during early-2000s weakness, the 2008–2010 Great Recession, and other downturns), not only during Burke’s tenure. Burke’s tenure was brief (around 2009–2011), so it is unlikely to be the sole time the state rate topped the national rate over a 25-year span.

claim: Says New Hampshire had the fourth-lowest unemployment rate in the country during Maggie Hassan’s time in the state Senate.
rationale: The claim is implausible as stated because unemployment rankings fluctuate month-to-month and New Hampshire’s rank varied during Maggie Hassan’s time in the state senate (mid-to-late 2000s); it was not consistently the fourth-lowest nationwide. Without a specific date or source, the assertion that NH held exactly the fourth-lowest rate 'during her time' is unsupported by broad Bureau of Labor Statistics time series which show changing ranks, especially around the Great Recession.

claim: "The state is set to recapture an additional $500 million in Robin Hood payments from taxpayers and not one penny of it will go to public education in Texas."
rationale: Texas 'Robin Hood' recapture payments are collections from property‑wealthy districts that are generally redistributed by the state to under‑funded school districts to support public education.
