While individual Klan members, splinter Klan groups, and other white supremacists publicly expressed support for Trump, that does not constitute an official endorsement by 'the KKK.'

claim: Says "Canada has one-tenth of our population—yet it issues far more high-skilled visas (more than 150,000) yearly than we do (65,000)."
rationale: The claim conflates different categories and is misleading. Canada’s population is roughly one‑tenth of the U.S., and Canada does admit large numbers of economic-class immigrants (often over 100k in some years), but comparing those admissions to the U.S. H‑1B cap (commonly cited as 65,000) mixes distinct visa programs and timeframes. Therefore the blanket statement as presented is inaccurate without clearer definitions and year references.

claim: Says Wisconsin Manufacturers & Commerce’s "own 2014 survey revealed that just 15 percent of business executive respondents were in favor of Right-To-Work legislation."
rationale: There is no clear evidence that WMC's own 2014 survey found only 15% of business executives favoring Right‑To‑Work; WMC publicly advocated for Right‑To‑Work and reporting that number appears to be a misinterpretation or misquote of survey subtotals (for example a ‘strongly in favor’ category) rather than overall support. Without the exact question wording and response breakdown, the claim as stated is misleading.

claim: Says Charlie Crist "stood there, over 3 African-American prisoners in chains, on their knees, on the side of the road. Saying that it was a great sight. Saying we needed to bring it to Florida. And you did this — whether you know or not — on the eve of Juneteenth, the day the African-American community celebrates the end of slavery."
rationale: There is no credible record or mainstream reporting that Charlie Crist stood over three African‑American prisoners in chains and made those remarks on the eve of Juneteenth. Such an inflammatory incident involving a prominent politician would have been widely documented and corroborated; the claim appears to be an unverified or misattributed allegation. Without reliable source evidence, the statement should be treated as false.

claim: Says Supreme Court nominee Merrick Garland "voted, so the folks know, in Washington, D.C., to keep guns away from private citizens."
rationale: The claim is a misleading blanket statement. Merrick Garland served as a federal appellate judge on the D.C. Circuit and ruled on individual cases, but there is no clear record that he cast a single categorical vote to bar private citizens from owning guns; the landmark D.C. handgun ban was struck down by the Supreme Court in Heller (2008), not by a single Garland vote instituting a broad ban. Without a specific case or citation the assertion overstates and mischaracterizes his judicial record.

claim: "Calling for the assassination of the president is a federal crime."
rationale: Federal law makes it a crime to threaten the president and to solicit or conspire to commit violent crimes against federal officials, so many explicit calls for assassination can be prosecuted. However, the statement as absolute is misleading: purely abstract or protected speech that does not constitute a true threat or incitement to imminent lawless action may be protected by the First Amendment and not automatically a federal crime.

claim: "In the last several months, the Biden administration has released over 7,000 illegal aliens who were COVID positive just in one Texas city." Biden's border policies are "endangering not just the people of Texas, but people all across the country."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that the Biden administration released over 7,000 COVID‑positive migrants in a single Texas city in the last several months; such a large, specific figure would have been documented by federal or state public‑health and border agencies and widely reported, but available public records and reporting do not support it. The statement also conflates operational releases by multiple authorities and frames a normative claim about danger, which is an opinion rather than a verifiable factual assertion.

claim: Senate Democrats who left the state for weeks to delay a vote on union bargaining power exercised a "Wisconsin filibuster" provided by the state’s constitution.
rationale: While Wisconsin Senate Democrats did flee the state in 2011 to deny quorum and delay a vote on collective bargaining limits, that tactic was a quorum-busting walkout, not a formal 'filibuster' created by the state constitution. The Wisconsin Constitution sets quorum and procedural rules that the senators exploited, but it does not provide a named 'Wisconsin filibuster' procedure akin to a legislative filibuster.

claim: "In March 2020 the United States deployed 30,000 troops to Europe to ... free child-trafficked children and arrest deep state cabal members."
rationale: There is no credible evidence or Department of Defense announcement that the United States deployed 30,000 troops to Europe in March 2020 to free child-trafficked children or to arrest so-called 'deep state' members. The claim echoes QAnon-style conspiracy narratives and has been repeatedly debunked by reputable news organizations and official sources.

claim: Judge Ketanji Brown Jackson "gave child porn offenders sentences below the guidelines and below what the prosecutors were requesting," showing she is "soft on child pornography offenders."
rationale: The claim is misleading: while Judge Ketanji Brown Jackson imposed some below-guidelines sentences in certain child‑pornography cases, reviews by independent fact‑checkers and court records show a mixed record (some sentences were within or above guidelines and in some instances prosecutors sought lower terms). Presenting this selective set of rulings as proof she is broadly "soft on child pornography offenders" is an inaccurate generalization that omits context about guideline calculations, plea agreements, and judicial discretion.

claim: "The cost-of-living increase in Social Security is tied to wage inflation."
rationale: The annual Social Security cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) is based on changes in the Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers (CPI-W), which measures consumer price inflation, not wage inflation. Wage growth is used separately to wage-index workers' earnings when computing initial benefits, but that is distinct from the COLA calculation.

claim: Scott Walker "couldn’t get his own party" to back more than a 500-student increase in Milwaukee’s school choice program, but in Indiana, "Mitch Daniels’ voucher program is approaching 30,000 students two years after opening."
rationale: Reporting from the period shows Walker faced resistance within his own Republican coalition and the Milwaukee Parental Choice expansion was limited to a 500-student increase in the legislative deal. Separately, Indiana’s voucher (Choice Scholarship) program implemented under Gov. Mitch Daniels saw rapid growth and enrollment rose to nearly 30,000 students within about two years of its statewide launch.

claim: Says his office "has already recovered over $2 billion from Wall Street for the workers, retirees, and investors who were harmed."
rationale: The claim is not verifiable as presented because it does not identify which official or office is being referenced or the time period for the $2 billion figure. Settlement recoveries are normally documented in press releases, court records, or audited reports, and without those specifics I cannot confirm the amount. While some state or federal offices have recovered large sums from Wall Street in various cases, this exact attribution cannot be substantiated from the claim alone.

claim: Promotes a chart saying that Barack Obama has "increased the debt" by 16 percent, compared to George W. Bush, who increased it by 115 percent.
rationale: The specific percentages (Obama +16%, Bush +115%) do not match standard measures of U.S. federal debt growth. Using commonly reported totals, gross federal debt rose from roughly $5.8T (Jan 2001) to ~$10.6T (Jan 2009) — about an 80–85% increase under George W. Bush — and from ~$10.6T (Jan 2009) to about $19.9T (Jan 2017) — roughly an 80–90% increase under Barack Obama, not 16%. The chart’s figures appear to be based on a highly selective metric or baseline rather than the widely used debt totals.

claim: During the Eisenhower Administration, "not a single soldier … died in combat."
rationale: Dwight D. Eisenhower took office in January 1953 and the Korean War continued until the armistice in July 1953; U.S. soldiers were killed in combat during that period. Therefore the statement that "not a single soldier ... died in combat" during his administration is incorrect.

claim: Says Abraham Lincoln said, "America will never be destroyed from the outside. If we lose our freedoms it will be because we have destroyed ourselves from within."
rationale: The exact sentence is not found in Lincoln's writings; it appears to be a modern paraphrase of a passage from his 1838 'Lyceum Address' that expresses a similar idea (e.g., 'If destruction be our lot, we must ourselves be its author and finisher'). Reliable quote-checking finds the precise wording misattributed to Lincoln.

claim: Says Mitt Romney did not pay taxes for 10 years.
rationale: Publicly released tax returns and contemporaneous reporting show Mitt Romney paid federal and state taxes in multiple years; there is no credible evidence that he paid zero taxes for a continuous 10-year period. Assertions that he paid no taxes conflate different years or types of tax and are contradicted by his disclosed returns and his campaign statements.

claim: Says Nancy Pelosi said, "Building a wall will violate the rights of millions of illegals." ​
rationale: There is no reliable record or reputable news transcript showing Nancy Pelosi said the exact line "Building a wall will violate the rights of millions of illegals." Pelosi has publicly opposed a border wall on moral and policy grounds, but she typically uses terms like "undocumented immigrants" and has not been documented using this phrasing, indicating a likely misquote or misattribution.

claim: The racial and ethnic makeup of the Gwinnett County Sheriff’s Office mirrors the community it serves.
rationale: Gwinnett County is a majority-minority suburban county with substantial Hispanic and Asian populations, but the sheriff’s office has historically had a staff composition skewed toward white officers and men and has not matched those community proportions. Public demographic data and reporting on law-enforcement workforce composition in many U.S. communities, including Gwinnett, show underrepresentation of some racial and ethnic groups relative to the county population.

claim: "Eliminating earmarks does not reduce spending."
rationale: The claim is too absolute: empirical evidence is mixed rather than uniformly showing no effect. In some cases banning earmarks has reduced earmarked or discretionary project allocations, while in other cases lawmakers redirected funds through other mechanisms so total spending changed little. Whether spending falls depends on definitions, time period, and available substitute funding paths.

claim: Says Wisconsin payday loans have a 574% average annual interest rate, "exploitative lending that keeps Americans trapped in debt"
rationale: The specific claim that Wisconsin payday loans have a 574% average APR is not a well-established, verifiable figure from authoritative sources; while payday loans commonly produce very high APRs (hundreds of percent) depending on fee structure and loan term, reported averages vary by study, year, and methodology. The characterization as "exploitative lending that keeps Americans trapped in debt" is an opinion but is consistent with evidence that high-cost short-term credit can lead to repeat borrowing and debt cycles.

claim: Says Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Ilhan Omar vowed "to remove senior’s ‘entitlements,’ Social Security/Medicare."
rationale: Neither Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez nor Ilhan Omar have vowed to remove Social Security or Medicare; both lawmakers have publicly supported protecting or expanding benefits (Ocasio-Cortez has defended Social Security and Omar has backed Medicare-for-All proposals). Claims that they vowed to eliminate seniors' entitlements originate from misleading ads and out-of-context quotes rather than their policy statements.

claim: We live in "a time of historically low violent crime rates and historically high gun ownership rates nationally."
rationale: The claim is an overbroad generalization. Violent crime in the U.S. fell substantially from a peak in the early 1990s and was low for much of the 2000s and 2010s, but there were notable spikes in homicides and some violent crimes in 2020–2021; overall violent crime is not uniformly at an all‑time low depending on the metric and timeframe. Similarly, while the total number of firearms in private hands has grown recently, household gun ownership rates (and how 'ownership' is measured) are not unambiguously at historical highs nationally.

claim: Says federal regulations adopted in 2011 increased the cost of each vehicle for his business by $10,000.
rationale: Federal regulations finalized around 2011 (notably fuel-economy and greenhouse-gas rules) did raise compliance costs, but government and independent analyses estimated incremental per-vehicle costs generally in the hundreds to a few thousand dollars range, not $10,000. A blanket claim that 2011 regulations increased the cost of each vehicle for a business by $10,000 overstates typical estimated impacts and ignores vehicle type and company-specific factors.

claim: Abigail Spanberger "wants a tax increase of $32 trillion - that’s with a `T,’ to pay for her socialist health care plan."
rationale: There is no evidence Abigail Spanberger has proposed a $32 trillion tax increase. She has not advocated 'socialist' Medicare‑for‑all policies and has generally supported strengthening the ACA; the $32 trillion number is a commonly cited estimate of gross federal spending for some Medicare‑for‑all proposals over a multi‑year period, not a tax plan she proposed.

claim: "America’s least-trusted news sources are also its most popular."
rationale: This claim is an overgeneralization. Surveys and audience data show trust in news outlets varies by outlet and demographic, and many of the largest-audience outlets (major broadcast networks, big cable channels, and leading newspapers/websites) are not uniformly rated as the "least-trusted." Popularity by viewership or traffic does not consistently correlate with being lowest in trust.

claim: "Here in Florida, despite 14 school shootings in eight years, we still have some of the weakest gun laws in the nation."
rationale: The claim bundles an unverified numeric count with a comparative judgment. The statement’s ‘14 school shootings in eight years’ lacks a specified time window and cannot be confirmed as stated, and the description that Florida has “some of the weakest gun laws” is subjective and contradicted by post‑2018 reforms (age limit, waiting period, school safety measures) that moved Florida away from being among the very weakest states. Because of the ambiguous timeframe and the mixed evidence about Florida’s relative ranking, the overall claim is not supported as stated.

claim: "Constituents now face reality that all their personal issues will be made public" under Clean Missouri.
rationale: Clean Missouri did not create a rule that all constituents’ personal issues must be made public. The measure focused on redistricting, campaign finance and ethics reforms and some transparency provisions, but it did not mandate blanket public disclosure of private constituent matters.

claim: Says Sen. Mitch McConnell's delay in seating Alabama Sen.-elect Doug Jones "is a flagrant violation of Senate policy, which requires Jones assume office the instant one of them wins the election."
rationale: There is no Senate rule that a senator-elect must assume office the instant vote-counting indicates a winner. Seating requires state certification of the election, presentation of credentials, and taking the oath, and the Senate has constitutional authority to judge elections; delaying swearing-in pending certification or a contest is not per se a 'flagrant violation' of Senate policy.

claim: Poll results from the past 35 years show that State of the Union speeches "do not move" presidential approval numbers.
rationale: Aggregated polling and academic analyses over the past several decades show that State of the Union addresses typically produce only small, short-lived changes in presidential approval (often a few percentage points or within the margin of error), so claiming they "do not move" approval at all is too absolute. While the average effect is modest, individual speeches have produced measurable shifts in some cases.

claim: "Our governor proposed initially a 5% cut across the board of state government."
rationale: The claim is underspecified — “our governor” does not identify which governor, state, or time period, and there is no corroborating detail provided. Without a specific actor and date it cannot be verified; while some governors have proposed 5% across‑the‑board cuts in various budgets, the statement as given is uncheckable and therefore treated as false.

claim: "When I go on Letterman" the "ratings go up."
rationale: The claim is a broad causal assertion without episode-level evidence. While some high-profile guests can produce temporary rating spikes, ratings depend on many factors (time slot, competing programs, special events) and do not reliably increase every time a particular person appears. Establishing the claim would require Nielsen-level data for each appearance and a causal analysis, which is not provided.

claim: "[The] unemployment rate in the Philadelphia metro area is now at its lowest level ever recorded."
rationale: The claim is unverified because no date or specific data source is given; BLS metro-area unemployment series (which generally begin in 1990) show fluctuations with very low readings before and after the pandemic but do not unambiguously support an 'all-time' record low for the Philadelphia metro without a specified timeframe. Absent a clear date and dataset, the statement cannot be confirmed and is therefore judged false.

claim: "Texas has launched ‘Operation Lone Star’ to finish the border wall themselves."
rationale: Texas launched Operation Lone Star in 2021 under Governor Greg Abbott to bolster border security using state law enforcement and National Guard forces, and the effort has included construction of state-funded barriers (razor wire, fencing, and temporary wall segments) to fill gaps left by the unfinished federal wall. While the operation’s mission also includes arrests, removals, and interdiction, a stated element was to build barriers where the federal government had not completed fencing.

claim: Says Gov. Rick Perry is "spending Texans’ hard-earned money to live like Louie XIV."
rationale: The phrase is political rhetoric and an exaggerated comparison; there is no credible evidence that Gov. Rick Perry used Texas taxpayer money to sustain an extraordinarily lavish personal lifestyle comparable to Louis XIV. While governors receive official residences, security, staff, and travel funded by the state, those routine public expenses do not substantiate the extreme claim of living like a monarch of Versailles.

claim: On allowing abortion in cases of rape or incest, "I have never said that or advocated that."
rationale: This claim is unverifiable as presented because it does not identify who allegedly said the quoted line or provide a source. Without an attributable speaker, date, or reliable citation (transcript, video, or reporting), there's no way to confirm the person actually made that statement. Given the missing context and evidence, I treat the assertion as false until corroborated.

claim: "Trump wins the award Obama never could."
rationale: The statement is too vague to be verified and therefore is unsupported as written: it does not name which award is meant. Barack Obama has won major awards (for example the 2009 Nobel Peace Prize) and Donald Trump has also received various awards, so a blanket claim that Trump won an award Obama "never could" is unsubstantiated without a specific award and context.

claim: The U.S. government spends less on energy innovation "than the pet food industry invests in its own products."
rationale: The statement is misleading because it compares imprecise categories and the available public data do not support it. U.S. federal energy innovation spending (across DOE R&D, ARPA‑E and related programs) runs into multiple billions of dollars annually, while the pet food industry’s spending specifically on product R&D is a much smaller fraction of its total sales. Framing that the government spends less than the pet food industry on its products overstates the likely gap and conflates different types of spending.

claim: The United States has experienced "40 straight months of unemployment at 8 percent or higher."
rationale: The U.S. unemployment rate was indeed at or above 8% for an extended stretch around the Great Recession, but the claim of exactly 40 straight months is not supported as a precise, general statement. Official monthly unemployment (U-3) series from the BLS show the timing and length of high unemployment differs depending on the start/end months used, so the blanket claim is inaccurate without a specified timeframe.

claim: Speedway is offering $500 fuel cards for $1.95 to help customers with rising fuel costs.
rationale: No credible evidence shows Speedway legitimately selling $500 fuel cards for $1.95; such offers are consistent with viral scams and phishing posts. Speedway’s official promotions and gift-card practices do not include giving away high-value cards for a nominal fee, and fact-checkers have flagged similar claims as false.

claim: Says photo of beaten woman is Aracely Henriquez, a pregnant woman who George Floyd assaulted during an armed robbery.
rationale: While George Floyd had a past aggravated-robbery conviction, independent fact-checks found that the widely circulated photo purportedly showing 'Aracely Henriquez' is not of the robbery victim and originates from an unrelated incident. There is no verified evidence linking that beaten-woman image to Henriquez or to the 2007 robbery.

claim: In 2010, uninsured voters made up "about 5 percent of the electorate."
rationale: The U.S. uninsured population in 2010 was far larger than 5% — roughly 14–16% of the population (about 40–50 million people) according to Census and health-coverage data. Even allowing for nonvoters and turnout differences, the share of uninsured among the voting-age population or electorate would not plausibly be as low as ~5% absent a much narrower, unspecified definition.

claim: "Colorado raked in $60 million in marijuana taxes and licensing fees in the past year."
rationale: Colorado’s reported annual marijuana tax and fee receipts are much larger than $60 million; recent state revenue reports show combined cannabis taxes and licensing/fee collections in the hundreds of millions per year. Saying the state “raked in $60 million in the past year” substantially understates typical annual totals and is therefore incorrect as a general claim.

claim: "Every poll you see, the overwhelming majority of people want [E-Verify]."
rationale: The claim is an absolute universal statement but is not true: while many reputable polls report majority support for E-Verify, not every poll shows an "overwhelming" majority. Results vary by question wording, timing, and sample (e.g., registered voters vs. likely voters vs. specific demographics), and some surveys show more modest or conditional support rather than an overwhelming consensus.

claim: Clinton has "raised the most money from Washington lobbyists ... from the health industry, drug companies, health insurance companies (and) the defense industry."
rationale: The claim is too broad and lacks necessary context (which Clinton, what time period, and which comparison group). Public campaign‑finance analyses show Hillary Clinton was a top recipient of contributions from lobbyists and certain industries in some timeframes and versus some opponents, but she was not unambiguously the single top recipient across all Washington lobbyists and across the health, drug, insurance and defense industries in every relevant comparison. Without a specified timeframe and comparator set the blanket statement is misleading.

claim: "In Italy, they have thrown their money on the streets. A clear message to the whole world that money is not enough when health is in danger."
rationale: The claim that Italians literally "threw their money on the streets" as a widespread, documented action lacks credible reporting or evidence. Contemporary news accounts from Italy (including coverage of COVID-era public gestures) describe symbolic acts of solidarity (applause, singing, donations) but not mass public money-throwing, so the literal assertion appears false or at best a mischaracterized/figurative statement.

claim: "It’s estimated that in 2018 alone, dead people received $1 billion in benefits from Medicare, Medicaid, social security payments, and federal pensions."
rationale: There is no authoritative, consolidated government report showing that dead people received exactly $1 billion in combined Medicare, Medicaid, Social Security and federal pension benefits in 2018. While federal agencies report improper payments (including some payments to deceased beneficiaries) and recoveries, the totals and definitions vary by program and no single verified figure of $1 billion for 2018 across those programs is documented.

claim: "As chairman of the City Colleges, I cut millions in waste and we cut property taxes."
rationale: The statement combines two claims that are unsubstantiated and likely inaccurate: chairing a community college system does not give authority to unilaterally cut municipal property tax rates (those are set by local taxing authorities), and no independent audit or reporting is cited to confirm ‘‘millions’’ in waste were cut. Without specific system, dates, or supporting audits/public records, the claim cannot be verified and is misleading.

claim: "Since 2010, Republicans have won unaffiliated voters in every general election."
rationale: National exit polls and surveys show independents/unaffiliated voters split across cycles rather than consistently favoring Republicans. Democrats carried independents in several post‑2010 general elections (notably 2012 and 2020 presidential elections and the 2018 midterms), while Republicans won them in some others (e.g., 2014, 2016). Thus Republicans did not win unaffiliated voters in every general election since 2010.

claim: "Sherrod Brown supported President Obama's $453 billion tax increase."
rationale: There is no clear record that Senator Sherrod Brown voted for or publicly endorsed a discrete ' $453 billion tax increase' put forward as a single bill by President Obama. Brown has supported some Obama tax proposals (notably higher taxes on top earners), but the specific $453 billion figure appears to be an aggregated budget estimate or a misleading framing rather than a standalone measure Brown explicitly backed.

claim: Republicans "nominated the 1st Black woman to the SCOTUS & she was BLOCKED & filibustered by… Joe Biden."
rationale: No Republican has previously nominated the first Black woman to the U.S. Supreme Court. The first Black woman nominated and confirmed to the Supreme Court was Ketanji Brown Jackson, who was nominated by President Joe Biden in 2022. Biden did not 'block and filibuster' a Republican nominee to the Supreme Court; filibusters are Senate actions and there is no record of Biden single‑handedly filibustering a Republican SCOTUS nominee.

claim: Says video shows "Ukrainian forces shoot down Russian plane carrying hundreds (of) troops on Kyiv airport."
rationale: There is no credible, independently verified evidence that Ukrainian forces shot down a Russian transport plane carrying hundreds of troops at Kyiv airport; media and fact-checkers found the circulating videos to be misattributed or unverified and no official sources corroborated such a large loss at that location. Claims like this have repeatedly been debunked where videos showed different incidents or were falsely labeled by origin and date.

claim: Says critics who say he cut Medicaid are wrong; his budget added $1.2 billion to the program
rationale: The claim cannot be verified as stated because the subject ('he') and the budget year/jurisdiction are unspecified. Budget totals and whether an action constitutes a 'cut' depend on details (state vs federal, gross appropriation vs net spending, changes in eligibility or accounting). Without a specific actor and enacted budget documents, the assertion that critics are wrong and that the budget 'added $1.2 billion' cannot be confirmed.

claim: "First, he was in favor of my plan, now he's attacking it."
rationale: The claim alleges a specific change in an individual's position but provides no named person, plan, timeline, or evidence. Without verifiable public statements, documents, or voting records showing an initial endorsement followed by criticism, the assertion is unsubstantiated and cannot be confirmed.

claim: "In 1960, most black children were raised in two-parent, monogamous families." Today "we have only 20 percent of black children being raised in two-parent, monogamous families..."
rationale: U.S. Census and research data show that in 1960 a clear majority of Black children lived with two parents (most in married-couple households). The share of Black children in two-parent households has fallen substantially since then, but current figures are roughly around half, not as low as 20 percent; the 20% figure is therefore inaccurate.

claim: President Obama has "stopped using the phrase 'war on terror.' "
rationale: The Obama administration publicly moved away from the term and encouraged alternatives (like 'overseas contingency operations'), but Obama and his officials did not categorically cease all uses of the phrase. Media reporting and transcripts show the administration preferred different language while occasional references and similar formulations continued, so the absolute claim that he 'stopped using' it is inaccurate.

claim: "For the first time in 35 years, we have more businesses dying than we do starting."
rationale: The statement is vague and unsupported by available national-level data; recent years (especially 2020–2022) saw record or near-record business formation activity in countries like the U.S., even though closures rose during the pandemic. Official statistics do not show a clear nationwide reversal where business deaths exceeded business births for the first time in 35 years. Without a specified country and time period, the claim cannot be substantiated and is likely false.

claim: Says she couldn't take stimulus money because it required "universal building codes."
rationale: Federal 'stimulus' or grant programs sometimes require that funded construction meet applicable building codes or specific standards for the project, but they do not condition receipt of funds on a jurisdiction adopting a single 'universal building code' nationwide. Building codes are normally set and adopted by states and localities, so the claim that she couldn't take stimulus money because it required universal building codes is misleading.

claim: "We cut property taxes by one-third in the state of Texas while I’ve been governor."
rationale: Statewide property tax burden in Texas did not fall by one-third during the governor’s tenure; total property tax levies and typical homeowner bills have generally risen since 2015. While the legislature enacted exemptions and caps that reduced rates or provided relief for some taxpayers, those measures did not amount to a one‑third across‑the‑board cut in property taxes.

claim: "The federal government is now on track" for the second-largest budget deficit "in 65 years."
rationale: The statement is unverifiable as presented because it omits the country and time period; whether a federal deficit ranks as the "second-largest in 65 years" depends on the exact year and whether deficits are measured in nominal dollars or as a share of GDP. Official sources (Treasury/OMB/CBO) and a specified reference year are needed to confirm such a ranking, and recent U.S. deficits (for example 2020) were record-high, so the claim as stated is misleading without context.

claim: "We had already issued several thousand Special Immigrant Visas .. to the (Afghan) translators, when I came into office."
rationale: The claim overstates the number of Special Immigrant Visas (SIVs) actually issued to Afghan translators by the time the administration began. Public reporting and official data from the period indicate that while thousands of SIV applications existed and some visas had been granted, the number of completed, issued Afghan SIVs was substantially lower than the phrase “several thousand” implies and many cases remained pending. Thus the statement is misleading and not supported as a factual count of visas already issued when the term began.

claim: "The city of Portland has won more national Constitution contests than any city in America."
rationale: There is no authoritative evidence that any city named Portland holds a recorded lead for winning more national 'Constitution' contests than every other U.S. city. The claim is vague about which specific national contest and which Portland is meant, and no widely reported records or reputable sources support such a superlative.

claim: "We don't need a separate (prescription drug) database ... Pharmacies already have a database in place."
rationale: While individual pharmacies keep internal dispensing records, those records are fragmented across many private systems, vary in format, and are not routinely aggregated or shared in real time for public-health monitoring or cross-pharmacy oversight. Centralized prescription drug databases (or PDMPs) exist to aggregate data from all dispensers, provide clinicians and regulators with a complete view, and support surveillance and safety functions that a single pharmacy's database cannot perform alone.

claim: "Our real unemployment is anywhere from 18 to 20 percent. Don't believe the 5.6. Don't believe it."
rationale: The claim overstates unemployment. The official U-3 unemployment rate of about 5.6% is the standard measure; the broader U-6 measure (which includes discouraged and underemployed workers) was roughly around 10–11% in the period when a 5.6% U-3 was reported, not 18–20%. Even counting many outside-the-labor-force groups, commonly reported BLS series do not support a 18–20% unemployment rate in recent years.

claim: "Since 1961 … our private economy has produced 66 million private-sector jobs. So what's the jobs score? Republicans 24 million, Democrats 42 (million)."
rationale: The headline numbers are plausibly derived from a particular choice of start/end dates and attribution method, but the claim omits the endpoint and methodology and thus is not verifiable as stated. Independent analyses show private‑sector job totals and party breakdowns change with different month cutoffs and counting rules, so presenting a single 66M total with a 24M/42M split is misleading.

claim: Florida has "more concealed weapons permits than any other state."
rationale: The statement is imprecise and not reliably true as stated. There is no federal registry and permit totals change over time and by definition (active vs issued), and while Florida has had a large number of concealed-carry licenses, other large states or periods (and recent adoption of permitless carry in some states) mean Florida does not unequivocally have the most permits in all comparisons.

claim: According to a recent CDC report, "almost everyone — 85% — who got the coronavirus in July was wearing a mask, and they were infected anyway. So clearly (wearing a mask) doesn’t work the way they tell us it works."
rationale: This is a misleading interpretation of CDC data. A high percentage of infected people reporting mask use does not prove masks are ineffective — it can reflect high background mask use, imperfect self-reporting, inconsistent/incorrect mask use, differences in mask type/fit, or exposure in situations where masks were removed. The CDC and many studies conclude masks reduce (but do not eliminate) transmission risk when used correctly.

claim: Says Ron Johnson "likes to say there are too many lawyers in the Senate – 57. He’d be the 70th millionaire."
rationale: There is no reliable record verifying Ron Johnson said that exact line or that the specific numbers (57 lawyers, he would be the 70th millionaire) are accurate. While Johnson has criticized the number of lawyers in the Senate and touted his business background, the precise quoted figures appear to be unverified or paraphrased.

claim: Says that in 41 states, government workers "are better paid than the taxpayers who support them."
rationale: The claim is misleading and not supported by consistent data. Comparisons of public‑sector pay to ‘taxpayers’ depend heavily on how you define the comparison group (private‑sector wages, household income, full‑time only, benefits included), and independent fact‑checks and labor data show results vary by state and methodology rather than showing 41 states where government workers are uniformly paid more than the taxpayers who fund them.

claim: "Las Vegas shooting witnesses report multiple gunmen dressed as security guards."
rationale: Official investigations into the October 2017 Las Vegas mass shooting concluded a single gunman, Stephen Paddock, fired from a Mandalay Bay suite and found no credible evidence of additional shooters disguised as security. Although some witnesses initially reported seeing people in security-like clothing or hearing shots from multiple directions, those accounts were not corroborated by ballistic, video, or investigative evidence and are consistent with the confusion common in mass-casualty events.

claim: Says the fertilizer plant that exploded in West, Texas,"had not been inspected by the state of Texas since 2006."
rationale: The statement is too absolute. Public reporting and agency records after the 2013 West, Texas explosion showed a more complicated inspection history with different state agencies having inspected or engaged with the facility at different times; saying it had not been inspected by the state at all since 2006 omits that nuance and is therefore misleading. Investigations and news accounts noted varying inspection dates across agencies rather than a single continuous absence of any state inspection since 2006.

claim: Virginia is "the No. 1 recipient of federal dollars."
rationale: The statement is too broad and misleading: which measure and year determine “No. 1 recipient” is unspecified. While Virginia ranks very high in federal contracting and often scores near the top for procurement dollars (especially Northern Virginia), it is not consistently the top recipient of total federal dollars overall — other large states often receive more in total federal spending or grants, and per‑capita rankings differ. Without a specific metric and timeframe the claim is incorrect as a blanket statement.

claim: "For perspective, Special Session costs you $50k, every single day. That’s roughly the average teacher’s salary in NC."
rationale: The statement bundles two claims that are either unsupported or misleading. Per‑day taxpayer costs for a “special session” vary widely by state, scope, and year and are not a fixed $50,000/day without a specific source; many official estimates show different figures or present one‑time and staffing costs rather than a simple daily price. North Carolina’s average teacher salary is nearer to the low-to-mid $50,000s in recent years, so calling $50k an exact match is imprecise.

claim: Wisconsin is "38th in the country in terms of proficiency standards" in student testing.
rationale: The claim gives no year, grade, subject, or source and there is no single, consistently used national ranking that universally places Wisconsin 38th on “proficiency standards.” State proficiency cut scores and rankings vary by assessment (state tests vs. NAEP), subject, and year, so the assertion as stated cannot be verified and is likely misleading. Without a cited study or context, the specific numeric rank should be treated as false.

claim: Says Tom Ford said about Melania Trump, "I have no interest in dressing a glorified escort who steals speeches and has bad taste in men."
rationale: There is no reliable contemporaneous record or credible news-source confirmation that Tom Ford uttered that exact line about Melania Trump. While some online outlets and social posts have circulated similar pejorative paraphrases regarding designers declining to dress Melania, the specific quoted sentence cannot be verified and appears to be a viral misattribution or embellishment.

claim: "Since Barack Obama became president of the United States, 95 percent of economic gains have been made by the richest 1 percent."
rationale: The statement is misleading and not universally true. The “95%” figure originated from analyses of a specific short recovery window (roughly 2009–2012) and referred to reported income gains concentrated at the very top, not a comprehensive, unambiguous measure of all economic gains over the entire period of Obama’s presidency; using different time spans or measures (wages, household income, wealth, stock market gains) yields very different distributions.

claim: Says he "never supported" federal health care individual mandate.
rationale: The claim as presented cannot be verified because it lacks a named individual, timeframe, or context. Different politicians have publicly both denied and later acknowledged support for federal individual mandates, so the blanket assertion cannot be checked as true. Without a specific subject and evidence, the statement is not verifiable and defaults to false per instructions to prefer FALSE when uncertain.

claim: "The Family Research Council, according to some government agencies, is a terrorist group."
rationale: No U.S. federal or state government agency has formally designated the Family Research Council (FRC) as a terrorist organization. The FRC has been labeled a hate group by the Southern Poverty Law Center, and it was the target of a 2012 shooting, but that is not the same as an official government terrorism designation.

claim: Says the word newspaper stands for "north, east, west, south, past and present event report."
rationale: This is a false etymology/backronym. The word 'newspaper' comes from 'news' (information about recent events) + 'paper' (the medium), not from initial letters standing for compass points or 'past and present event report.'

claim: Says President Barack Obama "came into office very concerned about" wiretappings but "then he became president of the United States, he got all the briefings … (and) he decided … the balance is probably pretty appropriately struck."
rationale: I cannot verify that President Obama or a named, reputable official actually said this exact sequence of lines; while officials and commentators have reported that Obama was initially concerned about surveillance and later accepted intelligence briefings, this specific quoted wording appears uncorroborated in my training knowledge. Without a clear, attributable source for the quotation, it should not be treated as a verified factual quote.

claim: Blames Mike McIntyre and Nancy Pelosi for the second straight year of no cost-of-living increases for Social Security beneficiaries.
rationale: Annual Social Security cost-of-living adjustments (COLAs) are determined automatically by the Social Security Administration based on the CPI-W inflation measure, not set by individual members of Congress. A zero COLA in consecutive years would reflect very low measured inflation, so blaming Mike McIntyre and Nancy Pelosi for a lack of increases is inaccurate and misleading.

claim: The U.S. Supreme Court decided in 1982 that non-citizen children must get free K-12 education.
rationale: In Plyler v. Doe (1982) the U.S. Supreme Court held that states may not constitutionally deny children of undocumented immigrants access to free public elementary and secondary education under the Equal Protection Clause. The decision requires public K–12 schools to admit and educate non-citizen children and struck down state laws that would bar or withhold funding for their schooling.

claim: "Al-Qaida operatives, have said, 'Hey, we want you to use this loophole (for purchasing guns despite being on a watch list) to attack and kill Americans.'"
rationale: There is no credible, verifiable evidence or reporting that al-Qaida operatives issued this specific quoted instruction about exploiting a gun-purchase 'loophole' while on a watch list. While extremist groups have broadly encouraged attacks in propaganda, the exact quoted claim appears to be unsubstantiated or misattributed in public records.
cited_knowledge: Review of public reporting and official statements about extremist propaganda, watchlist/NICS issues, and absence of a verified source for this exact quote.
safety_notes: Ambiguous wording and lack of source make misattribution possible; the claim could conflate general extremist exhortations with a specific, unverified quote.

claim: "The American economy is continuing its longest monthly streak of job growth in history, with 3.9 million jobs added since President Trump was elected."
rationale: The claim mixes measures and is misleading: while the U.S. experienced an extended streak of monthly job gains after the 2009 recession that continued into the Trump years, it was not uniquely the longest in all of history and the "3.9 million" figure depends on which series and end date you pick. BLS payroll and household surveys give different totals and independent fact-checkers have found the Trump-era totals and the "longest ever" wording to be inaccurate or unsupported without additional qualifiers.

claim: "Prescription drug companies are charging Americans prices that are on average 4x higher than what's charged in other countries."
rationale: U.S. prescription drug prices are generally substantially higher than in other high‑income countries, but multiple reputable analyses (RAND, OECD and health policy studies) typically find average markups closer to about 2–3 times rather than a uniform 4× multiple. Some individual drugs or categories can cost 4× or more in the U.S., but the blanket claim that Americans pay on average 4× higher across the board overstates typical findings.

claim: "Obama’s daughters caught on camera burning US flag at DC protest."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Malia or Sasha Obama were filmed burning a U.S. flag; reputable fact-checkers and news reports have traced the viral images and videos to other individuals and contexts, showing the claim is a misidentification. The allegation appears to be misinformation spread via social media rather than a verified event involving the Obama daughters.

claim: "Joe Biden just confirmed that he is running for president in 2020 and it has America applauding!"
rationale: Joe Biden announced his 2020 presidential campaign in April 2019, so he did not 'just confirm' a 2020 run. Additionally, the claim that 'it has America applauding' is a broad, unsubstantiated generalization—public reaction to his campaign was mixed, not uniformly celebratory.

claim: "They talk about this problem with binding arbitration. It doesn’t make a lot of sense to me to have somebody from Los Angeles fly into Zanesville and impose a wage settlement on you ... and then they’re on the plane back to Los Angeles."
rationale: The statement describes a real feature of binding arbitration: parties often use neutral arbitrators drawn from national rosters who may travel in from other cities and issue a binding decision. The speaker’s claim that such an outsider can impose a wage settlement and then leave is an accurate description of how binding arbitration can operate, though the judgment that it 'doesn’t make a lot of sense' is normative.

claim: "‘MAGA bomber’ identified as former CNN employee who donated to heavily to Hillary Clinton."
rationale: The person arrested in the 2018 pipe-bomb mailings was Cesar Sayoc, a documented Trump supporter; credible reporting and public records do not show he was a former CNN employee or a heavy donor to Hillary Clinton. The claim appears to be a social-media falsehood; available employment history and FEC contribution records do not support those assertions.

claim: "Pfizer vaccine now completely worthless in Israel as >80% of all COVID-19 patients were previously vaccinated."
rationale: The claim combines a misleading statistic with an absolute conclusion. Even if a large share of reported cases in Israel at certain times were among vaccinated people, that can reflect high vaccine coverage and waning immunity—not that the Pfizer vaccine is "completely worthless." Israeli data have shown reduced protection against infection over time and increased breakthrough infections, but vaccines have continued to substantially reduce risk of severe disease, hospitalization, and death, especially after booster doses.

claim: "Ultraviolet Radiation is administered into the body as a disinfectant to kill bacteria and viruses and this has been used for a while now."
rationale: Ultraviolet (UV) light is widely used to disinfect air, surfaces, and water, but it is not administered inside the body as a routine systemic disinfectant because UV damages living tissues. There are limited medical procedures involving UV-treated blood outside the body (e.g., extracorporeal photopheresis) and historical/alternative‑medicine uses of ultraviolet blood irradiation, but these are not the same as administering UV into the body as a general disinfectant and are not broadly used for treating infections.

claim: Says the WIC program was created by the Black Panthers to help feed single mothers and children in their communities.
rationale: The Special Supplemental Nutrition Program for Women, Infants, and Children (WIC) was created by the U.S. federal government and first authorized in 1972 as a public nutrition program; it was not founded by the Black Panther Party. The Black Panthers did operate community food programs (notably free breakfast programs) that raised awareness of child hunger and likely put pressure on policymakers, but they did not create or administer the WIC program.

claim: A Virginia principal "expelled two kids for wearing a crucifix around their necks  saying, ‘there is no place for religion at school.’"
rationale: There are no credible reports substantiating that a Virginia principal expelled two students for wearing crucifixes and said 'there is no place for religion at school.' Public-school students are generally allowed to wear passive religious symbols (like crosses) under U.S. First Amendment precedent, so an outright expulsion for that reason would be legally dubious and would have been widely reported; similar viral claims have repeatedly been debunked or mischaracterized.

claim: Alison Alter "has exploited a campaign finance loophole to obtain over $64,000 in public dollars to fund her campaign."
rationale: I cannot verify the specific allegation that Alison Alter exploited a campaign finance loophole to obtain over $64,000 in public dollars. The claim names a precise figure and wrongdoing but I found no corroborating, verifiable evidence in widely known public sources; public financing programs do distribute matching or public dollars legally, and misuse allegations require documentation from campaign finance filings or reputable investigations.

claim: "The same federal government that offers some money for a program is walking away from another health care program."
rationale: The statement is too vague to verify as a general fact because it does not identify which federal government, which programs, or the timeframe. While it is common for governments to fund some programs and cut others, the claim as written is unprovable and therefore cannot be confirmed.

claim: Says the California congressional district he represents "has a higher GDP than Russia."
rationale: Russia’s national GDP is on the order of trillions of US dollars, while even the wealthiest California congressional districts or metropolitan areas produce economic output measured in hundreds of billions at most. No credible economic estimates show a single U.S. House district exceeding Russia’s total GDP, so the claim is incorrect.

claim: Says Joe Biden "blackmailed Ukraine with a billion in tax dollars to drop an investigation into his son and Democrats want to impeach President Trump for simply asking if it was true?"
rationale: Although Joe Biden publicly threatened to withhold about $1 billion in U.S. loan guarantees to pressure Ukraine to fire prosecutor Viktor Shokin, independent reporting and international actors indicated Shokin was widely seen as corrupt and not actively investigating Burisma (where Hunter Biden was a board member). Multiple investigations have found no evidence Biden acted to protect his son, and the impeachment of President Trump centered on allegations of conditioning military aid and soliciting foreign interference for political benefit, not merely asking a question.

claim: Says Sen. Bill Nelson "has aligned himself with communists and dictators," "went to Venezuela to admire Chávez’s revolution" and "supports murderers."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Sen. Bill Nelson formally "aligned himself with communists and dictators," publicly went to Venezuela to praise Chávez’s revolution, or declared that he "supports murderers." Senators sometimes meet foreign leaders or participate in delegations, but Nelson’s public record and reporting do not show endorsements of Chávez’s regime or statements supporting murderers; these phrases resemble partisan attack rhetoric rather than documented facts.

claim: Says the U.S. gives Israel "$3 billion annually" in aid and zero to Detroit.
rationale: The U.S. does provide Israel roughly $3–3.8 billion per year in military assistance under the 2016 10‑year MOU, so the "$3 billion" figure is an approximation but close; however it is incorrect to say the U.S. gives "zero" to Detroit. Detroit and other U.S. cities receive federal funding through grants and programs (HUD, FEMA, Community Development Block Grants, and substantial COVID/American Rescue Plan allocations), so the statement that Detroit gets no federal aid is false.

claim: "Bill Nelson voted for higher taxes 150 times."
rationale: The claim is unsubstantiated and misleading: independent fact-checkers and roll-call analyses have not found a clear, verifiable tally showing Bill Nelson voted to raise taxes 150 times. Whether a vote 'raises taxes' depends on definitions (e.g., revenue measures, fee changes, budget reconciliations), and many cited votes do not directly increase taxes or are mischaracterized by political ads.

claim: Says the Obama administration spent taxpayer dollars on electric cars in Finland (and) windmills in China.
rationale: The claim is misleading. While some Obama-era loans and grants went to U.S. companies that had foreign subsidiaries or sourced components abroad, there is no clear evidence the administration directly funded the purchase of electric cars in Finland or systematically bought windmills made in China; most stimulus and DOE loan funds were directed to U.S.-based firms and domestic projects, though isolated cases involved foreign-made parts or factories.

claim: "In 2009, Mitch McConnell was the person that’s saying, 'Hey, we should get all the ethics information in before we do the hearings.' "
rationale: There is no public record or reliable news report documenting Mitch McConnell saying that exact line in 2009. While Senate leaders sometimes urged disclosure of ethics information around nominations, the precise quoted statement cannot be verified and appears to be a misattribution or paraphrase.

claim: "More black babies are aborted in NYC than born."
rationale: Public vital statistics from the New York City Department of Health and multiple fact-checks show that in recent years the number of live births to Black mothers in NYC exceeds the number of induced terminations recorded for Black women. The claim is vague about year and definitions (race of fetus vs mother, resident vs non‑resident), and when correctly measured it does not hold.

claim: Louisiana gets "not one single penny" from Gulf Coast offshore oil revenues.
rationale: The claim is false. Louisiana receives payments tied to Gulf offshore oil including federal revenue-sharing under the Gulf of Mexico Energy Security Act (GOMESA), state severance taxes and royalties on state-owned offshore production, and significant Deepwater Horizon settlement/RESTORE distributions. Therefore the state does receive substantial money related to Gulf offshore oil.

claim: The impeachment process against Donald Trump "provides fewer due process protections and fewer protections for minority rights than what we have seen in previous impeachment efforts."
rationale: The claim is a broad comparative assertion that lacks specified metrics and a clear reference point (which Trump impeachment and which protections). Impeachment procedures are set case-by-case by the House and Senate and have varied historically (e.g., witness rules, committee investigations, access to counsel), so it is not demonstrably true as a general statement that Trump’s proceedings uniformly provided fewer due-process or minority-rights protections than all prior impeachments.

claim: "I can send every qualified person to a four-year college in their state for $150 billion."
rationale: The claim is implausible as stated because it gives no timeframe or definition of who is “qualified,” and $150 billion is unlikely to cover sending every eligible person to a four‑year in‑state college on an ongoing basis. U.S. undergraduate enrollment and average in‑state tuition imply annual price tags on the order of tens to low hundreds of billions depending on scope (one cohort vs all current students) and do not include room, board, aid, or capital costs. Reasonable cost estimates for broad free‑college proposals vary widely and often exceed or recur beyond $150 billion.

claim: Says Nancy Pelosi passed a bill awarding a $9 billion contract to her husband’s company.
rationale: There is no evidence that Nancy Pelosi passed any bill that directly awarded a $9 billion contract to her husband’s company. Congressional legislation does not directly grant government contracts to specific private entities, and fact-checking organizations and public records show no such transaction or targeted award to Paul Pelosi’s business linked to legislation she sponsored or passed.

claim: "There are 100 members of the U.S. Senate. Fifty-seven of them, including Russ Feingold, are lawyers. There are zero manufacturers and one accountant."
rationale: While the U.S. Senate has 100 members, the specific occupational counts in this claim are incorrect or unsupported. Russ Feingold is a former senator (not currently serving) and though many senators are lawyers, exact tallies like “57 lawyers, 0 manufacturers, and 1 accountant” are not consistent with public biographical records and vary by time and classification.

claim: Says Connie Mack "is protecting Chevron oil from a multi-billion dollar lawsuit over pollution of rivers and rainforests."
rationale: There is no clear, credible public record showing that Connie Mack (the Florida politician) personally acted to protect Chevron from the multi‑billion‑dollar Ecuador pollution lawsuit. The Chevron v. Ecuador litigation and related allegations of corporate influence are well‑known, but accusations that Connie Mack protected Chevron appear to be political assertions without substantiating evidence linking him to blocking or quashing the suit.

claim: Says in Chicago, "we take more guns off the streets than New York or L.A."
rationale: The statement is misleading and not supported without qualification: public data and reporting practices vary by city and year, but historically NYPD and LAPD have reported as many or more gun recoveries than Chicago PD. Comparisons that claim Chicago takes more guns off the streets ignore differences in time period, agency jurisdiction, counting methods (seizures vs recoveries vs traced crime guns), and city population sizes.

claim: Says James Mattis said, "If you burn the American flag you’ll spend two years in the military. I promise you, you’ll be cured of the desire to burn a flag ever again."
rationale: There is no credible evidence or verified source that James Mattis ever said this; searches of his speeches, interviews, and reputable fact-checkers turn up no attribution. The claim also conflicts with U.S. legal protections for flag burning as expressive conduct and with how the military and courts operate, making the quote implausible as stated.

claim: Says Gov. Scott Walker’s proposed budget "would sell off Wisconsin’s state parks."
rationale: Governor Walker’s budget proposals cut DNR funding and at times sought to close parks, shift them to county control, or expand private management/fee-recovery, but they did not include an explicit program to sell off Wisconsin’s state parks outright. Reporting and budget summaries described closures, transfers, and privatization of services rather than direct sale of park lands.

claim: Says Mitt Romney flip-flopped on abortion.
rationale: Mitt Romney publicly expressed pro‑choice positions earlier in his political career (notably in the 1990s and as a Massachusetts politician) and later campaigned and governed with pro‑life positions during his presidential runs, and he has acknowledged his views evolved. That documented change in stated positions is commonly described as a flip‑flop.

claim: The debt limit deal "allows President Obama to borrow unlimited amounts of money."
rationale: Debt-limit agreements sometimes raise or temporarily suspend the statutory U.S. debt ceiling so the Treasury can issue additional debt up to a new limit or until the suspension expires, but they do not give the president unilateral or perpetual authority to borrow unlimited sums. Congress controls the statutory borrowing limit and the Treasury (not the president personally) issues debt within that authority.

claim: Says the estate tax is a threat to family farms.
rationale: As a general statement the claim is misleading: in the U.S. federal estate tax applies only above relatively high exemption thresholds and there are specific reliefs for farms (special‑use valuation, payment options, and other provisions) so most family farms do not owe the tax at death. That said, very large or highly appreciated farm estates or those in jurisdictions with lower state exemptions can still face estate tax liability.

claim: "It costs nearly five times as much in California to build and maintain a mile of road as it does in the rest of the nation."
rationale: California does have substantially higher road construction and maintenance costs than the national average, but reliable analyses and federal data do not support a near-fivefold difference. Most comparisons (depending on metric, year, and whether lane-miles or centerline miles are used) show California costs are higher by tens of percent to perhaps 2–3 times in some cases, not nearly 5x. The claim overstates the gap without specifying metrics, time period, or source.

claim: "Kelly Ayotte voted to give big oil more than $20 billion in tax breaks."
rationale: The claim is misleading. While Senator Kelly Ayotte did vote for some tax-extender measures that included fossil-fuel tax provisions, the assertion that she "voted to give big oil more than $20 billion" presents an inflated, context-free dollar figure not clearly tied to a single roll-call. Estimates of the cost of specific oil-and-gas provisions vary and are generally lower or spread across multiple years/measures, and Ayotte was not the decisive vote for a single $20+ billion package.

claim: "Today, the five largest financial institutions are 38 percent bigger than they were back in 2008, when they were too big to fail."
rationale: The claim is imprecise and cannot be verified as stated: it doesn’t specify which five institutions, which size metric (assets, market value, deposits), or the exact comparison date for “today.” Different datasets and definitions produce different percentage changes since 2008 (some measures show larger increases, others smaller), so the categorical 38% figure is unsubstantiated without clearer parameters.

claim: Says J. David Cox, "the boss" of the jail guards "who were supposed to keep" suspected sex trafficker Jeffrey Epstein alive, is also "friends with Bill and Hillary Clinton."
rationale: J. David Cox is the president of the American Federation of Government Employees (a union leader), not the supervisory 'boss' of the Metropolitan Correctional Center guards, and there is no credible public evidence that he is a personal friend of Bill and Hillary Clinton. Reporting shows union political activity and contacts with Democratic officials, but that is not the same as documented personal friendship with the Clintons.

claim: AIDS was transmitted to humans because "one guy" had sex with "a monkey" and then started "having sex with men."
rationale: Scientific evidence shows HIV resulted from multiple zoonotic transfers of simian immunodeficiency viruses (SIV) into humans—most plausibly via exposure to infected primate blood during hunting or butchering—not from a single person having sex with a monkey. The pandemic strain (HIV‑1 group M) emerged in central Africa in the early 20th century and later spread through human sexual networks, urbanization, and other transmission routes.

claim: Early morning election results from Michigan and Wisconsin show voter fraud.
rationale: There is no credible, verified evidence that 'early morning' election results in Michigan and Wisconsin demonstrate voter fraud. Official canvasses, audits, recounts, and court rulings in recent high-profile elections did not find widespread or outcome-changing fraud, and the late appearance of vote totals is commonly explained by normal processing of absentee and mail ballots.

claim: "The ‘tax plan’ rolled out by @realDonaldTrump would have cut his taxes by $30 million in 2005 (the only year we have returns for)."
rationale: Contemporary analyses by major news organizations applying Trump’s 2016 tax plan to the 2005 return he released estimated a tax reduction on that year on the order of about $30–$35 million, supporting the claim’s round figure. 2005 was the only full year of returns Trump made public at that time, so the parenthetical is also accurate.

claim: "I personally am pro-choice. I always have been. And I made no qualms about that when I was elected governor."
rationale: This statement is not verifiable as presented because it uses 'I' without identifying the speaker, the time, or the jurisdiction. Claims about a specific governor’s long‑standing personal stance and what they communicated at the time of election require checking that individual’s public record and campaign materials; absent that evidence, the assertion is unsubstantiated.

claim: "We have cut taxes more than 40 times in four years."
rationale: The claim is unverifiable as stated because it gives no actor, jurisdiction, or list of the alleged tax cuts. Politicians frequently aggregate many distinct measures (rate changes, credits, fee adjustments) to reach large counts, so without a specific, itemized list for a named government and four-year span this broad assertion is unsubstantiated.

claim: "Chris Christie has led New Jersey to a record-breaking 9 credit downgrades."
rationale: While New Jersey experienced multiple credit-rating downgrades during Chris Christie’s tenure, there is no credible evidence that he caused a “record-breaking 9” downgrades. Rating actions come from several agencies at different times, and counts attributing nine downgrades specifically to Christie are unsupported and conflates separate agencies and years.

claim: Says Ayn Rand said, "The question isn’t who is going to let me; it’s who is going to stop me."
rationale: This line is widely attributed to Ayn Rand, but there is no clear primary-source citation in her novels or essays confirming she actually wrote it. Because reliable sourcing is lacking and the quote appears largely on secondary websites, the attribution is questionable and should not be treated as established fact.

claim: "She’s voted for 60 tax increases, hurting the middle class and small businesses."
rationale: The claim is unverifiable as stated because it does not identify who “she” refers to and whether the count includes distinct bills, amendments, procedural votes, or budgetary provisions. Claims of a precise number of "tax increases" typically depend on a specific counting methodology and timeframe; without that context there is no reliable evidence to confirm 60 votes for tax hikes. Therefore the assertion as phrased is false/unsupported.

claim: A provision in the first bill passed by House Democrats would "allow the billions of dollars of aid we send to other countries to be used for abortions."
rationale: U.S. law (notably the Helms Amendment) has long restricted use of federal foreign assistance for abortions, and a provision in a House-passed bill would not by itself overturn those statutes without passage in the Senate and the president’s signature. Claims that a single House bill immediately 'allows the billions of dollars of aid' to be used for abortions misstate both the content and effect of typical provisions (which often seek policy changes or exceptions) and the limits of a bill that has only passed one chamber.

claim: In the United States, we’ve had "12 years in a row of wages declining."
rationale: This claim is not supported by standard US wage data. Commonly used series (nominal average hourly earnings from the BLS and median wage/household income data from the Census/BEA) do not show 12 consecutive years of declines; nominal wages have generally risen year-to-year and real/median measures have not fallen for a 12-year straight period nationally.

claim: That Donald Trump said in 1998 if he were to run for president he would run as a Republican because "They’re the dumbest group of voters in the country. They believe anything on Fox News. I could lie and they’d still eat it up. I bet my numbers would be terrific."
rationale: There is no reliable primary-source evidence that Trump said this exact quote in 1998; major fact-checkers and contemporaneous reporting do not document him saying those words and the line appears to be a circulating misattribution. While Trump has made disparaging comments about media and voters at various times, the specific phrasing and 1998 attribution cannot be substantiated.

claim: "We have an increase in murder within our cities, the biggest in 45 years."
rationale: The statement is too vague to verify and is likely incorrect as presented because it omits the country, which years are compared, and whether ‘increase’ refers to count or rate. In many places (for example the United States) homicides rose in 2020–2021 but did not exceed the large peaks of the early 1990s, so it is not supportable to claim a city-wide rise that is the 'biggest in 45 years' without specifying jurisdiction and timeframe.

claim: "Every time the weight of that vehicle is reduced by a hundred pounds, your chances of dying are going to go up by about 5 percent. Peel three hundred pounds off – you’re 15 percent more likely to die in that car."
rationale: This is an overgeneralized claim. Research does show vehicle mass influences crash outcomes and lighter vehicles can have higher occupant fatality risk, but the effect size varies by study, vehicle class, crash partner, speed, and safety features; it is not a universal fixed 5% increase in fatality risk per 100 pounds removed.

claim: President Joe Biden will "control health care costs by slapping a 95% tax on prescription drugs."
rationale: There is no Biden administration policy or enacted law that imposes a blanket 95% tax on prescription drugs. Biden's actions have emphasized Medicare drug price negotiation, inflation rebates, caps on certain out‑of‑pocket costs, and other measures to lower prices, not a 95% tax; some statutes include targeted penalties or excise taxes for noncompliance but nothing approaching a universal 95% levy.

claim: "5.7 million -- that’s how many illegal immigrants might have voted" in 2008.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that 5.7 million undocumented immigrants voted in 2008. Multiple academic reviews and official investigations have found only isolated instances of noncitizen voting (typically small numbers, often tens or at most low thousands across many years), and the mechanics of registration and voting make millions of illegal votes implausible.

claim: Says Virginia Del. Mark Cole "wants schools to check children’s genitals before using bathroom."
rationale: There is no reliable evidence that Delegate Mark Cole explicitly advocated that schools physically inspect children's genitals before bathroom use. He has supported policies requiring students to use facilities matching their biological sex, but reporting and available quotes do not document a call for genital checks; the claim appears to be a mischaracterization or hyperbolic paraphrase.

claim: Says Aaron Rodgers "is not the highest tax rate payer" in Wisconsin, it's "the single mom getting 24 grand in benefits with two kids who will lose 80 cents on the dollar if she goes and takes a job."
rationale: The statement is an unverified and misleading paraphrase: while benefit 'cliffs' can create high effective marginal tax rates for low‑income families, there is no evidence that a Wisconsin single mother receiving $24,000 in unspecified benefits universally faces an 80% marginal loss or is the person paying the highest tax rate. Wisconsin’s statutory income tax rates are far lower than 80%, and whether a claimant faces such an extreme effective rate depends on which specific benefits (federal, state, and local), phase‑outs, and taxes are counted. Without precise program-by-program accounting the 80% claim is not supported.

claim: "More people without health care since George Bush took office; more children in poverty since George Bush took office."
rationale: During George W. Bush’s presidency (2001–2009) the number of uninsured Americans rose and child poverty measures increased by most standard counts. Census and poverty analyses show higher counts or rates of uninsured people and elevated child poverty by the late 2000s compared with the start of his term, in part due to economic downturns.

claim: "There are more pain clinics in Broward County than there are McDonald's in Broward County."
rationale: There is no reliable evidence that pain clinics in Broward County outnumber McDonald’s restaurants. McDonald’s operates many dozens of outlets in large suburban counties like Broward, while reports of numerous “pain clinics” (including past pill-mill concerns) reflect a smaller, fluctuating number that has been reduced by enforcement. Without a current authoritative count showing more pain clinics than McDonald’s, the claim is unsupported.

claim: "The VA negotiates prescription drug prices. Medicare doesn't do that."
rationale: The VA does have statutory authority and a centralized system that lets it secure lower prescription prices through formulary and contracting tools. However the claim that “Medicare doesn't do that” is misleading: private Medicare Part D plans have long negotiated drug prices with manufacturers, and the federal government was historically barred from direct negotiation for Part D but the 2022 Inflation Reduction Act creates limited Medicare negotiation authority for certain high‑cost drugs starting in the mid‑2020s.

claim: HR 1 will allow members of Congress to draw a second salary "worth an estimated $600,000 per year!"
rationale: The claim is false. H.R. 1 (the For the People Act in recent Congresses) is legislation on voting, campaign finance, and ethics reform and contains no provision authorizing members of Congress to collect a separate $600,000-per-year salary. Congressional compensation is set by statute and any such large additional pay would be explicit in bill text and widely reported; the $600,000 figure appears to be a misrepresentation or fabrication circulated on social media.

claim: "You have 200,000 to 400,000 military veterans on the street in this country on any given day."
rationale: Official point‑in‑time counts in the United States show roughly 30,000–50,000 veterans experiencing homelessness on a single night, far below 200,000–400,000. Even annualized or cumulative estimates are not consistent with the claimed range, so the statement significantly overstates established counts.

claim: "During his 18-year Senate career, (Russ Feingold) supported judges who voted to deny your individual Second Amendment right. … (He) promises to protect those rights, but that's not what his record shows."
rationale: The claim is vague and unsubstantiated: it names no specific judges or rulings and presents a broad allegation about Feingold’s confirmations. While many lower-court decisions before the 2008 Supreme Court decision in D.C. v. Heller did not recognize an individual Second Amendment right, I find no clear, documented pattern that Feingold specifically and repeatedly “supported judges who voted to deny” an individual right. Without naming nominees and votes, the assertion cannot be verified as stated.

claim: Toledo Mayor "Mike Bell (once) lost his job as a firefighter because his city ran out of money."
rationale: There is no reliable evidence that Toledo Mayor Mike Bell once lost a firefighting job because his city ran out of money. Public biographical information about Mike Bell’s career does not document a termination for budgetary insolvency; the claim appears anecdotal and unsubstantiated.

claim: Orrin Hatch co-sponsored a 1993 health care bill that had an individual mandate.
rationale: There is no credible legislative record showing Orrin Hatch as a co-sponsor of a 1993 federal health-care bill that included an individual mandate. While proposals for individual mandates have appeared in various years and had some bipartisan support, fact‑checking and historical records do not substantiate the specific claim about Hatch co‑sponsoring such a 1993 mandate bill.

claim: "Bryce Reeves chaired a group bankrolled by a New York billionaire who fired hundreds of Virginia workers and sent their jobs to China."
rationale: Public reporting and available records do not support the specific claim that Virginia state senator Bryce Reeves chaired a group funded by a named New York billionaire who personally fired hundreds of Virginia workers and sent their jobs to China.
