While several million people saw individual, noncompliant plans cancelled when ACA standards took effect, independent analyses and CBO/CMS work did not support a clear, permanent figure of 'up to 20 million' Americans irreversibly losing plans they preferred; many cancellations were temporary, for short-term noncompliant policies, and administrative fixes allowed some renewals. The claim conflates different categories (individual vs. employer coverage), timeframes, and policy compliance issues to reach the large 20 million figure.

claim: "Under the Obama plan . . . all the health care in this country is eventually going to be run by the government."
rationale: The statement is false: the Affordable Care Act (the 'Obama plan') expanded regulation, subsidies, Medicaid, and created insurance marketplaces but did not convert all U.S. health care into government-run care. Private insurers, employer-sponsored coverage, and private providers remained central to the system after the law’s implementation.

claim: Dr. Anthony Fauci has not spoken or appeared publicly for several weeks.
rationale: This is a time-sensitive claim I cannot verify with my training cutoff; Dr. Anthony Fauci has been a frequent public commentator and guest in recent years, and a multi-week public silence by a figure of his prominence would normally be widely reported. Without current news or official sources confirming several weeks of no public appearances, the claim is likely false.

claim: Says Gov. Chris Christie’s "poll ratings have been going up."
rationale: The statement cannot be verified as presented because it lacks a timeframe and poll source; Chris Christie’s approval ratings have fluctuated over his career (for example they rose after Hurricane Sandy in 2012 and fell at other times). Without specifying which polls and what period, the blanket claim that his poll ratings “have been going up” is not supported. Therefore the claim as stated is unreliable.

claim: "The health care price tag for childhood obesity in Georgia is $2.4 billion annually and rising."
rationale: There is no widely cited, authoritative estimate that Georgia’s annual health-care cost for childhood obesity is exactly $2.4 billion. State-level and national estimates of obesity’s costs vary widely by year, age range, and whether they include only direct medical costs or broader economic impacts, and I could not confirm a consensus figure of $2.4 billion for childhood obesity in Georgia.

claim: A 50-50 public-private split for paying for a new Milwaukee Bucks arena would "be much better -- in terms of the portion of the public financing -- than most of the other arena projects done around the country."
rationale: Arena financing has varied widely across the country and time; while some projects relied on majority public financing, many recent arena deals have had a larger private share or roughly even splits. There is no clear evidence that a 50-50 split would be 'much better' than most other projects nationwide because the typical public share is not uniformly above 50%.

claim: Says Governor Cooper has vetoed "every single teacher pay raise we've ever passed."
rationale: The statement is an absolute claim that is not supported by the record. Governor Roy Cooper did veto several budget proposals and some pay-raise packages, but he did not veto every teacher pay raise the legislature passed; some raises were signed into law or enacted in budgets he approved or that became law without his veto. Public budget and news records show examples of teacher pay increases that were not vetoed by Cooper.

claim: "We spent $3-million of your money to study the DNA of bears."
rationale: The claim is vague and unverified: it gives no speaker, jurisdiction, time period, or citation to confirm that exactly $3 million of taxpayer money was spent specifically to study bear DNA. While governments and research agencies have funded genetics studies of bears, there is no clear public evidence tying a $3,000,000 taxpayer-funded line-item to that exact description. Without a specific source or context the statement cannot be substantiated and is treated as false.

claim: "Atlanta just lost 75% of its police force"
rationale: There are no credible reports or official statements indicating that the Atlanta Police Department suddenly lost 75% of its officers. Staffing changes and turnover have occurred over time, but a one-time loss of three-quarters of the force would have been widely reported by multiple reliable outlets and by city officials, which has not happened.

claim: "Victory! Republicans by 2 to 1 vote to endorse Mark Neumann on first ballot at GOP convention."
rationale: The claim asserts a specific 2-to-1 first-ballot endorsement but provides no date or location, and I have no verifiable record in my training data of a GOP convention where Republicans endorsed Mark Neumann by that exact margin on the first ballot. Without contextual details or corroborating sources this precise assertion cannot be confirmed and is treated as false.

claim: "An 8-year-old Ukrainian girl confronts a Russian soldier telling him to go back to his country."
rationale: There is no reliably verified evidence confirming that the specific footage shows an 8‑year‑old Ukrainian girl confronting a Russian soldier and telling him to go home. Many similar clips circulated during the conflict with misleading captions, and reputable fact‑checks require independent verification of age, location and participants, which is absent here.

claim: "Ten percent of violent deaths in the U.S. each year are due to strangulation."
rationale: Available mortality data and law-enforcement statistics show that the large majority of violent deaths in the U.S. are caused by firearms, with methods like strangulation/asphyxiation representing only a small fraction of homicides. While strangulation is an important and serious form of violence—particularly in intimate-partner contexts—it does not account for 10% of all violent deaths annually in the U.S.

claim: Says Quaden Bayles committed suicide.
rationale: There are no credible reports that Quaden Bayles committed suicide; mainstream news outlets and his documented public appearances after the 2020 viral bullying video show he remained alive and active in advocacy and media. The claim appears to be a rumor or misinformation rather than a verified fact.

claim: "National Guard doctors find hospitals empty of COVID patients."
rationale: The claim is an overbroad generalization. National Guard medical teams reported widely varying conditions: in some places and times they encountered underused facilities or empty wards, while in many other locations they found hospitals overwhelmed with COVID-19 patients. Without a specific time and place the blanket statement is misleading.

claim: Says "if current trends continue, by 2040, one out of three Texas workers will not have a high school diploma."
rationale: Available demographic and labor-force data show that high-school completion rates have been rising and the share of adults and workers without a high-school diploma has been falling; a projection that one-third of Texas workers would lack a diploma by 2040 contradicts those broad trends and typical official projections. Without a credible source showing a countervailing reversal, the specific 1-in-3 claim is not supported.

claim: Says when Rhode Island Lottery was proposed, "state residents were enticed to vote for it with the promise that the money would be used for education."
rationale: When Rhode Island’s state lottery was put to voters in the 1970s, supporters explicitly framed it as a revenue source for public purposes including education, and the referendum was promoted on that basis to win public approval. Historical accounts of the state lottery’s establishment show education funding was a central promise used to entice voters.

claim: The typical anglerfish is seven feet long.
rationale: Most anglerfish species are relatively small — typically a few centimeters to at most under a meter for large females, and males are often tiny parasitic dwarfs. A typical anglerfish is nowhere near seven feet long; reports of multi-foot specimens are rare exceptions rather than the norm.

claim: Says "New Jersey’s $1 billion horse racing industry … employs 13,000 individuals and ensures the preservation of 176,000 acres of horse farmland."
rationale: I could not corroborate the precise trio of figures from independent government or academic sources; similar numbers appear in industry promotional materials but are not verified by state agricultural or economic reports. The claim mixes an economic impact estimate with a jobs total and an acreage figure whose definition (‘ensures the preservation’ of 176,000 acres of ‘horse farmland’) is ambiguous and likely inflated or defined differently across sources.

claim: Says Dick Cheney "supported gay marriage sooner" than Hillary Clinton.
rationale: Hillary Clinton publicly endorsed same-sex marriage in March 2013. While Dick Cheney has expressed personal support for his daughter and favored gay rights in various ways, there is no clear public record showing Cheney formally endorsed marriage equality earlier than Clinton; many of his past comments were about civil unions or private support rather than an earlier public endorsement of marriage.

claim: "Lindsey Graham threatens to convert to Democrat if Republicans don’t Dump Trump."
rationale: There is no credible record of Senator Lindsey Graham publicly threatening to switch to the Democratic Party if Republicans do not abandon Donald Trump. Major news coverage and Graham's public statements show he has criticized Trump at times but has remained a Republican, and no reputable outlet has reported such a binding ultimatum. The claim appears to be a mischaracterization or unverified rumor.

claim: Says the case of a Texas judge who refused to perform heterosexual weddings exposes a double standard in the case against Kentucky clerk Kim Davis.
rationale: There is no well-documented instance of a Texas judge refusing to perform heterosexual weddings that was treated as a direct parallel to Kim Davis. Most reported refusals during the same period involved officials declining to issue or perform same-sex marriages after the Obergefell decision, not refusing opposite-sex ceremonies. Therefore the claim that such a Texas case exposes a double standard is unsupported by available reporting.

claim: "I've either balanced every budget or we turned back a surplus."
rationale: The statement is an absolute claim that cannot be verified as written because it lacks a named speaker, time period, and definitions of key terms. Public fiscal records for most governments show some years of deficits, so asserting that one person or administration "balanced every budget or turned back a surplus" is implausible without detailed evidence. Given the missing context and the sweeping nature of the claim, it is not supported.

claim: "The unemployment rate among (the) non-college-educated is well into the double digits in America. It's 4 percent or 5 percent for people who have college degrees."
rationale: Recent U.S. labor‑force data show that unemployment for workers without a college degree is generally in the single digits (often mid‑single digits), not "well into the double digits," while unemployment among those with a bachelor’s degree or higher has typically been around roughly 2–5% in recent years. The claim exaggerates the non‑college unemployment rate and omits timing and precise education categories.

claim: Ebola is "incredibly contagious," "very transmissible" and "easy to catch."
rationale: This is misleading: Ebola is not easily caught by casual airborne exposure like measles or influenza. Transmission requires direct contact with the blood or other bodily fluids of a symptomatic person (or contaminated objects), so its basic transmissibility (R0) is modest; however, without proper infection control it can spread readily in healthcare and funeral settings.

claim: "Studies have shown that voter fraud is non-existent in Texas."
rationale: The claim is false because multiple academic analyses, government reports, and prosecutions show that illegal voting in Texas is extremely rare but not zero. Documented investigations and isolated convictions demonstrate that voter fraud has occurred in the state, so the absolute statement that it is "non-existent" is unsupported.

claim: "The $5 billion website for Obamacare … never worked. Still doesn't work."
rationale: The claim is false because although HealthCare.gov had major technical failures at its October 2013 launch, those problems were largely fixed within weeks to months and the site subsequently processed millions of enrollments. The oft-cited "$5 billion" figure is exaggerated or conflates broader ACA implementation costs; it does not reflect that the website 'never worked' or that it still does not work.

claim: Says U.S. Rep. Sean Duffy is among seven "Tea Party freshmen" who "spent an average of $15,000 on cars for themselves."
rationale: I could not verify a reliable source showing Rep. Sean Duffy was specifically one of seven 'Tea Party freshmen' who collectively spent an average of $15,000 on cars for personal use. Campaign finance filings show some candidates purchased or leased vehicles for campaign or official travel, and coverage that aggregates such spending often conflates campaign vehicle purchases with personal purchases or omits context, making the precise claim unsupported as stated.

claim: "When the national debt reaches $15 trillion, it means that U.S. debt-to-GDP ratio will reach 99.7 percent of our debt and this is $47,900 for every living American."
rationale: Both parts of the claim are time-dependent and not universally true. Whether $15 trillion equals about 99.7% of GDP depends on the U.S. nominal GDP used (which has varied around $14–18 trillion in recent years), and the per‑person figure depends on the population base; simple division can produce numbers near $47,900 only for specific GDP and population estimates. Because the statement presents these numbers as fixed truths without specifying the date or data sources, it is misleading.

claim: Says Texas high school graduates must pass Algebra II to be eligible for automatic admission to state's public universities.
rationale: There is no single statewide rule that every Texas high school graduate must pass Algebra II to be eligible for automatic admission. Texas automatic-admission (top-percent) rules require completion of specified college-preparatory curricula, and many of those curricula include Algebra II, but graduation plans and exact automatic-admission course requirements vary and are set by law and by individual institutions. Thus Algebra II is often required in practice but not an absolute, standalone statewide prerequisite for automatic admission.

claim: The impeachment inquiry hearings "going on behind closed doors over which Congressman Schiff is presiding—they are consistent with the rules" of the U.S. House of Representatives.
rationale: House committees have longstanding authority under House rules to take depositions and conduct closed-door interviews, and impeachment inquiries have historically been initiated and run by committees without a prior full-House floor vote. The Intelligence Committee under Rep. Adam Schiff conducted closed-door depositions and the House later adopted a resolution formalizing procedures, so the practice was consistent with House rules and precedent even though it was politically contested.

claim: "Drunk" Nancy Pelosi "was removed from the House floor for cursing at Republicans."
rationale: There is no credible evidence or House record that Nancy Pelosi was intoxicated and removed from the House floor for cursing at Republicans. Viral clips making this claim have been debunked or shown to be misleading/miscontextualized, and major fact‑checkers and news outlets found no incident matching that description.

claim: "...Over 30 years, federal spending on education has grown by 375 percent, but test scores remain flat."
rationale: The statement is misleading and unsupported as written. Federal education spending in the U.S. has risen substantially in nominal terms over decades, but the magnitude depends on the 30‑year window and whether figures are inflation‑adjusted, and most K–12 spending comes from state and local governments rather than the federal government. Likewise, standardized test trends vary by subject, grade, and period: NAEP shows substantial gains in earlier decades with flatter or mixed results in more recent years, so the blanket claim that scores remain flat over a 30‑year span is not generally accurate without precise definitions.

claim: When President Donald Trump walked across Lafayette Square to a church, he held the Bible upside down.
rationale: Video and photographic evidence analyzed by multiple news organizations and fact-checkers show Trump held a closed Bible in front of him and did not intentionally display it upside down; a few still images and angles created the appearance that it might be inverted. Independent reviews concluded the claim that he held it upside down is a misinterpretation of the visuals.

claim: "Pads and tampons (are) still taxed when Viagra and Rogaine are not."
rationale: The claim is an overgeneralization. Sales-tax treatment of sanitary products, prescription drugs (like Viagra), and over‑the‑counter treatments (like Rogaine) varies by country and U.S. state — many jurisdictions have abolished the "tampon tax," prescription medicines are commonly exempt, while OTC products may or may not be taxed. Saying pads and tampons are still taxed when Viagra and Rogaine are not is inaccurate without a specific jurisdiction.

claim: "The nine-day deer hunt contributes more than $1.3 billion in revenue to the state of Wisconsin."
rationale: The commonly cited ~$1.3 billion figure refers to the overall economic impact or hunter spending associated with Wisconsin’s deer hunting season, not direct revenue flowing into the state government. Saying it 'contributes more than $1.3 billion in revenue to the state' conflates total economic activity with state tax or budgetary revenue, which is much smaller.

claim: "Eleven individuals who make over $30 million each got $22 million credit" from Wisconsin's manufacturing and agriculture tax credit.
rationale: I cannot find credible support for the precise claim that exactly eleven individuals each earning over $30 million received a $22 million credit from Wisconsin’s manufacturing and agriculture tax credit. Wisconsin’s Manufacturing & Agriculture Credit is claimed by businesses or pass‑through entities and flows to owners proportionally, so headlines that single out a small set of ultra‑wealthy individuals or attribute a single $22 million payment to each are likely a mischaracterization or conflation of aggregated credits. Without clear sourcing, the numbers and framing appear inaccurate.

claim: "There are 63 million abortions a year in this country."
rationale: The statement is implausible and unsupported: global estimates of induced abortions are on the order of ~70–75 million per year, so 63 million in a single country would be nearly the entire global total. National figures (for example, the United States) are orders of magnitude lower (hundreds of thousands per year), and even the largest countries do not currently report 63 million annual abortions.

claim: "COVID ends next Wednesday."
rationale: There is no factual basis to assert that COVID "ends" on a specific upcoming Wednesday. Infectious disease trajectories are unpredictable, variants and ongoing transmission make a fixed imminent end date implausible, and no major public health authority has announced a blanket end date.

claim: "Donald Trump is the first president in modern history (who) did not start a new war."
rationale: The claim is incorrect because several post–World War II U.S. presidents did not initiate new large-scale wars; for example, Gerald Ford (1974–1977) and Jimmy Carter (1977–1981) did not start new wars. While Trump did not launch a major new conventional war, he is not the first modern president with that record. The statement also rests on a vague definition of 'modern history' and 'start a new war.'

claim: "I said two years ago that the Fannie and Freddie thing was a very serious problem and we had to work on it."
rationale: The claim as presented is unverifiable: it gives no speaker, exact date, or source for the alleged remark. Without attribution and contemporaneous evidence (transcript, recording, or news report) that someone said those words two years earlier, there is no basis to confirm the statement.

claim: "In seven years that (nuclear) deal will have expired, and Iran is free to go ahead and create nuclear weapons."
rationale: This is inaccurate. The 2015 Iran nuclear deal (JCPOA) contains staggered expiration (‘sunset’) clauses for specific limits over different timeframes, not a single seven-year expiration, and Iran remains bound by the Non‑Proliferation Treaty and subject to IAEA safeguards. Even if some JCPOA limits lapse later, weaponization would violate international law and trigger sanctions and other responses, so Iran would not be simply "free" to build nuclear weapons without consequences.

claim: "Democrats oppose any effort to secure our border."
rationale: This is an overbroad absolute claim. While many Democrats oppose particular measures (for example a border wall or certain enforcement practices), Democratic leaders and members frequently support various border-security efforts such as funding for personnel, technology, ports of entry, and asylum system reforms. Positions differ by person and proposal rather than a blanket opposition to all security efforts.

claim: "The minimum number of infrastructure (needs) in Atlanta is $900 million."
rationale: The claim gives a specific minimum dollar figure without specifying scope, timeframe, or source. There is no single, universally accepted $900 million "minimum" for Atlanta's infrastructure needs—estimates vary widely by which systems, projects, and planning horizon are included—so the assertion as stated is unsupported.

claim: "Across the country, more than half of the U.S. attorney seats remain without a prosecutor chosen by Obama."
rationale: The statement is time‑ambiguous and misleading: there are 93 U.S. attorney offices and while many were temporarily filled by holdovers or interim officials early in Obama's term, presidents nominate and gradually fill these posts and Obama ultimately appointed a majority of U.S. attorneys during his presidency. Without a specific date the blanket claim that "more than half" remained without an Obama‑chosen prosecutor is not verifiable and is likely false as a general assertion.

claim: "Missouri has one of the highest rates of uninsured children in the country."
rationale: Recent national survey data (ACS/Census and child-health metrics) do not show Missouri among the states with the highest child uninsured rates; states such as Texas, Oklahoma, and Florida have consistently had substantially higher rates. Missouri’s child uninsured rate in recent years has been near or below the national median rather than at the top of the list.

claim: The FEMA health care workers replacing the noncompliant nurses and doctors are NOT required to get vaccinated via the CDC."
rationale: The claim is misleading: the CDC issues public-health guidance but does not itself 'require' individual vaccinations. Whether FEMA health‑care workers must be vaccinated depends on employer and federal policies (and on whether they are federal employees, detailees, or contractors) rather than a CDC mandate. At times during COVID, federal vaccine requirements applied to many federal workers and contractors, and agencies could impose vaccination conditions for deployed personnel.

claim: Says Tom Barrett "has directed that tens of millions of City of Milwaukee tax dollars be used for the construction of a downtown trolley at the expense of: health and public safety; repair and replacement of public infrastructure; public education; and, job creation and economic development."
rationale: This claim misstates and overattributes budget decisions. While Mayor Tom Barrett supported the Milwaukee downtown streetcar (The Hop) and the city did commit local funds (including TIF/parking and other local sources), the project was funded by a mix of federal, state, and local sources and required Common Council approvals — Barrett did not unilaterally "direct" tens of millions of city tax dollars. There is no clear evidence that those local contributions were explicitly taken out of budgets for health/public safety, public education, and other listed priorities as a direct one-to-one diversion.

claim: Mercedes-Benz USA  moving its headquarters to Atlanta will create at least 800 jobs.
rationale: When Mercedes‑Benz announced its U.S. headquarters move to the Atlanta area in 2015, company and state officials stated the project would create roughly 800 jobs as part of the relocation and incentive agreement. The 800‑job figure was the number reported in the company’s press release and by state economic development officials at the time.

claim: "Our minority graduation rate went from levels below Milwaukee and Madison, to above 80%" when I was Beloit school superintendent.
rationale: I cannot verify the specific claim with available information: it names a rise in Beloit’s minority graduation rate from below Milwaukee and Madison to above 80% during an unnamed superintendent’s tenure but gives no dates or sources. Without year-by-year cohort graduation data for Beloit, Milwaukee, and Madison and a clear definition of “minority,” the claim is unverified and thus judged false in this fact-check context.

claim: Oregon Health Plan rations "covered procedures under certain circumstances"
rationale: Oregon Health Plan (OHP) applies coverage policies, medical-necessity rules, prior authorization requirements, and historically a prioritized services list to determine which procedures it will pay for, and can limit or deny coverage in specific circumstances. Those policy mechanisms effectively result in rationing of covered procedures under defined conditions.

claim: "By any measure, New Jersey has one of the most segregated school systems in the country."
rationale: The statement is overly broad. New Jersey does rank near the top nationally on several measures of school segregation (particularly racial isolation and concentrated poverty in some recent studies), but rankings vary by metric, subgroup, and year, so it is inaccurate to claim it is one of the most segregated "by any measure."

claim: "Biden concedes 6 million votes."
rationale: The statement is false as written: there is no credible record of President Joe Biden 'conceding' 6 million votes. In U.S. political usage, 'concede' means the losing candidate acknowledges defeat; Biden did not concede the 2020 election and did not announce conceding any number of votes. No reliable reporting supports this claim.

claim: Georgia ranks 49th for women serving in elected state and federal offices.
rationale: The claim is presented without a year or source and therefore is not supported as stated. Rankings for women in elected state and federal offices vary by dataset and year (e.g., CAWP state rankings, congressional delegation counts, statewide offices), and commonly cited measures do not consistently place Georgia as 49th in recent tallies. Without a specified timeframe and metric, the absolute claim that "Georgia ranks 49th" is misleading.

claim: Newt Gingrich has been a proponent of selecting a president by popular vote instead of the Electoral College.
rationale: There is not a clear record of Newt Gingrich being a sustained proponent of replacing the Electoral College with a direct national popular vote; he has more often defended the Electoral College and aligned with Republican positions supporting it. While he has made occasional critical or nuanced comments about the system, those do not amount to a consistent, public advocacy for abolishing the Electoral College in favor of a pure popular vote.
cited_knowledge: General knowledge of Gingrich's public statements and Republican policy positions, and lack of a well-known, sustained campaign by Gingrich to replace the Electoral College with a national popular vote.
safety_notes: Ambiguity: Gingrich may have made isolated remarks at times that could be interpreted as sympathetic to reform; specific quotes or dates would be needed to confirm any single-instance advocacy.

claim: Says Amber Alerts are issued for white kids "but not Black kids in Milwaukee."
rationale: Amber Alert systems use standardized criteria (such as age, suspected abduction, imminent danger, and sufficient identifying information) that do not include race, and issuing an alert depends on meeting those criteria rather than the victim’s race. While there have been documented concerns and studies about racial disparities in media coverage and in some missing-person responses, the categorical claim that alerts are issued for white children but not for Black children in Milwaukee is an unsupported overgeneralization of policy and practice.

claim: "Coca-Cola has lost $4 bil in market value as people are boycotting Coke for their ‘try to be less White’ statement."
rationale: While news reports noted Coca‑Cola’s market capitalization dropped by roughly $3–4 billion on a trading day after the internal DEI phrase 'try to be less white' became public, there is no clear evidence tying that move solely to a consumer boycott. Stock‑price changes reflect many factors (broader market moves, investor reaction, trading flows) and attributing the entire decline to boycotting is unproven and misleading.

claim: "There's not a major bill I know with Hillary's name on it."
rationale: There is no widely recognized major federal law formally named for Hillary Clinton. While she was associated with the 1990s reform effort nicknamed "Hillarycare" and has sponsored/co-sponsored legislation as senator, there is no major enacted bill commonly titled with her name.

claim: The United States "is the only major country that taxes its own exports."
rationale: The U.S. federal government is constitutionally barred from levying taxes on exports and in practice the United States does not impose general export taxes. Many other major countries do levy export duties or surcharges on certain commodities (for example Argentina, India, Russia, Indonesia and Brazil), so the statement is incorrect.

claim: The president's health care proposals will cause "most Americans to have their premiums increased, not decreased, and hundreds of millions of people lose their current insurance coverage."
rationale: The claim overstates likely effects: nonpartisan analyses of major U.S. health-care proposals (e.g., CBO, KFF) typically project coverage losses in the tens of millions under repeal scenarios, not "hundreds of millions," and premium impacts are heterogeneous — some groups could see increases while others see decreases. Without naming a specific president's proposal and timeframe, the broad assertion that "most Americans" would pay higher premiums and that hundreds of millions would lose coverage is inconsistent with established estimates.

claim: "The vast majority of our public school students are receiving less state support than their private voucher peers."
rationale: The claim is unsubstantiated as stated: in most jurisdictions public per-pupil funding (counting state, local, and federal contributions) typically equals or exceeds common voucher amounts, which often cover only part of private tuition. While some voucher programs or specific students may receive payments that approach or exceed local public per-student spending, that is not the general, nationwide pattern and depends heavily on state, district, and program details.

claim: Georgia has saved $20 million through changes in criminal sentencing.
rationale: The claim is ambiguous and I cannot confirm a reliable, specific source that Georgia (state or country) definitively 'saved $20 million' solely through changes in criminal sentencing. While U.S. states including Georgia have reported cost reductions tied to sentencing reforms, reported savings figures vary by study and timeframe and are often contested. Without a precise jurisdiction, timeframe, and accounting method, the specific $20 million claim cannot be validated.

claim: "Babysitter on crystal meth eats 3-month-old baby."
rationale: There is no credible evidence or reporting from reliable news organizations that a babysitter on crystal meth ate a 3-month-old baby; the story matches patterns of sensational viral hoaxes. Such an extreme crime would have generated broad, verifiable coverage and official records, which are absent.

claim: An anonymous e-mail says that Hillary Clinton advocates communism.
rationale: It is plausible and well-documented that anonymous chain e-mails and online messages have circulated alleging that Hillary Clinton advocates communism. The claim only asserts that such an anonymous e-mail exists (not that the content is true), which is consistent with known patterns of political misinformation distributed by anonymous sources.

claim: "Sen. Obama's chair in New Hampshire is a lobbyist. He lobbies for the drug companies."
rationale: The claim is vague about who 'Sen. Obama's chair in New Hampshire' refers to and there is no reliable reporting identifying any New Hampshire campaign chair for Obama as a pharmaceutical lobbyist. Major news coverage and campaign disclosure records from Obama's Senate and presidential campaigns do not support the specific allegation that his NH chair lobbied for drug companies.

claim: Says only about 250 Texans have been killed in action since 9/11.
rationale: Department of Defense casualty tallies and multiple state-by-state lists of service members killed in the post‑9/11 wars show that the number of Texans killed in action is far higher than 250; Texas has consistently been among the states with the largest numbers of combat fatalities. The claim that only about 250 Texans have been killed since 9/11 contradicts those public casualty records and memorial lists.

claim: Says professional football coach Rex Ryan "won championships in New York. The AFC, I think, twice."
rationale: Rex Ryan’s New York Jets reached the AFC Championship Game twice (2009 and 2010 seasons) but lost both games; he did not win the AFC Championship in New York twice. Saying he "won championships in New York — the AFC, I think, twice" incorrectly asserts conference championships rather than appearances.

claim: Says the CBO said "it's not that people are getting pushed off a plan; it's that people will choose not to buy something they don't like or want."
rationale: There is no clear record of the Congressional Budget Office using that exact informal phrasing. While CBO analyses do distinguish between people losing coverage involuntarily and people choosing not to buy insurance under different policy scenarios, the quoted sentence appears to be a paraphrase or summary rather than a documented verbatim CBO statement.

claim: "The number of uninsured people in Massachusetts is about the same as it was when the mandates were passed in 2006."
rationale: Massachusetts’ 2006 health reform substantially reduced the uninsured population; uninsured rates dropped markedly after the mandates and have remained far lower than pre-reform levels. Current counts and rates of uninsured people in the state are not “about the same” as in 2006 but are materially lower.

claim: Photos show cemeteries and war memorials damaged during George Floyd demonstrations.
rationale: The blanket claim is misleading: although some war-related statues and memorials were defaced or removed amid the George Floyd protests, many widely shared photos purportedly showing cemeteries or war memorials damaged were misattributed or came from other times and places. Major fact-checkers reviewed numerous viral images and found several were reused from earlier incidents or different locations rather than showing damage that occurred during those demonstrations.

claim: "President Trump marshalled the full resources of our federal government from the outset. He directed us to forge a seamless partnership with governors across America in both political parties."
rationale: The claim overstates the federal response and glosses over widely documented problems and disputes. Federal resources were not fully mobilized immediately (use of the Defense Production Act and large-scale federal distribution were delayed), and there were numerous public conflicts between the Trump administration and governors of both parties over testing, supplies, and guidance rather than a uniformly "seamless partnership."

claim: "Why should you get a break for racehorses and not get a break for child care?"
rationale: The statement is a rhetorical claim implying governments universally give breaks to racehorses but not to child care; this is misleading. In reality, policies vary by jurisdiction—many governments provide tax credits, subsidies or support for child care, while some also give favorable tax treatment or subsidies to the horse-racing industry.

claim: The Biden administration inherited gains of "50,000 jobs a month. We're now finally back to 500,000 jobs a month. We inherited a country where 4,000 people a day were dying from Covid. That's now down 75%."
rationale: The statement bundles several time-sensitive claims that are inaccurate or misleading. Monthly payroll gains at the start of the Biden term were not simply '50,000 jobs a month' — job growth figures varied widely and earlier recovery months showed larger gains — and while some months in 2021 did see ~500,000+ jobs, the monthly average did not consistently match that single figure. Likewise, daily COVID deaths around the January 2021 peak were roughly in the low thousands, but the claim of a uniform 75% reduction depends on the specific dates used and ignores subsequent waves that changed the trajectory.

claim: "Whole of Italy goes into quarantine."
rationale: In March 2020 the Italian government issued a nationwide decree (announced March 9) imposing strict movement restrictions and closures to curb COVID-19 transmission, effectively placing the entire country under quarantine/lockdown. While there were exemptions and evolving rules, the action was widely described and implemented as a nationwide quarantine.

claim: "Julia Roberts claims ‘Michelle Obama isn’t fit to clean Melania’s toilet’ "
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Julia Roberts ever made this remark; the alleged quote has circulated on social media and fringe sites but was not reported by reputable news outlets or confirmed by Roberts' representatives. The phrasing matches a pattern of fabricated celebrity quotes used to inflame partisan sentiment. Given the absence of reliable sourcing, the claim is false.

claim: "Greg Casar passed paid sick leave."
rationale: As an Austin City Council member Greg Casar authored and led the effort for Austin’s paid sick leave ordinance, which the council passed in 2018; he has also continued to champion paid-sick-leave proposals at the federal level. The claim is true in the sense that he was the sponsor and helped get a municipal paid sick leave law passed while on the council.

claim: To abide by Environmental Protection Agency rules when mining or drilling you have "to take caution not to disturb bodies of water barely bigger than a puddle."
rationale: This claim is misleading. The EPA (with the Army Corps) enforces the Clean Water Act over “waters of the United States,” which can include some very small streams and wetlands if they are connected or have a significant nexus to navigable waters, but it does not categorically forbid disturbing every tiny water feature or 'puddle.' Jurisdiction is determined case-by-case and has been narrowed and clarified by court decisions and changing agency rules.

claim: Says Keanu Reeves gave a speech that began, "I cannot be part of a world where men dress their wives as prostitutes by showing everything that should be cherished ..."
rationale: There is no reliable record — video, transcript, or reputable news coverage — of Keanu Reeves giving a speech that begins with that line. The wording appears in viral posts and quote compilations but has been widely circulated without verifiable sourcing and is consistent with common misattributions of provocative quotes to celebrities.

claim: President Barack Obama’s latest executive order "mandates the apprehension and detention of Americans who merely show signs of ‘respiratory illness.’ "
rationale: There is no known Obama executive order that orders blanket apprehension and detention of Americans merely for showing signs of a respiratory illness. Federal public-health quarantine authority is limited to specific contagious diseases, governed by statutes and CDC regulations with legal and due-process checks, and fact-checkers have repeatedly debunked viral claims that Obama issued such a sweeping detention order.

claim:
Says U.S. Sen Sherrod Brown "promised that the first stimulus bill would fund the
Brent Spence Bridge."
rationale: There is no clear public record that Sen. Sherrod Brown explicitly 'promised' the very first COVID stimulus bill would fund the Brent Spence Bridge. While Brown has advocated for federal support for the Brent Spence Bridge and later infrastructure packages included bridge funding discussions, stimulus laws early in the pandemic (e.g., CARES Act) were not structured to guarantee specific local bridge projects. The statement appears to conflate advocacy with a binding promise tied to the first stimulus bill.

claim: Under a public health care option, 120 million Americans will "lose what they now get from private companies and be forced onto the government-run rolls as businesses decide it is more cost-effective for them to drop coverage."
rationale: The claim presents a specific, certain outcome (120 million losing private coverage and being forced onto government rolls) that is speculative and unsupported as a general rule. Empirical evidence and official analyses of public-option proposals show a range of possible effects (some crowd-out in certain designs), but not a deterministic mass shift of that magnitude; employer incentives, legal and contractual factors, and policy design strongly affect results.

claim: "Mass media destroyed! Blackout for mass arrests event!"
rationale: The statement claims a coordinated destruction of mass media and a blackout to enable mass arrests, but there is no credible evidence or independent reporting of any such widespread event. Incidents of that magnitude would generate verifiable coverage from multiple reputable outlets and official sources, which are absent; the language resembles sensational or misleading rhetoric.

claim: Says a picture he posted on Facebook of a man posing in front of five decapitated human heads is "one of the subhuman mongrels our president set free."
rationale: This claim cannot be verified as stated: it names neither the poster nor provides a date, link, or corroborating reporting for such an inflammatory Facebook post. High‑profile posts with violent imagery and explicit dehumanizing language are typically documented by reliable media; absent such evidence, the allegation is unsubstantiated.

claim: The Republican election platform "was actually written with the help of a former lobbyist for AIG and a former lobbyist for Exxon-Mobil."
rationale: The statement is ambiguous and presented as an absolute claim about the entire Republican platform. While news reports from past cycles have documented that former industry lobbyists (including those formerly affiliated with AIG and ExxonMobil) helped draft or suggested language for specific planks, that is not the same as the entire platform 'being written' by them. The claim overstates and generalizes the documented, limited involvement of such lobbyists.

claim: "Jeff Greene can buy anything" ...  he owns two mansions.
rationale: The claim is a hyperbole: owning two mansions indicates substantial wealth but does not mean a person can literally buy anything. Purchasing power is limited by finite assets, liquidity, legal/regulatory restrictions, and availability of goods or services. There is no evidence that Jeff Greene has limitless resources enabling him to buy anything imaginable.

claim: Says Hillary Clinton sold 20 percent of America’s uranium to Russia and then "the Russian government gave $145 million to the Clinton Foundation." Former FBI Director and special counsel Robert Mueller "delivered it."
rationale: The claim mixes several inaccuracies. The 2010 Uranium One transaction transferred control of a portion of U.S. uranium production capacity through a corporate sale reviewed by the multi-agency CFIUS, not a unilateral sale of '20 percent of America’s uranium' by Hillary Clinton; she did not personally approve or receive proceeds. Independent fact-checking and reporting show the Clinton Foundation did not receive $145 million from the Russian government (donations from Russian-linked sources were far smaller and mostly disclosed), and there is no evidence that Robert Mueller 'delivered' any funds.

claim: The ACLU didn't call for an investigation (of the Newark police department), they called for an immediate federal monitor.
rationale: Public statements by the ACLU (and ACLU of New Jersey) around reports of misconduct at the Newark Police Department have typically called for a Department of Justice pattern-or-practice investigation and for immediate federal oversight or a monitor; it is unlikely they categorically refused an investigation while only asking for a monitor. In other words, the organization has commonly sought both a formal federal investigation and federal monitoring/oversight rather than exclusively one or the other.

claim: Says "Cost of Mueller’s investigation: $3,200,000; Benghazi "investigation": $7,000,000; Trump’s golfing trips: $83,000,000; New debt from Republican tax bill: $1,500,000,000,000."
rationale: The claim mixes accurate and inaccurate or misleading figures. The Mueller probe cost was reported at roughly $32 million, not $3.2 million; the $1.5 trillion figure for the Republican tax bill roughly matches CBO/JCT 10-year deficit estimates; the Benghazi and Trump-golfing costs are highly dependent on which investigations, agencies, time periods, and accounting methods are used and cannot be stated definitively as those single amounts.

claim: Quotes Winston Churchill as saying "Diplomacy is the art of telling people to go to hell in such a way that they ask for directions."
rationale: This pithy line is frequently attributed to Winston Churchill but quotation research finds no verifiable primary source of him saying or writing it. The phrase appears in later compilations and popular usage without contemporary evidence linking it to Churchill, so the attribution is likely incorrect.

claim: Bath and Body Works products are not recommended during pregnancy because they are suspected of "damaging fertility or the unborn child."
rationale: There is no authoritative public health guidance or regulatory classification that singles out Bath & Body Works products as suspected reproductive toxicants that should be avoided in pregnancy. While some individual cosmetic ingredients (for example certain retinoids, high-dose salicylic acid, or some fragrance-associated chemicals like some phthalates) have been flagged for caution in pregnancy, Bath & Body Works products are not broadly labeled or recommended against by major health agencies for 'damaging fertility or the unborn child.'

claim: Old photograph shows a group of women in KKK attire holding a sign that reads "Women of the Democrat Party."
rationale: The widely circulated photo has been debunked: reverse-image searches and fact-checkers trace the picture to historical Ku Klux Klan parades or related images, but the banner reading 'Women of the Democrat Party' is a later miscaption or digital alteration rather than the original text. Original photographs show Klan women or different banners, not an explicit Democratic Party sign.

claim: "In this country, we have a 25 percent dropout rate."
rationale: The statement is unverifiable as written because it does not name which country, which education level, what definition of 'dropout rate' is used, or which year. Dropout rates vary widely across countries and by definition, so the blanket claim cannot be treated as a factual statement without supporting data.

claim: The coronavirus "was constructed in the Wuhan Institute of Virology."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that SARS-CoV-2 was engineered or 'constructed' at the Wuhan Institute of Virology. Published genomic analyses and statements from major scientific bodies find features consistent with natural evolution, and investigations and intelligence reviews have not produced proof of deliberate construction at that lab.

claim: Says many public-employee unions falsely told their Wisconsin members his budget-repair bill sought 12 percent to 13 percent of their incomes for health insurance premiums.
rationale: There is not clear evidence that many public-employee unions uniformly and falsely told members the bill would require 12–13% of their incomes specifically for health insurance. Wisconsin's 2011 budget-repair law required public employees to make pension contributions and to pay a share of insurance premiums, but the exact percent of income varied by plan and the law did not uniformly impose a 12–13%-of-income health-premium requirement. Some union communications did cite high combined contribution figures or worst-case examples, but characterizing a widespread, categorical falsehood across many unions is not clearly supported.

claim: "In Minnesota, well over 6,200 election-day registrations from 2008 proved fraudulent."
rationale: Multiple official reviews and contemporary news fact-checks found no evidence that 'well over 6,200' 2008 same-day registrations in Minnesota were proven fraudulent. While thousands of voters used same-day registration that year, investigations and the Minnesota Secretary of State reported only a small number of isolated fraudulent cases rather than thousands.

claim: Says Israel Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu "didn't change his position" on a two-state solution.
rationale: Netanyahu has made public statements both endorsing a conditional two-state framework (notably his 2009 Bar-Ilan speech) and later rejecting a fully sovereign Palestinian state or insisting on heavy conditions; describing him as having "not changed his position" is misleading because his rhetoric and policy positions have shifted over time and depend on how "two-state" and its conditions are defined. Multiple public statements and policy proposals show variation rather than an unchanging stance.

claim: "Barack Obama’s real father is Communist Party propagandist Frank Marshall Davis."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Frank Marshall Davis was Barack Obama’s biological father. Obama’s father is documented as Barack Obama Sr., a Kenyan man, in Obama’s memoirs, public records, and contemporary accounts; the claim that Davis was his real father is a long-debunked conspiracy theory.

claim: Says Joe Biden "will destroy your protections for pre-existing conditions."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Joe Biden proposed or promised to ‘destroy’ protections for pre-existing conditions; throughout his campaign and presidency he has repeatedly stated support for preserving and strengthening the Affordable Care Act’s protections. Claims that he will remove those protections are political attacks or misrepresentations rather than descriptions of his policy positions or record.

claim: Says when Republicans took over the state legislature in 2010, New Hampshire’s tax rate for employers was 50th in the nation, and unemployment had more than doubled under Democrats.
rationale: The statement bundles two contested assertions that lack clear supporting evidence: New Hampshire being ranked 50th in 'tax rate for employers' in 2010 depends entirely on which tax and which ranking is used and is not a well-established fact, and the increase in unemployment in 2008–2010 occurred during the national Great Recession and cannot straightforwardly be attributed solely to Democrats in state government. Without a specific tax measure, year, and clear causal attribution, the claim is misleading.

claim: "Tell me what Madeleine Albright’s position was on the War on Iraq. I wouldn’t be surprised if she supported it."
rationale: Madeleine Albright publicly expressed support for the 2003 U.S. invasion of Iraq and for removing Saddam Hussein. She spoke and wrote in favor of action and did not join the major public opposition to the war, though later comments and analyses occasionally noted reservations about the post-invasion planning and consequences.

claim: Decriminalizing marijuana "will save the state anywhere from $4 (million) to $11 million dollars."
rationale: The claim is too specific without specifying which state, what timeframe, or which costs are counted. Estimates of savings from decriminalizing or legalizing marijuana vary widely by jurisdiction and methodology; some analyses report savings in the low millions for particular states and periods, while others project much larger or negligible net effects. As a blanket statement that decriminalization "will save the state anywhere from $4 million to $11 million" it is unsupported and misleading.

claim: "I'm probably one of the four or five best-known Americans in the world."
rationale: The claim is subjective and unverifiable as stated: it names neither the speaker nor provides evidence. Ranking someone among the "four or five best-known Americans in the world" would require contemporaneous, global recognition data across populations, which is not provided and unlikely to be demonstrably true.

claim: Ed Gillespie’s "firm even lobbied for five foreign governments, including a dictator now awaiting trial for war crimes."
rationale: Publicly available lobbying disclosures and reporting on Ed Gillespie’s post-White House firm document some corporate and foreign clients but do not substantiate the specific claim that his firm lobbied for five foreign governments including a dictator later awaiting trial for war crimes. The allegation is vague about timing and the dictator’s identity and appears unsubstantiated by the record of registered lobbying clients.

claim: Says series of 11 photos are "from the 1918 flu pandemic."
rationale: I cannot verify that an unspecified series of 11 photos are from the 1918 influenza pandemic without provenance, original metadata, or archival sourcing. Many images circulated online are misattributed or taken in different eras or contexts, so claiming they are definitively from 1918 is not supportable based on the claim as given.

claim: Opposition to having a fully elected Chicago Board of Education is in the "super minority."
rationale: The assertion that opposition is in a “super minority” cannot be substantiated without a specific poll or timeframe; available reporting and polls about a fully elected Chicago Board of Education have shown varying levels of support and opposition, often with a clear plurality or majority favoring elections but not with opposition reduced to a tiny "super minority." Because public opinion has fluctuated and depends on timing and question wording, the blanket claim is unsupported.

claim: In the 100 days since its passage, the economic stimulus has "saved or created nearly 150,000 jobs."
rationale: This wording matches an early administration claim about the 2009 stimulus (ARRA) that cited state reports and internal estimates of jobs “saved or created” in the first 100 days. Independent economists and fact-checkers noted those figures were short-term estimates based on self-reports and modeling, not directly verifiable counts, so the claim is misleading as a definitive fact. Without clearer attribution and methodology, the precise figure cannot be taken as an established fact.

claim: Says she "wiped out" the state Agriculture Department’s inspections of eggs at retail sites like grocery stores.
rationale: The claim lacks identifying details and no corroborating evidence is provided that a named official completely eliminated state Agriculture Department inspections of retail eggs. Most states have statutory or regulatory inspection responsibilities (and federal standards) that cannot be entirely removed by a single person without formal rulemaking or legislation; at most an official could reduce or reallocate inspections. Given the missing context and usual legal constraints, the absolute phrasing “wiped out” is not supported.

claim: Says CNN President Jeff Zucker ordered employees to downplay Bill Clinton’s relationship with Jeffrey Epstein and make it look like Epstein was "Trump’s partner in all of this."
rationale: There is no credible, verifiable evidence or published internal CNN documentation showing Jeff Zucker instructed staff to downplay Bill Clinton’s links to Jeffrey Epstein or to portray Epstein as primarily associated with Trump. CNN publicly reported on Epstein’s connections to multiple prominent figures, and the specific quote and directive cited in the claim have not been substantiated by reliable mainstream reporting. The claim appears to originate from partisan or unverified sources rather than confirmed internal communications.

claim: "9,871,525 is the number of registered voters in AZ according to FB. AZ population is 7,270,000."
rationale: The claim is implausible because the asserted number of registered voters (9,871,525) exceeds Arizona's total population (~7.27 million). Official and widely reported Arizona voter registration totals are on the order of about 4–5 million, not nearly 10 million, so the FB figure is incorrect or misattributed.

claim: Says "Obama’s deadliest cover-up (in an explosion that killed 29 miners) has been uncovered" by internal government documents.
rationale: While an explosion at the Upper Big Branch mine in April 2010 killed 29 miners, there is no credible evidence that 'internal government documents' have revealed an Obama-led cover-up. Investigations and public records attribute the disaster to mining-company safety failures and resulted in regulatory and criminal actions against company personnel, not to a concealed executive-branch cover-up by President Obama.

claim: Says James Clapper "and virtually everyone else" said "there is no collusion" in the Russia investigation findings.
rationale: While former DNI James Clapper did publicly say he saw no evidence of collusion, it is incorrect to claim that "virtually everyone else" said the same. Public reactions to the Russia investigation and the Mueller report were mixed: Attorney General Barr initially summarized no conspiracy, but many officials, lawmakers, and commentators argued Mueller did not exonerate the president and disputed the blanket "no collusion" framing.

claim: In Wisconsin, because a key provision of the Voting Rights Act was not in effect,  "somewhere between 40,000 and 80,000 people were turned away from the polls (in 2016) because of the color of their skin" and other factors.
rationale: There is no credible evidence or official count showing that 40,000–80,000 people were physically turned away from Wisconsin polling places in 2016 because of their race. Shelby County v. Holder (2013) did invalidate the Voting Rights Act coverage formula (preclearance), but that ruling did not produce documented mass, race-based turnaways of that magnitude; empirical studies and reporting on Wisconsin found far smaller and more contested numbers related to voter ID issues and administrative barriers. The claimed large range appears to conflate different estimates (e.g., people lacking ID, registered but not voting) and lacks a reliable source tying those numbers to being turned away for skin color.

claim: Says Chuck Todd said the Roy Moore story "felt completely orchestrated."
rationale: I find no credible transcript or reliable reporting showing Chuck Todd explicitly saying the Roy Moore story 'felt completely orchestrated.' The phrase appears to circulate on social media as an attribution without supporting video or reputable news-source confirmation, suggesting misattribution or paraphrase rather than a verifiable direct quote.

claim: When he was Milwaukee County executive, "eight years in a row we pushed through budgets that did not increase the tax levy from the previous year."
rationale: Independent reviews of Milwaukee County budgets during Scott Walker’s tenure as county executive found that while he frequently proposed budgets that kept the county tax levy flat, the levy did increase in at least one year and some so‑called freezes relied on one‑time revenues or accounting shifts. Therefore the precise claim of eight consecutive years with no increase in the tax levy is not fully accurate.

claim: Jim Renacci "voted repeatedly to end Medicare."
rationale: During his time in the House, Jim Renacci voted for multiple Republican budgets and bills that proposed converting Medicare from its traditional defined-benefit model to a premium-support/market-based system or cut its spending—changes widely described as effectively ending Medicare as currently structured. Those votes are the basis for claims that he 'voted repeatedly to end Medicare.'

claim: Says Oregon ranks 43rd in education.
rationale: The claim gives no source or year and presents an absolute ranking. State education rankings differ by publisher and year, and Oregon is not universally ranked 43rd across reputable lists, so the assertion as stated cannot be verified and is likely false.

claim: Letting the Bush tax cuts expire would raise taxes on small businesses.
rationale: Many small businesses are organized as pass-through entities (sole proprietorships, partnerships, S-corporations) whose profits are taxed at individual income tax rates. The Bush-era tax cuts reduced individual rates and capital gains/dividend taxes, so allowing those cuts to expire would generally raise tax liabilities for owners of such small businesses.

claim: Says TikTok found Cassie Compton, who has been missing from Arkansas since 2014.
rationale: I am not aware of any credible reporting or law-enforcement confirmation that TikTok located Cassie Compton, who was reportedly missing from Arkansas since 2014. Social-media claims about finding long-missing people frequently circulate but require verification from police or reputable news outlets, which is absent in this case up to my knowledge cutoff.

claim: Florida is "second in the nation in the uninsured."
rationale: The statement is presented as an absolute fact but lacks a timeframe and metric (rate vs. raw number), and rankings of uninsured people vary by year and measure. While Florida has had a high number and rate of uninsured residents in some years, Texas and other states often rank higher depending on the dataset and year, so the blanket claim is incorrect without qualification.

claim: The poorest counties in the U.S. are in Appalachia and "happen to be more than 90 percent white."
rationale: This is an overgeneralization. While many very poor counties are in Appalachia, the poorest counties nationally are concentrated across the rural South (including the Mississippi Delta) and some Native American areas; numerous poorest counties are majority Black or Native American rather than 'more than 90 percent white.'

claim: Fox News changed its accreditation to "entertainment."
rationale: There is no authoritative evidence that Fox News formally changed its official accreditation to a single category labeled 'entertainment.' The claim appears to stem from misreading corporate descriptions, program labels, or filings that list Fox as providing both news and entertainment or from isolated regulatory descriptions of specific programming, not a wholesale reclassification.

claim: Says Beto O'Rourke's "father-in-law, a billionaire real estate developer who bankrolled a Super PAC to buy Beto a congressional seat…"
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Beto O'Rourke's father‑in‑law is a billionaire real‑estate developer who personally bankrolled a Super PAC to buy O'Rourke a congressional seat. Reporting on O'Rourke’s campaigns and public campaign finance records do not show a family member single‑handedly funding a Super PAC to secure his House seat; his early congressional races were funded through ordinary campaign fundraising and outside groups, not a known billionaire in‑law.

claim: "I got a letter from 20 people who said they wanted their money back, 14 never gave me a penny."
rationale: This is a specific, personal anecdote that cannot be independently verified from the claim alone. Without documentary evidence (the letter, identities, or transaction records) there is no reliable basis to accept the precise numbers stated.

claim: Georgia and other states with weak gun laws have more crime.
rationale: This statement is an overgeneralization. Empirical research often finds that weaker gun laws are associated with higher firearm homicide and suicide rates, but overall crime levels (violent or property crime) depend on many factors—poverty, policing, urbanization, demographics—and do not uniformly track gun-law strength; Georgia does not consistently have the highest overall crime rates because of those confounders.

claim: One Wisconsin school district "is so worried about losing state funding that it has stopped giving milk to elementary school kids during snack time."
rationale: I find no reliable, corroborated reporting that a Wisconsin school district stopped giving elementary students milk specifically out of fear of losing state funding. State school aid formulas and USDA school nutrition reimbursement programs generally do not condition basic state funding on whether districts serve milk at snack time, making the claim implausible without a named district and credible sources.

claim: "The National Academy of Medicine points to a significant correlation between marijuana and psychosis, schizophrenia, and other psychotic disorders, particularly in teenagers where the risk of developing schizophrenia increases three fold."
rationale: The National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine (2017) concluded there is substantial evidence of an association between cannabis use and increased risk of psychosis and schizophrenia, particularly with earlier and heavier use. However, the report did not state a specific "threefold" increase for teenagers; effect sizes across studies vary and the academy emphasized association and dose-response rather than a single universal risk multiplier.

claim: Tide gauges measuring sea level in Rhode Island since 1930 have risen "maybe about 10 inches since that time."
rationale: NOAA tide-gauge records for Rhode Island (e.g., Providence/Narragansett area) show a relative sea-level rise on the order of ~3 mm/yr over the 20th century, which accumulates to roughly 9–11 inches since about 1930. Saying sea level has risen "maybe about 10 inches" is a reasonable, rounded characterization of the observed gauge trends.

claim: "Forty-seven percent of (members of Congress) are millionaires."
rationale: The share of members who are millionaires depends on the year, chamber, and how 'millionaire' is defined; recent estimates have hovered around but not consistently equaled 47%, with reported values varying from the high 30s to the low 50s. Without a specific Congress and methodology the precise figure 47% cannot be verified as a general fact.

claim: The COVID-19 vaccine could lead to prion diseases, Alzheimer’s, ALS and other neurodegenerative diseases.
rationale: There is no credible scientific or epidemiological evidence that COVID-19 vaccines cause prion diseases, Alzheimer’s, ALS, or other neurodegenerative diseases. The vaccines produce transient expression of antigen (or deliver inactivated/viral-vector material) and do not change host DNA or produce mechanisms known to induce prionopathies; long‑term safety monitoring and multiple studies have found no causal link. Isolated case reports, theoretical papers, or raw adverse‑event reports do not establish causation and have not been supported by robust data.

claim: Ché Guevara "wrote extensively about the superiority of white Europeans over people of African descent."
rationale: Ernesto 'Che' Guevara's published writings and speeches emphasize anti-imperialism, international solidarity, and opposition to racism; he worked in revolutionary Cuba on policies addressing racial inequality. While some private diary entries (notably from his Congo mission) contain derogatory or paternalistic descriptions of African fighters, this does not amount to him 'writing extensively' in favor of white European superiority as an ideological position.

claim: "A golf course closes somewhere in America every 48 hours."
rationale: There is no sustained, verifiable statistic showing a golf course closes somewhere in America every 48 hours as a constant rate. Industry tracking (e.g., National Golf Foundation reports and media analyses) shows closure rates vary by year and region and are often lower or presented as net losses over multi‑year periods; the “every 48 hours” phrasing is a recurring anecdote rather than a documented, continuous fact.

claim: Says Joe Biden called ANTIFA "courageous Americans."
rationale: Joe Biden did not explicitly call ANTIFA 'courageous Americans.' Clips that claim he did have been manipulated or taken out of context — Biden praised some peaceful protesters and criticized violent actors, but he did not label ANTIFA as 'courageous Americans.'

claim: Under Gov. Tom Corbett, "Pennsylvania ranks 49th in job creation."
rationale: The statement is presented as an absolute but is misleading: Pennsylvania’s ranking for “job creation” depends on the exact time window and metric used. During Tom Corbett’s 2011–2015 term some short intervals or specific measures put Pennsylvania near the bottom nationally, but authoritative BLS payroll and employment-rate measures for his full term do not uniformly place the state at 49th, and independent fact-checkers found the claim cherry-picks timeframe and data.

claim: There are "49 different federal job training programs that report to eight agencies."
rationale: Authoritative counts of federal job-training programs vary by source and year, and I am not aware of a consistent, supported claim that exactly 49 programs report to eight agencies. Government reviews (GAO and congressional analyses) have commonly reported different totals (for example, figures like 47 programs spanning multiple departments) and the number changes depending on definitions and time. Because program listings and organizational responsibility have shifted, the precise phrasing in the claim is not reliably accurate.

claim: "AIG insures the pension trust of the United States Congress!"
rationale: The congressional pension is part of the federal retirement systems (FERS/CSRS) administered and backed by the federal government (OPM/Treasury), not covered by a private insurer. There is no basis to say AIG insures the United States Congress pension trust.

claim: Says for every dollar the state spent on audits last year, it delivered $64 in cost savings.
rationale: The statement is unsupported and ambiguous: it does not identify which state or audits it refers to and a $64 return per $1 spent is an unusually large ROI compared with typical audit results. Without a verifiable source, time period, and methodology for calculating 'cost savings,' the claim cannot be accepted as factual.

claim: In the past three years, state legislatures have "enacted more of these restrictions (on abortion) than in the previous 10 years combined."
rationale: Available public tracking (e.g., research and news summaries) confirms a surge in state abortion restrictions after the 2022 Dobbs decision, but the specific blanket claim that the last three years produced more restrictions than the previous ten combined is not reliably supported without a clear definition of which measures count and which exact years are compared. Different trackers and analyses count laws, bills, and rules differently and produce different totals, so the claim overstates a simple, verifiable numeric comparison.

claim: "We have the lowest corporate tax rate since 1968."
rationale: The claim is ambiguous—'we' and which tax measure (statutory federal rate, combined federal+state, or effective tax rate) are not specified—so it cannot be verified as stated. Corporate tax rates vary by country and over time, and determining whether a current rate is the lowest since 1968 requires specifying the jurisdiction and the exact rate measure. Without that context the assertion is unsupported.

claim: "Under the ruling of the Supreme Court, any lobbyist could go into any legislator and say, if you don't vote our way on this bill, we're going to run a million-dollar campaign against you in your district."
rationale: The Supreme Court’s campaign finance rulings (e.g., Citizens United) expanded the ability of outside groups to spend independently on political speech, but they did not authorize illegal threats, bribery, or coordinated contributions. A lobbyist explicitly threatening a legislator with retaliation in exchange for a vote would likely be criminal (bribery, extortion, or coercion) and not protected by those rulings. Independent expenditures are also subject to rules against coordination with candidates.

claim: Bill Nelson’s vote for the Affordable Care Act "cuts $500 billion from Medicare to pay for new government programs."
rationale: Bill Nelson voted for the Affordable Care Act, and the law was scored by the Congressional Budget Office and others as reducing projected Medicare spending by about $500 billion over the first decade. Those reductions came largely from lower payment rates and slowed growth (including cuts to Medicare Advantage overpayments and provider payment changes) and were used in part to finance coverage expansions, subsidies, and deficit reduction rather than direct new benefit increases for Medicare enrollees.

claim: "There's not a single, solitary example that" signing the bill to end Glass-Steagall "had anything to do with the financial crash."
rationale: The claim is incorrect: numerous analysts, official reports, and academic studies have linked the repeal/erosion of Glass–Steagall (culminating in Gramm–Leach–Bliley) to greater bank consolidation, expanded commercial banks' investment activities, and increased systemic risk that contributed to the 2007–08 financial crisis. Examples frequently cited include the post‑repeal growth of universal banks (e.g., Citigroup) that took on large mortgage‑backed securities and trading exposures and suffered major losses. While the crisis had many causes and the extent of Glass–Steagall's role is debated, it is false to claim there are no examples or analyses making the connection.

claim: "Because of #TaxReform, 4 million American workers have received raises and bonuses, and 90% of Americans are seeing bigger paychecks this month."
rationale: The headline numbers are misleading. The "4 million" figure reflects aggregated corporate announcements of bonuses and pay actions (many one-time payments) rather than a verified count of workers receiving permanent raises, and the claim that "90% of Americans" saw bigger paychecks conflates IRS withholding-table changes and payroll timing; far fewer people were demonstrably receiving larger paychecks that specific month.

claim: GOP candidate for California governor Travis Allen "on the floor vote … refused to join Republicans opposing driver licenses for illegal aliens."
rationale: Official record and contemporary news reporting show Travis Allen voted with Republicans opposing legislation that granted driver licenses to undocumented immigrants (notably the AB 60 votes), so the claim that he "refused to join Republicans opposing" is incorrect. He publicly opposed and voted against those measures.

claim: "Dems have removed any mention of ‘God’ from their Platform."
rationale: The claim is misleading. The Democratic Party did not issue a universal change that removed all mentions of 'God' from every platform document — in 2024 the DNC chose not to adopt a traditional full platform and instead promoted policy priorities, and prior Democratic platforms and many party materials have continued to include references to faith or God in various forms. Whether a specific document omits the word 'God' depends on which year or text is being referenced, so the blanket claim is false.

claim: The newly created state Immigration Enforcement Review Board "can actually prosecute, and get them [violators] into jail, if we bring in the attorney general."
rationale: A state administrative review board generally does not have independent criminal prosecutorial power or authority to incarcerate people. Only prosecutors (a state attorney general or local district attorney) can file criminal charges and seek jail time, and most immigration violations are enforced at the federal level, which limits state ability to prosecute purely immigration offenses.

claim: Ron Johnson didn’t "show up" for a day of impeachment hearings.
rationale: The statement is vague and provides no date or specific impeachment proceeding; I find no clear, reputable documentation that Senator Ron Johnson entirely skipped a full day of impeachment hearings as a notable, reported event. Senators do occasionally miss sessions for other official business, but without a specific hearing date this claim cannot be verified and is therefore unsupported. Absent concrete evidence, the blanket assertion is not reliable.

claim: "More people, almost twice as many, pay the penalty or take the waiver than signed up for (Obamacare)."
rationale: Public data from the Affordable Care Act open-enrollment periods show millions of people signed up for marketplace coverage (commonly 8–12 million in early years), while far fewer taxpayers actually paid the individual mandate penalty or claimed exemptions in a given tax year. Therefore the claim that almost twice as many people pay the penalty or take a waiver than signed up is not supported by available enrollment and IRS penalty/exemption data.

claim: Biden was responsible for "ending genocide in Bosnia."
rationale: The statement greatly overstates Joe Biden’s role. The Bosnian genocide and war were ended through a combination of NATO military pressure and diplomatic negotiations culminating in the 1995 Dayton Accords brokered by U.S. administration figures (notably Richard Holbrooke) under President Bill Clinton; Biden was a senator who supported intervention but was not the person responsible for ending the genocide.

claim: Says Russ Feingold said that with Obamacare, "we could keep our doctors and our plans, it was rated as the Lie of the Year."
