rationale: The claim gives a precise per-resident dollar amount but provides no source or date and does not match the range reported by major congestion studies. Annual per-driver congestion costs for Atlanta reported by organizations like the Texas A&M Transportation Institute and INRIX vary by year and methodology and in recent reports are often higher than $924 (or vary substantially), while other studies produce different figures. Without specifying year, whether it means per commuter or per resident, and the valuation method for time and fuel, the $924 number is not reliably supported.

claim: "Now remember, property taxes went up 70 percent in the 10 years before I became governor."
rationale: The claim is unverified and likely misleading because it gives no jurisdiction, dates, or definition of “property taxes” (rate, assessed value, or total bills). Property-tax changes vary widely by state, county, and city, and a 70% increase in the 10 years before a given governor took office cannot be confirmed without specific locality and time-period data. Because the statement lacks necessary context and precise measurement, it should not be accepted as fact.

claim: "You're more likely to be the victim of a violent crime in Milwaukee than in 96 percent of the country."
rationale: The statement gives a precise percentile without a year or defined comparison group; crime-rate rankings for Milwaukee vary by dataset, year, and whether you compare cities, counties, or all populated places. While Milwaukee frequently ranks among U.S. jurisdictions with high violent-crime rates, available FBI and city-level statistics do not consistently place it higher than 96% of all U.S. places across years and metrics, so the blanket claim is unsupported.

claim: Says he "raised graduation rates to nearly 90 percent."
rationale: The statement is missing any named subject, time period, location, or source, so it cannot be verified as presented. Without those specifics and supporting data (district or state graduation statistics before and after the claimed intervention), the assertion that "he raised graduation rates to nearly 90 percent" is unsubstantiated.

claim: "The United States is 3rd in murders throughout the world. If you remove Chicago, Detroit, Washington, St. Louis and New Orleans, the United States is then 189th out of 193 countries in the entire world."
rationale: The United States is not third in the world in homicides; other countries (e.g., Brazil, Mexico, India, South Africa, Colombia, Venezuela) report comparable or larger numbers or higher rates. Removing the five cited cities (Chicago, Detroit, Washington (D.C.), St. Louis and New Orleans) would not reduce U.S. homicides enough to make the country rank 189th of 193 — those cities account for only a small fraction of national murders and many countries have far lower totals and rates.

claim: The United States has "10,000 IRS agents making sure that you don't take an improper charity deduction," but to fight terrorism, it has "less than two dozen people focusing on countering violent extremism at home."
rationale: The claim misstates staffing. There is no evidence that 10,000 IRS agents are dedicated solely to policing charity deductions — IRS examiners and revenue agents audit a wide range of tax issues and the 10,000 figure, if cited, would not be limited to charitable deductions. Likewise, federal countering-violent-extremism efforts (across DHS, FBI, DOJ and partner agencies) involve far more than “less than two dozen” people; these programs and task forces employ dozens to hundreds of personnel at multiple levels.

claim: The majority of revenue generated by a proposed Kenosha casino would be sent to the Seminole tribe in Florida.
rationale: Tribal casinos are typically owned by the local tribe and retain the bulk of gaming revenue to fund tribal government and services; commercial operators or brand owners (Hard Rock/ Seminole) normally receive management fees and royalties, not the majority of gross receipts. Thus it is very unlikely that a proposed Kenosha casino's majority revenue would be sent to the Seminole Tribe of Florida.

claim: "The Austin school district calendar lists 64 different dates for either a state-mandated test or make-up test."
rationale: I cannot find evidence that a single Austin school district calendar enumerates 64 distinct dates for state‑mandated tests or makeups. State testing (e.g., Texas STAAR) is scheduled in defined test windows with a limited number of administration and makeup days, and district calendars typically summarize those windows rather than listing dozens of unique dates.

claim: Says "the Kardashians donate whopping sum to Las Vegas mass shooting victims"
rationale: There is no credible, contemporaneous reporting or charity documentation showing that the Kardashian family collectively made a large, publicized donation to victims of the Las Vegas mass shooting. While many celebrities donated after that event, reliable sources do not list a 'whopping' Kardashian contribution, so the claim is unsupported.

claim: "We never had an earthquake in Youngstown until John Kasich was elected Governor,"
rationale: While a widely reported sequence of earthquakes near Youngstown began in 2011 (after John Kasich won the 2010 gubernatorial election), the blanket claim that Youngstown "never had an earthquake" before his election is inaccurate. Ohio and the surrounding region have recorded seismic events before 2010, and the 2011–2012 sequence was notable because it was linked to injection wells, not because earthquakes were previously impossible there.

claim: No one showed up for this Joe Biden and Kamala Harris joint campaign event in Arizona.
rationale: The categorical claim that "no one showed up" is extremely unlikely and not supported without a specific event and date. Media coverage, campaign photos, and reporting from Biden–Harris appearances in Arizona show that these joint events have had attendees, so the absolute statement is false.

claim: Georgia has had the nation’s busiest Court of Appeals for a decade or more.
rationale: The claim is vague and likely incorrect: while Georgia’s appellate courts are busy, nationwide caseload statistics historically show larger systems (notably California’s Courts of Appeal, several Texas appellate districts, and some federal circuits) handling greater volumes. There is no clear authoritative evidence that Georgia has been the single "nation’s busiest" Court of Appeals continuously for a decade or more.

claim: Every child in Colorado who has been given medical marijuana for treatment for seizures has had diminished seizure activity.
rationale: The claim is a universal statement for which there is no evidence. Controlled trials of cannabidiol (a component of medical marijuana) show reduced seizure frequency for some specific epilepsy syndromes (e.g., Dravet, Lennox-Gastaut) but not every treated child responds, and other medical‑marijuana products and diagnoses have mixed or insufficient evidence and can cause adverse effects.

claim: Speaking of an HIV outbreak in Indiana during his time as governor, says "we immediately deployed health resources."
rationale: The claim that officials "immediately deployed health resources" during the Indiana HIV outbreak is inaccurate. Reporting and public-health accounts of the 2015 Scott County outbreak show the state initially resisted CDC-recommended harm-reduction measures (notably syringe exchange) and only authorized temporary syringe services and other interventions after significant delay and external pressure.
cited_knowledge: Contemporary reporting and public-health documentation of the 2015 Scott County, Indiana HIV outbreak describing initial hesitation to implement syringe exchange and later authorization after CDC/public pressure.
safety_notes: The term "immediately" and "health resources" are somewhat vague; the state did undertake some testing/outreach early, but major harm-reduction measures were not promptly authorized.

claim: "Here's the fact: The No. 1 source of income into Mexico are Mexicans working here and sending the money back."
rationale: Remittances from Mexicans working abroad (mainly in the U.S.) are a very large and growing source of foreign currency for Mexico and have overtaken specific categories like oil or tourism in some years, but they are not the single largest source of income overall. Mexico's merchandise exports (manufactured goods) and other external inflows (trade receipts and foreign investment) exceed remittances in total value, so the blanket claim that remittances are the No.1 source is misleading.

claim: "An April study found that about 70 percent of ads in this election cycle have been negative [due to SuperPACs], up from only 9 percent through the same period in 2008."
rationale: I could not verify an April study that reports exactly 70% negative ads this cycle versus 9% through the same period in 2008. While independent analyses have documented a large increase in negative advertising by outside groups and Super PACs, the specific 70%/9% comparison appears to be unsupported or taken out of context.

claim: Says U.S. Senate rival Tommy Thompson ran Medicare "into the ground" and "nine years closer to bankruptcy."
rationale: The claim attributes a precise quantitative effect and a definitive qualitative judgment to Tommy Thompson that is not supported by clear evidence. Medicare trust‑fund solvency projections change year to year based on many factors (enrollment, health costs, legislation) and no authoritative source shows Thompson alone ‘ran Medicare into the ground’ or moved projected insolvency exactly nine years. The language is also partisan and subjective rather than an empirically established fact.

claim: "More than 9,000 Rhode Island voters used the Moderate Party master lever mechanism and they didn't have a single Moderate on their ballot."
rationale: I find no reliable evidence that more than 9,000 Rhode Island voters used a “Moderate Party master lever” while no Moderate candidates appeared on their ballots. The claim appears to conflate or misinterpret ballot mechanics — Rhode Island does not report a standalone party-only total in that way and official results do not show a separate 9,000+ party-only tally for a Moderate Party.

claim: "Like every budget passed by the Senate since I have been lieutenant governor, Senate Bill 1 is within the spending limit set by the Texas Constitution."
rationale: The claim is an absolute statement that every Senate budget since the speaker became lieutenant governor complied with the Texas Constitution’s spending limit. Whether a budget 'is within the spending limit' depends on formal comptroller certification and on accounting choices about what funds count; there have been disputes and differing analyses over past Texas budgets. Without clear, documented comptroller certifications for each bill and an agreed accounting method, the blanket assertion is not supported.

claim: Dollar General "added 2,500 stores and 20,000 jobs" during his four-year tenure as CEO.
rationale: I cannot verify that exact claim as stated: it lacks a named CEO and a specific four-year period, and publicly available company reports and press coverage typically give different or more specific figures for store openings and jobs over given periods. While Dollar General has grown substantially and added many stores and employees over years, the precise claim of 2,500 stores and 20,000 jobs in a single four-year CEO tenure is unverified and likely inaccurate without a clear time frame or source.

claim: "Governor Evers' budget would increase property taxes by the largest amount in a decade"
rationale: The claim is unverified and likely false as stated because it gives no year or metric and there is no widely reported, authoritative finding that any Governor Evers budget produced the largest decade‑long increase in property taxes. Property tax changes depend on local levies, state aid formulas, and whether the claim refers to dollars, percentage change, or average levy — comparisons that require detailed fiscal analysis which is not provided.

claim: Says Sen. Jeanne Shaheen’s "wealth has surged while in public office."
rationale: The claim is vague and not supported by clear, widely reported evidence that Sen. Jeanne Shaheen’s personal wealth dramatically surged while holding public office. Public financial-disclosure filings show some fluctuations and modest increases over time, but there is no consensus reporting of a large, unexplained windfall tied to her tenure.

claim: "No Republicans voted for" recent hikes in the income tax, payroll tax, capital gains tax, dividend tax and estate tax. "These taxes were all passed under … Obamacare."
rationale: The Affordable Care Act did create an additional 0.9% Medicare payroll tax on high earners and a 3.8% Net Investment Income Tax that affects capital gains and dividends for high‑income taxpayers, and the law passed without Republican votes. However, it did not broadly raise ordinary income tax rates or enact a general estate‑tax hike, so the claim that all the listed tax hikes (income, payroll, capital gains, dividend and estate tax) were passed under "Obamacare" is inaccurate.

claim: "Since that famous day in February where the governor campaigned with Barack Obama on behalf of the stimulus program, 211,000 Floridians have lost their jobs."
rationale: The statement gives a precise job-loss number but omits a clear start and end date and an authoritative data source, so it cannot be verified as stated. Official employment statistics (BLS and state reports) are reported monthly and the number of jobs lost in Florida depends entirely on the defined period; without that context the specific claim is unsubstantiated and likely misleading.

claim: As a result of Roe vs. Wade, "America’s maternal mortality rate dropped dramatically."
rationale: Roe v. Wade (1973) legalized abortion nationwide, which led to a large reduction in deaths from unsafe, illegal abortions — a significant component of maternal mortality at the time. Overall U.S. maternal mortality fell in the years after legalization, and scholarly analyses attribute a meaningful portion of that decline to access to safe, legal abortion.

claim: "We have about six school districts that are in school 140 to 150 days this year."
rationale: The claim is unverified and likely incorrect as stated because it gives no jurisdiction or source; most U.S. public school districts have around 170–180 instructional days, so asserting 'about six' districts with only 140–150 days is implausible without local data. Without a specific state, county, or list of districts and the calendar year, the claim cannot be confirmed.

claim: The Buffalo protester pushed to the ground "had been previously arrested 300 times. 82 times for incitement. Riots is what he does for a living."
rationale: Independent news reports and multiple fact-checks established the man shoved in Buffalo was Martin Gugino, a 75-year-old peace activist and retired professional. There is no credible evidence or official record that he had been arrested 300 times or 82 times for incitement; those figures were fabricated and circulated on social media.

claim: A monthly "police and fire protection fee" on all Wisconsin phone bills does nothing to support police and fire.
rationale: The statement is too absolute. In Wisconsin, monthly line-item fees labeled for police and fire protection are typically statutory emergency/911 or public-safety surcharges that are collected to fund 911 systems, dispatch, public-safety communications and other services that support police and fire operations. Allocation can vary by statute and locality and not every dollar necessarily goes directly to municipal payrolls, but it is incorrect to say such fees do nothing to support police and fire.

claim: Since 2009, "millions of Americans have lost their health care plans."
rationale: Multiple sources and official estimates during the Affordable Care Act rollout documented that several million people received cancellation or nonrenewal notices when pre-ACA individual and some group plans were discontinued, and over a longer period many more have experienced lapses or changes in coverage. The statement is broad but accurate in that the scale of plan losses since 2009 reaches into the millions.

claim: "If Biden wins the election, there are people out there planning on mass murdering poc and lbgtq+ people. Please stay inside during the election and a few days after."
rationale: There is no publicly available, credible evidence that a coordinated, widespread plan exists to mass-murder people of color and LGBTQ+ people specifically if Biden wins. While isolated threats and extremist violence have occurred around elections, claiming a general, organized plot requires verified intelligence which is not present in public reporting. The blanket warning as stated is unsupported and appears to be fear-inducing speculation.

claim: "The American people don't want us to raise taxes."
rationale: This blanket statement is inaccurate because American public opinion on tax increases is mixed and context-dependent. Polling and electoral outcomes show many Americans oppose broad tax hikes but will support increases aimed at specific purposes (e.g., infrastructure, healthcare) or higher taxes on the wealthy, so it is incorrect to assert that the American people universally don't want taxes raised.

claim: "Whether you like to admit it or not, half our general revenue goes to education."
rationale: The statement is presented as a general fact but is ambiguous about which government or level (federal, state, local) and usually untrue. In most countries and in the U.S. federal budget, education is a small share of total revenue; while education can be the largest single item in many state or local general funds, it rarely equals exactly half of total general revenue across jurisdictions. Because the claim is blanket and lacks specificity, it is not supportable as stated.

claim: "Breaking: Santa Fe killer expresses his love for Obama."
rationale: There are no credible news reports or verified evidence that the Santa Fe shooter publicly expressed love for Barack Obama. Coverage of the Santa Fe High School shooting described the shooter's posts and symbols but did not include any statement praising Obama; the claim appears to be a fabricated or misleading social-media assertion.

claim: Says Dan Feehan "would vote with Pelosi for open borders and amnesty, putting Minnesota families at risk."
rationale: There is no clear public record of Dan Feehan explicitly saying he “would vote with Pelosi for open borders and amnesty.” The claim collapses multiple charged assertions (pledging to back Pelosi for speaker, supporting “open borders,” and endorsing blanket amnesty) into a single statement; available public statements and campaign materials do not support that exact combination of promises and the terms used are rhetorical and misleading.

claim: Says Mike Enzi is "getting about 84 percent of his campaign funds from Washington-based PACs. That's more than any senator of either party."
rationale: There is no reliable campaign-finance evidence showing Mike Enzi received about 84% of his funds from Washington-based PACs or that this was the highest share of any senator. Campaign reports (FEC/OpenSecrets) show senators receive PAC contributions from a variety of sources and years, and an 84% concentration from DC-based PACs would be an extreme outlier that isn’t supported by published data. The claim likely misstates the time period, the definition of "Washington-based PACs," or confuses specific small-time slices of fundraising.

claim: Says Kanye West got 40,000 votes in the presidential election in Kentucky.
rationale: Kanye West did not receive 40,000 votes in Kentucky in the recent presidential election cycle; his nationwide total in 2020 was only about 60,000 votes and his share in any single state was far smaller. Kentucky’s certified results do not show a 40,000-vote tally for him, so the specific claim is incorrect.

claim: "We have a fire marshal that said, 'Oh we can't allow more people’ ...  And the reason they won't let them in is because they don't know what the hell they're doing."
rationale: This statement attributes a direct quote and a judgment about a fire marshal’s competence, but there is no verifiable transcript, recording, or independent reporting provided to confirm the quote or the claim about why people were not allowed in. Without corroborating evidence, the assertion that a fire marshal said that and that the reason is incompetence cannot be treated as factual. It may be rhetorical or a paraphrase by the speaker rather than an accurate quotation.

claim: "Covid-19 is now the leading cause of death in the United States."
rationale: Current U.S. mortality data in recent years show heart disease and cancer remain the top causes of death; COVID-19 mortality has fallen significantly from pandemic peaks and has not been the single leading cause in the most recent full-year CDC reports. The statement’s use of “now” is ambiguous, but on available up-to-date national mortality statistics COVID-19 is not the leading cause of death.

claim: John McCain's tax plan will give no reduction "for 100-million American families."
rationale: The precise statement is misleading. Nonpartisan analyses of John McCain’s tax proposals (particularly his 2008 campaign plan) showed that many households would receive tax reductions and that characterizing exactly “no reduction for 100 million American families” misstates the distributional findings and omits key context such as the year, definition of ‘families,’ and which components of the plan are counted.

claim: "Roy Barnes proclaimed Mexican workers good for Georgia."
rationale: There is no well-documented, verbatim proclamation by former Georgia governor Roy Barnes stating the simple claim 'Mexican workers are good for Georgia.' While Barnes has commented on immigration and the economy at times, I could not find a reliable, widely reported source for this exact proclamation; the claim appears to be a paraphrase or misattribution rather than a documented, explicit quote.

claim: "Mar-A-Lago (was) destroyed by (Hurricane) Irma (and) Jared Kushner (is) still missing."
rationale: Both parts are false: Mar-a-Lago was not destroyed by Hurricane Irma (it sustained some storm effects but remained standing and in use), and Jared Kushner is not missing — there are no credible reports that he disappeared and he has continued public and private activities. The claim appears to conflate rumor or exaggeration with reality.

claim: Rhode Island voters are moving away from the Democratic party to non-affiliation
rationale: Recent Rhode Island voter-registration trends show the Democratic share declining modestly while the share of voters registered as unaffiliated (no party) has risen, with unaffiliated voters surpassing Republicans in enrollment. This pattern indicates a movement of some voters away from the Democratic party toward non-affiliation.

claim: "Joe Biden’s great-grandfather Joseph J. Biden was a slave-owner and fought" for the Confederacy.
rationale: Contemporary genealogical research and media fact-checking find no credible evidence that President Biden had a great-grandfather named Joseph J. Biden who owned slaves or fought for the Confederacy. Claims appear to conflate or misattribute 19th-century individuals with similar names; Biden’s documented direct ancestors do not appear in slaveholder rolls or Confederate service records as his great‑grandfather.

claim: Louisiana is turning down $100 million "that would require us to change our unemployment law, that would have actually raised taxes on Louisiana businesses."
rationale: The claim bundles several specific assertions (a $100 million offer refused, a required change to state unemployment law, and that the change would have raised taxes on Louisiana businesses) without citation; I find no corroborating public reporting tying those three facts together. Federal/state program offers and unemployment trust fund adjustments are common but vary by program and time, so the blanket claim as stated cannot be verified and is likely misleading.

claim: The state and local tax deduction is a major benefit for moderate-income households because "50% of households that claim State & Local Tax deduction make under $100K."
rationale: The claim is misleading: even if roughly half of filers who claim the SALT deduction have incomes under $100K in some years, the dollar value of the deduction is heavily concentrated among higher‑income households. Analyses from tax experts and IRS/Tax Policy Center data show that higher earners receive a much larger share of the total SALT tax benefit, so it is not primarily a major monetary benefit for moderate‑income households.

claim: Says there’s "no wait list" for private school vouchers
rationale: The statement is an overbroad universal claim and cannot be true in general: private school voucher programs vary by jurisdiction and many are capped and have wait lists when demand exceeds funding. Without naming a specific program, time, and place the claim is not verifiable and is likely false as stated. Some individual voucher programs may indeed have no wait list, but that does not make the blanket claim correct.

claim: "A family of four can make up to $88,000 a year and still get a subsidy for health insurance" under the new federal health care law.
rationale: Subsidy eligibility under the Affordable Care Act is based on a household’s income as a percentage of the federal poverty level (FPL), not a single fixed dollar amount like $88,000. The 400% FPL threshold for a family of four varies by year (and is generally higher than $88,000 in recent years), and temporary pandemic-era changes also modified eligibility rules for some years.

claim: Says he is the "ranking member" of the House select committee investigating the Jan. 6 attack on the U.S. Capitol.
rationale: The claim is ambiguous about who “he” is and is likely incorrect: the House January 6 select committee did not have an officially recognized Republican "ranking member". House GOP leaders attempted to name members but Speaker Pelosi did not accept McCarthy’s picks, and the committee instead included two Republicans appointed by the Speaker (including Liz Cheney), with no formal minority "ranking member" role.

claim: "More people have watched ‘Morning Joe’ than CNN and HLN 5 years in a row."
rationale: The claim is imprecise about which metric (total viewers, average viewers, timeslot) and which five consecutive years are meant. Nielsen ratings fluctuate year to year and while Morning Joe has at times outperformed CNN or HLN in the morning timeslot, a blanket claim that it had more viewers than CNN and HLN for five straight years cannot be verified without specific yearly Nielsen data and is therefore not supportable as stated.

claim: The fiscal cliff agreement was "the largest tax increase in history."
rationale: The 2012 "fiscal cliff" deal (American Taxpayer Relief Act) raised taxes on high earners and ended a payroll-tax holiday, but the revenue increase was modest compared with major historical U.S. tax hikes. Much larger tax increases occurred during periods such as World War II and other major tax acts, both in absolute dollars and as a share of GDP, so calling the fiscal cliff the largest in history is incorrect.

claim: "The states that are locked down are increasing at twice the rate we are" in Florida
rationale: The statement is vague and unsupported: it fails to define what is "increasing" (cases, hospitalizations, deaths), the timeframe, or which states are meant. COVID-19 trends varied widely by state and period, and there is no consistent evidence that states with lockdowns were universally increasing at exactly twice Florida’s rate. Verifying or falsifying the claim requires a specific metric, dates, and data sources.

claim: "(Brendan) Doherty wants to raise the eligibility age for Social Security benefits for anyone born after 1960, with no regard for the challenges it would cause for people working in physically demanding occupations."
rationale: I find no reliable public record or reporting that Brendan Doherty has proposed raising Social Security eligibility specifically for everyone born after 1960; current law already sets full retirement age at 67 for those born in 1960 or later. The statement that he would do so 'with no regard' for people in physically demanding jobs is an attribution of motive not supported by cited statements. Without a specific sourced policy proposal or direct quote, the claim is unverified and likely false.

claim: "Bernie Sanders voted in favor of every war during his tenure."
rationale: Bernie Sanders has a long record of opposing major U.S. wars and authorizations of force — most notably he voted against the 2002 Iraq War authorization and has publicly opposed many subsequent military interventions. While he has sometimes supported specific military funding or limited operations, he did not vote in favor of every war during his tenure.

claim: "Most of these killers tend to be 18, 19 years old."
rationale: The claim is vague and unsupported: without specifying which category of 'killers' (homicide offenders, mass shooters, serial killers, etc.), there is no basis to assert that most are ages 18–19. Empirical crime statistics and criminology research show offender age distributions vary by crime type and jurisdiction and rarely concentrate such a large majority at two specific ages.

claim: Says Sri Kulkarni attended "notorious desert drug parties" and was arrested for cocaine.
rationale: There is no credible reporting or public arrest record showing that Sri Preston Kulkarni was arrested for cocaine or that he attended 'notorious desert drug parties.' The allegation appears to stem from partisan attack materials and unverified social media claims rather than verified law-enforcement or major news reporting.

claim: The Wisconsin state Assembly chambers extend to the bathroom and the parlor, and rules allow members to vote for each other if the member is in the chambers.
rationale: Wisconsin Assembly voting rules require a member to be physically present in the chamber (or the designated voting area) to cast a vote; there is no general rule that the chamber legally 'extends' into bathrooms or parlors. Members are not permitted to cast votes on behalf of absent colleagues simply because those colleagues are nearby — proxy voting or voting for another member is not allowed under normal Assembly rules.

claim: "Paul Ryan has blocked all action to strengthen our gun laws."
rationale: The claim is overly broad and inaccurate. While Speaker Paul Ryan used his control of the House floor to oppose or decline to bring certain gun‑control proposals (especially broad background‑check measures), he did not single‑handedly block every possible action to strengthen gun laws — Congress considered and passed other related measures and states pursued their own reforms.

claim: Says science shows the physiological effects of wearing masks include hypoxemia, hypercapnia, shortness of breath, toxicity and increased muscle tension.
rationale: Multiple studies and public health agencies conclude that wearing surgical or cloth masks does not produce hypoxemia, hypercapnia, systemic toxicity, or objectively increased muscle tension in healthy people; some individuals may experience perceived shortness of breath or discomfort. Tight-fitting respirators (N95) worn for long periods can cause discomfort, headaches, or transient symptoms in some users, but this is not the same as the physiological harms claimed.

claim: John McCain and George W. Bush want to spend "a trillion dollars in Iraq over the next 10 years."
rationale: There is no clear record that John McCain or George W. Bush formally proposed or pledged to spend exactly “a trillion dollars in Iraq over the next 10 years.” Independent analysts and government budget offices produced estimates that long-term Iraq costs could approach or exceed $1 trillion under certain scenarios, and both supported continued funding for operations, but that is not the same as an explicit $1 trillion, 10-year spending plan they declared they “want” to enact.

claim: A second impeachment means Donald Trump loses his lifetime pension, travel allowance, Secret Service detail, and his ability to run for public office.
rationale: An impeachment by the House alone does not remove benefits or bar someone from office; only a Senate conviction can remove a president and the Senate may additionally vote to disqualify a person from holding future federal office. Statutory benefits (former presidents' pension, travel allowances, and Secret Service protection) are governed by federal law and are not automatically forfeited by impeachment or even by conviction—stripping those benefits would require separate legislative action or specific statutory authority.

claim: Says drug dealers have "overdosed on purpose" to avoid prosecution.
rationale: The claim generalizes that drug dealers have deliberately overdosed to avoid prosecution, but there is no evidence that this is a common or established tactic. Overdoses are overwhelmingly accidental or due to substance use disorder, and while isolated individuals might feign or induce medical crises to delay arrest, that does not support the broad assertion.

claim: A space shuttle the National Museum of the United States Air Force near Dayton would be "within a day's drive of 60 percent of the U.S. population."
rationale: There is no authoritative evidence that placing a shuttle near Dayton would put 60% of the U.S. population within a single "day's drive." The term "day's drive" is undefined and under typical interpretations (around 8–10 hours or ~500–600 miles) many large population centers on the West Coast and in the far Southwest would be outside that range, making the 60% figure unlikely.

claim: Florida students take "an array of standardized high stakes tests which eat up as much as 45 school days per year."
rationale: The 45-school-day figure is an overstatement for typical Florida students. State-mandated exams in Florida (FSA, end-of-course exams and similar assessments) generally require roughly one to two weeks of formal administration; even when add-ons like makeups and district interim tests are included, statewide averages fall well below 45 full school days. The larger number appears to come from advocacy estimates that count every short classroom quiz, test-prep activity, and local benchmark as a full testing day.

claim: Say video "shows massive alligator strolling across Florida golf course."
rationale: There is insufficient information to verify that the referenced video actually depicts a ‘massive alligator’ on a Florida golf course. While alligators do commonly appear on Florida golf courses, viral clips are often miscaptioned, taken elsewhere, or digitally altered, so the claim as stated cannot be confirmed without provenance or geolocation.

claim: Says Mitt Romney wants to "get rid of Planned Parenthood."
rationale: During his 2012 presidential campaign Mitt Romney publicly said he wanted to defund and effectively "get rid of" Planned Parenthood, telling audiences he would work to end federal funding for the organization. Multiple contemporary news reports and his campaign statements reflect that position.

claim: Says the Koch brothers want to "protect tax cuts for companies that ship our jobs overseas."
rationale: The Koch network has consistently advocated for broad corporate tax cuts and opposed policies that would eliminate tax advantages for multinationals or penalize offshoring. Political reporting and advocacy analyses show they supported maintaining tax provisions and cuts that benefit companies that shift profits or operations abroad, so characterizing their position as protecting such tax breaks is accurate.

claim: "A federal judge just ordered Wisconsin must have all ballots counted by 8 p.m. on the day of the election."
rationale: There was no recent federal court order requiring Wisconsin to finish counting all ballots by 8 p.m. on election day. Wisconsin law sets an 8 p.m. deadline for absentee ballots to be received, but counting and processing commonly continue after polls close and courts have not imposed a blanket federal deadline to stop counting at 8 p.m.

claim: "War for the soul of the TxDems: 57% of Dem incumbents for Tx House LOST their primary."
rationale: The statement gives no year and is inconsistent with typical Texas House primary outcomes; in recent cycles only a small number of Democratic incumbents lost primaries, not a majority. Public election returns and reporting do not support a 57% incumbent loss rate for Texas House Democrats in any recent statewide primary.

claim: Says Donald Trump offered his hotel "to our troops to sleep in after they were put in a car garage."
rationale: There is no credible public evidence or contemporaneous reporting that Donald Trump offered his hotel for National Guard troops who were reported to have slept in parking garages after the Jan. 6 response. Major news accounts and fact-checkers document the housing controversy but do not corroborate an offer of Trump hotel space, so the specific claim is unsubstantiated.
cited_knowledge: General knowledge of reporting around the Jan. 6 National Guard housing controversy and absence of verified reports or official confirmations that Trump offered his hotel to those troops.
safety_notes: Timing and phrasing are ambiguous (who 'said' this and when); if the claim refers to a private, undocumented offer it cannot be verified from public records.

claim: Obamacare "will provide insurance to all non-U.S. residents, even if they are here illegally."
rationale: The Affordable Care Act does not provide insurance to all non-U.S. residents; undocumented immigrants are generally ineligible for Medicaid and are barred from receiving federal premium tax credits or subsidized Marketplace coverage. Some undocumented people can buy private insurance at full price or receive care through state/local programs or emergency services, but the law does not grant universal coverage to those here illegally.

claim: As state Commerce secretary, Mary Burke drafted, sponsored and promoted "budgets that raised taxes by billions, created high structural deficits and raided funds to finance huge spending hikes."
rationale: Mary Burke served as Wisconsin's Secretary of Commerce (an appointed cabinet role) and was not the legislator who drafted or sponsored state budgets. Budget bills are prepared and enacted by the governor's administration and the legislature; while the Doyle administration enacted budgets with revenue changes in the mid-2000s, attributing 'drafted, sponsored and promoted' multi‑billion tax increases and intentional 'raids' solely to Burke is inaccurate and misleading.

claim: Rhode Island's unemployment insurance system "is the most expensive such system in the country."
rationale: The claim is unqualified and no consistent, widely accepted metric shows Rhode Island as categorically the single "most expensive" unemployment insurance system in the U.S. Costs (benefit levels, employer tax burdens, and trust-fund solvency) vary by metric and year, and other states (e.g., Massachusetts, New Jersey, Alaska, Connecticut) have at times ranked higher on various measures. While Rhode Island has occasionally been among higher-cost states on specific measures or in certain years, it is not reliably identifiable as the most expensive across the board.

claim: In the case of a catastrophic event, the Atlanta-area offices of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention will self-destruct.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that the CDC’s Atlanta offices are designed to 'self-destruct' in a catastrophe. Federal emergency and continuity-of-operations plans focus on evacuation, data protection, and relocation rather than destroying facilities. A literal self-destruct mechanism for an occupied federal building would be unsafe and unlawful.

claim: Says U.S. Sen. Ron Johnson "opposes faster broadband internet in small towns" and "got nearly $90,000 in campaign contributions from the telecom special interests."
rationale: The claim bundles a vague policy charge with a specific dollar figure in a way that is not verifiable as stated. Ron Johnson has opposed certain broadband regulations and subsidies favored by critics, and he has accepted contributions from telecom industry PACs, but saying he broadly 'opposes faster broadband in small towns' mischaracterizes nuanced votes and he has received more/less money depending on the time period—the flat “nearly $90,000” figure lacks necessary time-frame and category specificity.

claim: Says a Congressional Budget Office report found low-income seniors in Florida will face "800 percent premium increases" under the American Health Care Act.
rationale: The CBO’s 2017 score of the American Health Care Act provided national-level estimates and did not report that low-income seniors in Florida would face an “800 percent” premium increase. While the CBO did project that older adults could face higher premiums under the AHCA and provided aggregate estimates of premium and coverage effects, it did not produce a state-specific finding of an 800% increase — that figure appears to be a misattribution or comes from other analyses or hypothetical scenarios.

claim: "The only people in this town that have voted to cut Medicare spending are the people who voted in favor of Obamacare. That’s a fact."
rationale: The claim is an absolute, locality-specific statement without supporting data and is not verifiable as stated. Votes on the Affordable Care Act and any measures described as 'cutting Medicare spending' occurred at different levels and involved many legislators and voters; it is implausible to assert exclusivity without precinct-level voting records and clear definitions. Additionally, the ACA contained complex Medicare payment changes rather than straightforward benefit cuts, so conflating votes is misleading.

claim: Twitter employee named Jackson Mulholland resigned in a tweet after Elon Musk joined the company’s board.
rationale: There is no credible reporting or verifiable evidence that a Twitter employee named Jackson Mulholland resigned in a public tweet after Elon Musk joined Twitter’s board. Major news coverage of Musk’s short-lived board appointment and employee reactions does not mention any such named resignation, and the name appears to be unverified or from parody/social posts.

claim: "Now there is a new threat that we’re seeing up close: the risk of exposure to powerful drugs that can kill in even tiny amounts."
rationale: Highly potent synthetic opioids (notably illicit fentanyl and its analogs) have very low lethal doses measured in micrograms to milligrams, so they constitute a new and serious public-health threat. However, the actual risk depends on route and amount of exposure—ingestion or inhalation of small quantities can kill, while brief skin contact is generally considered unlikely to cause overdose.

claim: There were "63 murders this weekend" in Chicago and Mayor Rahm Emanuel’s legacy is "more murders in his city than ever before."
rationale: No official reporting from the Chicago Police Department or reputable news outlets documented 63 homicides in a single recent weekend; viral figures of that size typically refer to shootings or incidents, not confirmed murders. Likewise, saying Rahm Emanuel’s legacy is "more murders in his city than ever before" is misleading—Chicago recorded far higher annual homicide totals in earlier periods (notably the early 1990s) and Emanuel’s mayoralty (2011–2019) did not produce an unprecedented all-time high. The claim conflates categories and omits date-specific sourcing.

claim: Says she helped lead the launch of curbside recycling.
rationale: The claim is unverifiable as written because it doesn't identify who 'she' is, when, or where the curbside recycling launch allegedly occurred. Without a named person, date, and reliable source documentation, the assertion cannot be confirmed and thus is treated as false for fact-checking purposes.

claim: Oregon’s "three largest employers, and 13 of the top 25, are health care providers."
rationale: Available employer rankings for Oregon show that the largest employers include non-health entities such as the State of Oregon, Intel, and major manufacturers/retailers; while several large hospital systems (Providence, OHSU, Legacy, Kaiser, PeaceHealth) are major employers, they do not occupy all three top positions nor make up 13 of the top 25 in typical lists. The claim therefore overstates the share of health-care providers among Oregon’s very largest employers.

claim: "President Obama took more money from Wall Street in the 2008 campaign than anybody ever had."
rationale: The claim overstates the facts. Barack Obama did raise record overall funds in 2008 and received substantial contributions from finance-industry individuals, but campaign finance data do not show that he took more "Wall Street" money than anyone in history; the term is vague and donations were spread across candidates and cycles.

claim: "(Assembly Democrats) wanted to raise the gas tax by $2.4 billion. We said no to that....They’re down on the ground. They’re sweating. They’re twitching. It’s ugly, ‘cause I keep saying no."
rationale: I cannot verify that Assembly Democrats formally proposed a specific $2.4 billion gas tax increase or that the quoted description of their physical reactions is factual. The statement mixes a concrete dollar figure with vivid, anecdotal language and lacks publicly verifiable context (which legislature, bill text, or official votes). Without corroborating legislative records or reporting tying Democrats to a $2.4 billion gas tax increase, the claim appears unverified or a rhetorical exaggeration.

claim: Says Jeb Bush tweeted "Ok boomer" at Donald Trump.
rationale: There is no credible evidence or contemporaneous media coverage that Jeb Bush tweeted “Ok boomer” at Donald Trump; such an interaction between two high-profile political figures would have been widely documented. Jeb Bush's known Twitter history and news archives do not show him using that phrase directed at Trump.

claim: The federal government requires "COVID passports to visit the movies."
rationale: There has been no U.S. federal requirement that people show 'COVID passports' to attend movie theaters; rules on proof of vaccination were set by states, cities, private businesses, or in some other countries by national governments. The claim as stated (a federal government requirement for movies) is therefore incorrect in the typical U.S. context.

claim: "mRNA Vaccines Show No Mortality Benefit - Danish Study"
rationale: The claim is an overgeneralization and mischaracterizes the evidence. While a specific Danish analysis may have reported no statistically significant change in all-cause mortality for a particular age group, numerous randomized trials and large population studies (including national data from multiple countries) show mRNA COVID-19 vaccines reduce COVID-19 hospitalizations and deaths; findings about all-cause mortality depend heavily on outcome definition, population, follow-up time and confounding. No single Danish study conclusively proves mRNA vaccines provide no mortality benefit in all contexts.

claim: "COVID19 PCR tests are scientifically meaningless."
rationale: PCR tests detect SARS-CoV-2 RNA by amplifying viral genetic material and have been clinically validated and widely used to diagnose and track COVID-19. While they have limitations—such as detecting non-viable viral fragments after recovery, variable cycle threshold (Ct) interpretations, and occasional false positives/negatives—these shortcomings do not make the method scientifically meaningless.

claim: Goldman Sachs was Barack Obama's "No. 1 private contributor."
rationale: The claim as stated is misleading: corporations cannot give directly to federal candidates, and while Goldman Sachs (its PAC and employees) were among the large private sources of contributions to Obama, they were not unambiguously the single "No. 1" private contributor without specifying year or whether one aggregates employee, PAC, and bundler donations. Campaign finance records show large support from the financial sector and from Goldman-linked donors, but the claim overstates a simple, singular ranking.

claim: 40,000 veterans in Texas won’t get health care because Perry rejected Obamacare's Medicaid expansion.
rationale: The specific claim that 40,000 Texas veterans 'won’t get health care' solely because Governor Perry refused Medicaid expansion is not supported. While Texas’s decision not to expand Medicaid under the ACA did leave many low-income adults uninsured, veterans are separately eligible for care through the VA and estimates of how many veterans would have gained coverage vary widely and do not establish a definitive 40,000 figure caused solely by the governor’s action.

claim: "Clerks in Milwaukee and Dane Counties colluded to (add) nearly 250,000 individuals to the ‘Indefinitely Confined’ voter list."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that clerks in Milwaukee and Dane Counties colluded to add nearly 250,000 people to the 'indefinitely confined' list. In Wisconsin the 'indefinitely confined' status is declared by voters (and recorded by clerks), and post‑election reviews and reporting found no substantiated coordinated scheme by those county clerks to mass‑enroll voters into that category.

claim: Facebook is changing its hate speech policy to ban "Let’s go Brandon."
rationale: As of my last reliable information through mid-2024, Meta/Facebook had not issued a blanket hate-speech ban specifically on the phrase "Let’s go Brandon." Platforms generally assess such slogans by context (e.g., whether they target a protected class or incite violence) and may remove posts for harassment or policy violations, but there was no widely reported policy change expressly banning that phrase across the site.

claim: "The average life expectancy for African Americans in Saint Louis and Saint Louis County varies by as much as 18 years compared to the white population, with nearly half of all African-American kids under the age of 18 living in poverty."
rationale: Multiple public-health analyses and local data have documented life-expectancy differences of roughly 15–18 years between predominantly Black neighborhoods and predominantly white neighborhoods in St. Louis City/County. Census and American Community Survey data also show very high child poverty rates for African-American children in St. Louis City — on the order of nearly half in several recent multi-year estimates.

claim: "More college graduates are living at home than in decades."
rationale: While overall rates of young adults living with their parents have risen in recent decades and spiked during economic downturns, the statement that 'more college graduates are living at home than in decades' is misleading. Data show the increases are concentrated among younger adults and those without college degrees, and trends for college graduates are smaller and vary by age group and time period.

claim: "Biden's plan is a 14% tax hike on middle class families."
rationale: The statement is vague and incorrect as phrased: Biden’s major tax proposals in 2020–21 primarily targeted high-income households (above $400k or $1M) and corporations, not broadly imposing a 14% tax hike on middle‑class families. Independent analyses (e.g., Tax Policy Center and other nonpartisan reviewers) found little or no comparable 14% increase in tax burdens for typical middle‑income households.

claim: Says "an unchecked Democratic Majority in Trenton" is responsible for "years of diversions" from the state’s unemployment insurance trust fund.
rationale: The claim is vague and attributes sole responsibility to an "unchecked Democratic Majority in Trenton" without specifying a time period. Historical problems with New Jersey’s unemployment insurance trust fund have resulted from a mix of factors — economic downturns, federal loans, statutory funding decisions and actions taken by both parties and multiple administrations — rather than a single-party, unchecked diversion over many years. There is no clear evidence that only an "unchecked Democratic Majority" caused years of diversions.

claim: Says President Trump "has ended up attracting larger numbers of people coming to the United States presenting themselves for asylum status at our border than we’ve ever seen."
rationale: While U.S. border encounters and asylum-seeking family unit crossings reached very high levels during parts of the Trump administration (notably FY2019), the statement that Trump "has ended up attracting larger numbers ... than we’ve ever seen" is misleading: it asserts causation and an absolute historical record without specification. Historical CBP data show peaks vary by year and category, and later years (after his term) also saw large numbers, so the blanket causal claim is not supported as stated.

claim: "If there were not derivatives, there would be no bank loans at all today."
rationale: Derivatives are risk-management and speculative instruments that can facilitate larger or more complex lending, but they are not a prerequisite for bank loans. Lending has existed for centuries long before modern derivatives markets, and many contemporary loans are made without use of derivatives. While derivatives can expand or reshape credit markets, the absence of derivatives would not eliminate all bank lending.

claim: Says Sen. Sherrod Brown "voted to block American energy production and increase energy taxes."
rationale: The claim is a broad, misleading summary with no single Senate vote in which Sherrod Brown explicitly 'voted to block American energy production' or enacted a blanket 'energy tax.' Brown has supported climate and clean‑energy legislation (including voting for the Inflation Reduction Act) and opposed certain fossil‑fuel projects, but those actions are regulatory or incentive‑based rather than a direct vote to ban domestic energy production or impose a general energy tax.

claim: Says 25 percent of Austin's public school buildings are "underutilized."
rationale: The statement gives a precise figure without a source; utilization percentages for school buildings depend on the district, year, and the definition of 'underutilized' and are not a fixed, universally agreed number. Without a cited AISD (or other Austin-area district) facilities report establishing 25% for a specific time, the claim is unverified and likely inaccurate.

claim: "Irish superstar Saoirse Ronan dies after on-set accident in St. Lucia."
rationale: There are no credible reports from major news outlets or official statements confirming that Saoirse Ronan died in an on-set accident in St. Lucia. Celebrity death hoaxes frequently circulate on social media, and such a high-profile event would be widely and reliably reported if true.

claim: "Not only is there no scientific evidence that CO2 is a pollutant, higher CO2 concentrations actually help ecosystems support more plant and animal life."
rationale: The claim is incorrect. Carbon dioxide is a well-established greenhouse gas and extensive scientific evidence links rising CO2 concentrations to global warming and broad harms to ecosystems and human systems; regulators (e.g., the U.S. EPA) treat CO2 as an air pollutant for climate impacts. While higher CO2 can stimulate plant photosynthesis in some experiments (the so‑called CO2 fertilization effect), those benefits are limited by nutrient, water, and pest constraints and are often outweighed by heat stress, drought, shifts in species interactions, and ocean acidification that harm marine life.

claim: Says Russ Feingold supported a stimulus plan that allowed a company to create 3,000 jobs in China.
rationale: While Senator Russ Feingold did vote for the 2009 federal stimulus (ARRA), there is no evidence that the legislation 'allowed' or directly caused a company to create 3,000 jobs in China. Stimulus laws provide funding and tax provisions aimed at stimulating the U.S. economy; they do not authorize companies to outsource or mandate where private firms hire. The claim appears to be a misleading causal attribution without specific supporting facts.

claim: Wisconsin's Lincoln Hills youth prison has a "66 percent recidivism rate," while "states like Missouri, that have more of a regional model -- 8 percent."
rationale: The two figures are misleadingly compared: Lincoln Hills has been reported to have a high recidivism rate under certain measures, but the 66% figure comes from a specific cohort and time window, while Missouri’s “8%” is a differently defined metric from its Division of Youth Services (often measuring return to secure confinement under a different follow-up period). Because the jurisdictions use different definitions, populations, and timeframes, the claim’s direct juxtaposition is inaccurate and not a valid one-to-one comparison.

claim: "We're not allowed to read it (the Trans-Pacific Partnership) before representatives vote on it."
rationale: Congressional members and designated, cleared staff were given access to the full TPP text before any final vote, though access was restricted (secure reading rooms, no public posting or uncontrolled copying). Saying 'we're not allowed to read it before representatives vote' is inaccurate if referring to members of Congress, though the public and many outside groups were denied access until later.

claim: "Toomey crossed party lines… to stop gun sales to suspects on the terror watch list."
rationale: While Senator Pat Toomey has at times worked across the aisle on gun policy (notably the 2013 Toomey–Manchin background-check effort), he did not cross party lines to support a ban on gun sales solely to people on the terrorist watchlist. Toomey opposed using the watchlist as an automatic basis to deny gun purchases, citing due-process and redress concerns during Senate debates after major attacks.

claim: "We had the highest number of (military) sexual assaults ever reported in the last year" and "we had the lowest conviction rate and the lowest prosecution rate."
rationale: The statement is unsubstantiated as written because it omits which country or service and which year are meant. Publicly released annual military sexual assault reports (for example, U.S. Department of Defense reports) show year-to-year variation in reports, prosecutions, and convictions, and do not support a blanket claim that the most recent year was both the highest-ever for reports and the lowest for prosecutions and convictions without specifying jurisdiction and checking the official data.

claim: "The senior senator from Arizona (John McCain) said he couldn't support repealing 'don't ask, don't tell' because of the economy."
rationale: John McCain did oppose repealing 'don't ask, don't tell' at times, but his publicly stated reasons focused on military readiness, unit cohesion and the timing of taking up a divisive social issue during wartime, not that he opposed repeal because of the economy. Contemporary news accounts and his floor statements attributed his objection to national security and timing concerns rather than economic reasons.

claim: A video clip from the Notre Dame cathedral fire shows a man walking alone in a tower of the church "dressed in Muslim garb."
rationale: While a short clip circulated showing a person in a tower during the Notre Dame fire, independent fact-checkers found no evidence the individual was 'dressed in Muslim garb' or that the footage proved a religiously motivated presence. The clothing in low-quality viral video is ambiguous and identity or religion cannot be determined from it, and reputable reporting did not corroborate the claim.

claim: "So Trump comes to Nashville to oversee damage from the tornado. He flies into the area in a helicopter to get there without further traffic problems in the city. He writes PERSONAL checks to those in need, with his personal accountant in tow."
rationale: There are no credible reports that Donald Trump personally wrote checks to tornado victims in Nashville or traveled there with his personal accountant to distribute money. While presidential travel often uses helicopters (Marine One) and officials sometimes visit disaster sites, the specific claim that he flew in to avoid traffic and handed out personal checks with his accountant accompanying him is unsubstantiated and implausible given standard federal disaster-response protocols.

claim: "We know mask mandates work. There’s enough evidence out there between counties that have done it and counties that haven’t."
rationale: A substantial body of evidence from observational comparisons of counties and regions with and without mandates, quasi-experimental analyses, meta-analyses, and some community randomized trials shows that mask mandates increase mask use and are associated with reduced COVID-19 transmission, hospitalizations, and deaths. Public health agencies have reviewed this evidence and concluded masks help limit spread, so the general claim that there is enough evidence between jurisdictions to conclude mandates work is supported.

claim: "When the union says I want to eliminate tenure, that’s not true."
rationale: The statement is a denial but provides no context (who is speaking, which union, or which form of 'tenure' is at issue), so it cannot be verified as true. Without specific evidence such as the speaker's policy statements, voting record, or the union's documented claims, the assertion that the union's claim is untrue is unsubstantiated.

claim: "As soon as Biden took office, he eliminated all subsidies for fossil fuels."
rationale: Biden did not eliminate all fossil-fuel subsidies upon taking office. He issued climate-focused executive orders (including pausing new federal oil and gas leasing pending review and rejoining the Paris Agreement) and proposed cutting some subsidies in budget proposals, but many federal tax preferences and other subsidies remained and would require congressional action to repeal.

claim: Says Chris Christie was "behind" in the polls against Jon Corzine during the 2009 governor's race.
rationale: Most statewide polls and polling aggregates during the 2009 New Jersey governor's race showed Chris Christie leading or tied with incumbent Jon Corzine for much of the campaign, and Christie ultimately won the election. While isolated individual polls at particular times might have shown Corzine slightly ahead, the overall polling picture did not have Christie behind.

claim: Republicans are "trying to create a fake unemployment insurance crisis."
rationale: The claim attributes a unified, deceptive intent to all Republicans and asserts they are "trying" to manufacture a fake unemployment insurance crisis — a specific coordinated intent that cannot be established as factual. While many Republican lawmakers have criticized unemployment insurance programs, proposed cuts, or highlighted fraud and solvency concerns, those actions and political rhetoric do not prove a coordinated effort to fabricate a crisis across the entire party.

claim: "NASA confirms earth will go dark for 6 days in December 2020."
rationale: There is no record of NASA confirming that Earth would go dark for six days in December 2020; NASA and other scientific agencies issued no such warning. No known astronomical event in December 2020 could have caused a global six-day darkness, and the claim matches common hoaxes and misinformation.

claim: It "is estimated that as many as 300,000 auto workers may be out of a job before the end of the year."
rationale: The statement is an unverified, round-number estimate presented without a source, timeframe, or specified country; such precise large-scale job-loss claims require attribution to labor statistics, company announcements, or credible analyses. Without a named source or date, the figure of "as many as 300,000" cannot be confirmed and is therefore treated as unsupported.

claim: Says he has supported "George Bush more than I have Barack Obama."
rationale: The claim asserts that someone said "I supported George Bush more than I have Barack Obama," but gives no named speaker, date, or source to verify the quote. Without an identified person or independent reporting, the statement cannot be corroborated, so it is treated as unverified and therefore labeled false per the instruction to prefer FALSE when uncertain. If a specific speaker and reliable source are provided, the quote could be checked.

claim: "There are actually only 30 countries that practice birthright citizenship."
rationale: The exact count depends on how you define "birthright" (unconditional jus soli vs. conditional jus soli) and whether you include territories; sources therefore give different totals. While some sources round to "about 30" for unconditional birthright, many more countries grant citizenship at birth under conditions (parental residency, legal status), and laws change over time, so the blanket statement that there are "only 30" is misleading and not reliably accurate.

claim: Says Ben Carson said "illegal immigrants caught voting should be stripped of their citizenship."
rationale: There is no credible record of Ben Carson saying the quoted line; major fact‑checks and news outlets found the attribution to be false. While Carson has advocated strong penalties for illegal voting and strict immigration policies at times, he did not publicly state that illegal immigrants who vote should be "stripped of their citizenship."

claim: "Simply being in this country without documentation is not a crime"
rationale: The statement as a universal claim is false because immigration laws differ by country. In some places (including parts of U.S. practice) mere unlawful presence is treated as a civil immigration violation, but illegal entry or reentry can be a criminal offense; other countries criminalize unauthorized presence more broadly.

claim: "I had prostate cancer, five, six years ago. My chance of surviving prostate cancer, and thank God I was cured of it, in the United States, 82%. My chances of surviving prostate cancer in England, only 44% under socialized medicine."
rationale: The stated figures are incorrect: modern prostate cancer survival in both the United States and England is far higher than 44% (five-year relative survival in both countries is generally in the high-80s to >90% for many recent periods). The claim appears to mix up metrics, timeframes, or stages and uses a misleading political label for the NHS rather than reporting actual survival data.

claim: "Nancy Pelosi just bought a 11,000 square foot $25 million mansion in Florida."
rationale: There is no credible reporting or public financial-disclosure evidence that Nancy Pelosi or her husband recently purchased an 11,000-square-foot, $25 million mansion in Florida. A purchase of that size by a high-profile politician would be widely reported and appear in public records, but no such evidence is available up to mid-2024.

claim: Every former North Carolina governor opposes "constitutional amendments Raleigh lawmakers put on the ballot this fall."
rationale: The claim asserts unanimous opposition from every former North Carolina governor, which is a categorical statement not supported by public records. Former governors have taken varied positions (some opposed, some supported, and some declined to comment) on ballot amendments, so there is no documented unanimity of opposition.

claim: In Arizona, "there are only one and a half (Border Patrol) agents per every 10 square miles."
rationale: The claim is misleading: Border Patrol staffing is reported and deployed by sector and along border miles, not evenly across an entire state’s total square mileage. Using Arizona’s full land area to compute 'agents per 10 square miles' understates concentrations of agents along the international border and ignores temporal variation in staffing levels, so the stated ratio is not a reliable factual statistic.

claim: "Obama has proposed 442 tax hikes since taking office."
rationale: Independent fact-checkers found the "442" figure results from a misleading tally method (counting many line items, repeated proposals across years, technical changes, and revenue offsets) rather than 442 distinct, unilateral tax rate increases on taxpayers. The claim conflates different types of budgetary provisions and double-counts items, so it overstates and mischaracterizes what was proposed.

claim: "@BernieSanders receives strong support from the conservative & most rural part of Vermont."
rationale: Bernie Sanders is broadly popular statewide and often wins many rural counties in Vermont, but it is inaccurate to say the conservative and most rural parts uniformly give him strong support. Many of Vermont’s most rural areas (for example parts of the Northeast Kingdom and other traditionally Republican counties) lean conservative and do not consistently provide overwhelming backing for a progressive white‑national‑senator label. Saying they 'receive strong support' overstates and homogenizes varied voting patterns.

claim: Rubio's "got more experience than Obama had."
rationale: The claim is presented as an absolute statement but is ambiguous and not clearly supported. Whether Rubio had "more experience" than Obama depends on which types of experience and which moment in time are compared: Obama had federal Senate experience and prior legal/community-organizing work before his presidential run, while Rubio had many years in Florida state government plus fewer years in the U.S. Senate. As a blanket assertion without context it is misleading and cannot be treated as true.

claim: Former Gov. Pat McCrory appointed liberals to the North Carolina Textbook Commission, which "mandated textbooks" pushing critical race theory.
rationale: There is no reliable evidence that Governor Pat McCrory appointed a bloc of 'liberals' to a North Carolina Textbook Commission that then 'mandated' textbooks promoting critical race theory. North Carolina's textbook adoption involves multiple review steps, public input, and state education bodies rather than a single governor-run fiat, and reported controversies around standards did not result in an official statewide mandate of CRT in K–12 textbooks.

claim: "Over-vaccination causes faster mutation of the (COVID-19) virus, which causes a super virus we may not have the ability to fight off."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that 'over-vaccination' causes faster mutation leading to an unstoppable 'super virus.' Viral mutation rate is driven by the amount of replication; by preventing infections and reducing viral replication, vaccines generally reduce opportunities for new variants to emerge. While immune pressure can in theory select for escape mutations, real-world data show vaccination lowers cases, hospitalizations, and overall viral spread rather than accelerating dangerous mutation.

claim: Unvaccinated people "are making the vaccinated people sick and die, but the unvaccinated people are not dead or sick."
rationale: The claim is an absolute and inaccurate characterization. For COVID-19 and similar infectious diseases, unvaccinated people do contribute disproportionately to transmission, hospitalizations, and deaths, but many unvaccinated people do get sick or die and vaccinated people can still become infected and occasionally die (though at much lower rates). Saying unvaccinated people "are not dead or sick" is factually false and blaming them as the sole cause of all vaccinated illness/death ignores breakthrough infections and other risk factors.

claim: "Sean Duffy backed plan to privatize Social Security."
rationale: There is no clear, widely reported record that Rep. Sean Duffy endorsed a plan to fully privatize Social Security. He supported Republican budgets and reforms aimed at reducing future liabilities (changes to retirement age or COLA formulas) but did not publicly champion a definitive full-privatization plan converting benefits into private accounts.

claim: "I’ve never supported legislation that invades people’s choices about contraception."
rationale: The claim is a universal negative about a person’s legislative history but provides no named speaker, timeframe, or record to verify. Without a specific individual and their voting/sponsorship history this cannot be confirmed, and many public officials have at times supported legislation that affects contraception.

claim: A Fox News affiliate reported on a shooting before it happened.
rationale: The claim is vague and there is no specific, verifiable instance provided. I am not aware of any reliably documented case in which a Fox News affiliate published a report of a shooting before the event occurred; while newsrooms sometimes make timing or prewritten-content errors, that does not confirm this assertion. Without a date, location, or source, the claim cannot be substantiated.

claim: Says Republican-approved changes to "make it more difficult to participate in Ohio elections include reducing in-person early voting from 35 days to six."
rationale: There is no clear evidence that Ohio Republicans enacted a statewide cut of in-person early voting from 35 days to just six. Recent GOP-backed measures did restrict aspects of voting (drop boxes, weekend hours, ID rules) and narrowed some early voting windows in specific proposals, but they did not uniformly reduce in-person early voting to six days statewide.

claim: "We could cut unemployment in half simply by reclaiming the jobs taken by illegal workers."
rationale: The undocumented/illegal workforce is much smaller than the total number of unemployed and many unemployed workers are not willing, available, or qualified to take the specific low-wage, sectoral jobs that undocumented workers often hold. Unemployment includes structural and frictional components (skills mismatch, geographic mismatch, search time) that cannot be eliminated simply by replacing one group of workers with another, so "reclaiming" those jobs would not plausibly cut unemployment in half.

claim: "Less mass shootings under Trump!"
rationale: The statement is an unqualified, comparative claim but lacks a defined time period and definition of “mass shooting.” Available datasets and reporting (definitions vary) do not support a simple claim of fewer mass shootings during Trump’s presidency; by many common definitions and trackers, mass-shooting incidents and casualties were stable or increased in 2017–2020 and several high-profile events occurred in that period. Therefore the blanket assertion is unsupported.

claim: "8 Syrians caught at Texas border in Laredo."
rationale: I cannot verify this specific claim: there are no corroborating reports or authoritative sources in my knowledge base up to June 2024 that confirm ‘‘8 Syrians caught at Texas border in Laredo.’’ Without a date, source, or official confirmation the claim remains unverified and should not be treated as established fact.

claim: With Medicare for All, "study after study has shown that ... the average middle-class families will save $3,000 each and every year on their health care bills."
rationale: There is no consensus 'study after study' showing a uniform $3,000 annual saving for the average middle‑class family under Medicare for All. Analyses reach divergent conclusions—some project substantial savings for many households, others project smaller savings or net higher costs once taxes replacing premiums are counted—because results depend heavily on how 'middle class' is defined and which costs (premiums, out‑of‑pocket, taxes) and plan features are included.
cited_knowledge: Multiple economic and policy analyses (from academic papers and think tanks) of single‑payer proposals produce widely varying estimates driven by differing assumptions about provider payment rates, tax financing, covered benefits, and baseline health spending.
safety_notes: Estimates vary by proposal design, household income definition, and whether taxes replacing premiums are counted; precise impacts would depend on specific legislative details.

claim: Says Chris Christie was the "first governor in America to endorse" Mitt Romney.
rationale: The statement as phrased is ambiguous and overbroad. Chris Christie did endorse Mitt Romney in January 2012 and was widely reported as the first sitting governor to back Romney in the 2012 Republican primary, but saying he was the “first governor in America to endorse” Romney without specifying the campaign/year is misleading because other governors (or former governors) had endorsed Romney in different cycles or contexts.

claim: "In 2011, texting surpassed alcohol as the leading contributing factor in teen driving deaths."
rationale: Contemporary federal crash data and independent fact-checkers do not support a clear finding that texting overtook alcohol as the leading contributing factor in teen driving deaths in 2011. Alcohol-impaired driving remained a major contributor, and estimates of texting/cellphone involvement were limited by underreporting and inconsistent definitions of distraction.

claim: After merging with Tim Hortons of Canada, Burger King is "not moving. … Our headquarters will remain in Miami" and "(we) will continue to pay all of our federal, state and local U.S. taxes."
rationale: Although Burger King executives said operational headquarters would remain in Miami and that U.S. operations would continue paying U.S. taxes, the 2014 merger created Restaurant Brands International, a Canadian-headquartered parent based in Toronto, and the deal was widely characterized as a tax inversion that reduced U.S. tax liability. The statements are therefore misleading and not accurate as presented.

claim: The Greenlight Pinellas transportation plan involves a "300% tax increase."
rationale: Greenlight Pinellas proposed a modest local sales surtax to fund transit improvements (a small fraction of a percent added to the sales tax, commonly described as a one-cent or similar county surtax), not a 300% tax hike. Describing it as a "300% tax increase" is a gross mischaracterization or miscalculation of the measure's actual tax rate change.

claim: "Given the results of the primary, the vote of one New Hampshire superdelegate is equal to the votes of about 10,000 grassroots activists."
rationale: The claim is misleading: a New Hampshire superdelegate casts a single delegate vote at a nominating convention, not a bundle equivalent to thousands of individual grassroots votes. Any numeric equivalence (e.g., 1 superdelegate = 10,000 activists) depends on an arbitrary division of popular votes or activists by a small number of superdelegates and is not an official or fixed conversion. Without a clear definition of “grassroots activists” or the specific primary figures used, the stated 10,000 ratio is unsupported.

claim: "In two years, Gov. McAuliffe has vetoed more bills that the previous three governors issued in each of their four-year terms."
rationale: The claim asserts that Gov.
