claim: "Biden won’t allow Delta-variant COVID patients to get proven and effective monoclonal treatments even though there are 50,000-100,000 Americans infected by Delta EVERY DAY."
rationale: This claim is false. The federal government has not banned monoclonal antibody treatments for Delta patients — several monoclonal antibody therapies retained FDA emergency use authorization and were procured and distributed by HHS and state partners, though specific monoclonal products were withdrawn or had their EUAs revised when evidence showed they were ineffective against certain variants. Daily U.S. COVID case counts have varied over time and are not reliably a constant 50,000–100,000 Delta infections every single day; access issues that occurred were typically due to supply, changing guidance, or state-level distribution, not an across-the-board prohibition by President Biden.

claim: California’s marijuana legalization initiative, Prop. 64 "allows marijuana smoking ads in prime time, on programs with millions of children and teenage viewers."
rationale: Prop. 64 did not broadly allow marijuana ads to be run in prime-time programs with large child and teen audiences. The measure explicitly prohibits marketing targeted at persons under 21 and gives regulators authority to restrict advertising placement and content to avoid targeting minors, so blanket claims that it permits prime-time ads on programs with millions of children are misleading.

claim: Says Rick Scott has "teamed up with a felon convicted of running a Ponzi scheme to smear Charlie Crist."
rationale: There is no credible public reporting or court record showing that Rick Scott formally 'teamed up' with a person convicted of running a Ponzi scheme to attack Charlie Crist. While Scott and allied groups have run negative ads and used outside donors against Crist, I could find no verified evidence tying those efforts to a Ponzi-scheme felon.

claim: "If you like your health care plan, you can keep your health care plan."
rationale: This statement was widely repeated about the Affordable Care Act but proved inaccurate in practice: millions of people received cancellation notices because their existing individual plans did not meet new ACA standards or insurers changed offerings. President Obama later acknowledged that the promise did not hold universally. While some plans that complied with new rules could be retained, the categorical claim was misleading.

claim: "People (are) paying more in taxes than they will for food, housing and clothing combined."
rationale: The claim is an overly broad generalization with no country, income group, or time period specified. Tax burdens and household spending patterns vary widely: for most households in most countries, combined spending on necessities (food, housing, clothing) is greater than the total taxes they pay, although some high-income households or residents of very high‑tax countries may pay more in taxes than those specific expenditures. Because the statement asserts a universal truth without qualifiers, it is incorrect as stated.

claim: "Klein did not hold a single town hall meeting (on health care) where the general public was invited to ask questions or present their views."
rationale: This claim is false. During Ralph Klein’s tenure there were multiple health‑care 'town hall' or public consultation events; while many were criticized for being tightly controlled or invitation‑only, contemporary reporting and records show some sessions were publicly advertised and allowed public questions or comments. The historical record indicates a mix of formats rather than an absolute absence of public‑invited Q&A.

claim: The House budget plan proposes "the largest discretionary spending cut in history."
rationale: The statement is ambiguous and unsupported as a blanket claim: whether a proposal is the "largest discretionary spending cut in history" depends on the baseline (nominal vs. inflation‑adjusted, one‑year vs. multi‑year, cumulative cuts vs. difference from current law). Independent scoring agencies and historical comparisons are required to substantiate such a superlative, and past events (for example sequesters and major budget acts) have produced very large discretionary reductions by some measures. Without a specific baseline or formal CBO scoring showing it exceeds all prior cuts, the claim is not verifiable and is therefore false as stated.

claim: "The amount of money that we put into running our own state legislature is nearly as much as we put into the University of Rhode Island."
rationale: State legislative operating budgets are typically a tiny fraction of a public university's funding. The University of Rhode Island receives tens to hundreds of millions in annual funding (state appropriations plus tuition and other revenue), whereas the cost to run a state legislature is generally only a few million per year, so they are not 'nearly as much.'

claim: "Governor (Perry), you were a Democrat, having worked for Al Gore as his campaign manager..."
rationale: The claim mixes a partly true fact with a false one. Rick Perry was affiliated with the Democratic Party early in his career but he never served as Al Gore’s campaign manager; there are no credible records showing Perry worked on Gore’s campaigns in that role (Gore’s campaigns had different senior staff).

claim: Hillary Clinton wants to "wave the white flag of surrender and set a date for withdrawal."
rationale: There is no reliable record that Hillary Clinton advocated 'waving the white flag of surrender and setting a date for withdrawal.' Her documented foreign-policy positions have typically emphasized conditions-based withdrawals and she has often rejected fixed timetables; the quoted phrasing appears to be partisan rhetoric rather than a factual statement of her policy or words. Without a specific time or source this claim is unsubstantiated.

claim: A video shows "the COVID-19 vaccine when it hits your blood."
rationale: Such videos are misleading: vaccine components (mRNA, proteins, lipid nanoparticles) are molecular or nanoscale and cannot be seen in ordinary video footage of blood. Investigations of viral clips have found they typically show artifacts, contaminants, unrelated fluids, or microscope imaging misinterpreted as 'vaccine hitting blood.'

claim: Says a "Canadian provincial prime minister came to Ohio for his medical treatment because of the delay in Canadian health care which would have endangered his life."
rationale: The claim is vague and unverified: Canadian subnational leaders are titled 'premiers', not 'provincial prime ministers', and there are no credible reports of a Canadian premier traveling to Ohio for life‑saving treatment because of dangerous delays in Canadian health care. A high‑profile medical evacuation of a sitting or recent premier for that reason would have been widely reported in major Canadian and international media, but no such documentation exists.

claim: "If you take into account all the people who are struggling for work, or have just stopped looking, the real unemployment rate is over 15 percent."
rationale: The claim is presented as a general truth but omits any country or timeframe, so it cannot be universally verified. For the U.S., the broader BLS unemployment measure (U-6), which includes discouraged and marginally attached workers, has exceeded 15% during severe downturns (e.g., 2009–2010 and April 2020) but is not consistently above 15% in normal periods. Therefore the blanket statement that the "real" unemployment rate is over 15% is misleading without specific context.

claim: "If Obamacare is fully implemented, 30 million people will still be without health insurance."
rationale: Major nonpartisan analyses and post-implementation data do not support a firm claim that exactly 30 million would remain uninsured. CBO and other projections generally forecast the remaining uninsured in the low-to-mid 20 millions under full implementation, and empirical counts after rollout were roughly in that mid-20 million range; estimates vary with assumptions about Medicaid expansion, undocumented immigrants, and take-up.

claim: Says Michael Bennet wants to close Guantanamo Bay prison and bring terrorists "right here to Colorado."
rationale: Sen. Michael Bennet has supported closing Guantánamo Bay and moving detainees into U.S. custody for trial or secure detention, but he has not said he wants to ‘bring terrorists right here to Colorado.’ Political ads have mischaracterized his position; transfers would be to federal or military facilities under DOJ/DoD authority and are not simply relocations a single senator declares.

claim: "Fluoride in the water, that was originally done by the Nazis!"
rationale: Community water fluoridation was introduced as a public-health measure in the United States in the 1940s (notably Grand Rapids) to reduce tooth decay, based on dental research, and was not an invention or policy originating with Nazi Germany. Claims that 'fluoride in the water' was 'originally done by the Nazis' are conspiracy theories that misinterpret or distort disparate historical facts about fluoride's industrial uses and isolated alleged abuses.

claim: "We didn't go out and take" information from the Hillary Clinton campaign.
rationale: The claim as stated is ambiguous about who 'we' refers to, but on the key matter of whether information from the Clinton campaign was obtained and used by outside actors in 2016, authoritative investigations found that Russian intelligence hacked accounts associated with the Clinton campaign (including Podesta) and those emails were later published. A blanket assertion that 'we didn't go out and take' such information contradicts those findings in the widely reported 2016 interference case.

claim: Actions by Joe Biden left "10,000 - 15,000 American citizens abandoned to terrorists in Afghanistan."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that 10,000–15,000 U.S. citizens were left behind and handed over to terrorists in Afghanistan. U.S. government statements and independent fact-checking placed the number of U.S. citizens remaining after the evacuation in the low hundreds at most, and many much larger figures cited by critics conflate U.S. citizens with Afghans with U.S. ties, green card holders, or visa applicants. While the withdrawal and evacuation had serious failures, the specific numeric claim is unsupported.

claim: "Exit polls indicate that Democrats get over 70 percent of LGBT votes in federal elections."
rationale: National exit polls and post-election surveys in recent U.S. federal elections have repeatedly shown that self-identified LGBT voters favor Democratic candidates by large margins, typically in the roughly 70–80% range. While year-to-year variation exists, multiple reputable polls report Democratic shares above 70% for LGBT voters in presidential and congressional contests.

claim: "House Bill 6627 also requires the applicant to attest to their eligibility to vote, as is required by the National Voter Registration Act and used by all other states that have (automatic voter registration)."
rationale: The federal NVRA does require an attestation of voter eligibility on the national mail registration form, and many automatic voter registration (AVR) systems incorporate an attestation step. However I cannot verify the text of a specific 'House Bill 6627' from the claim without knowing the jurisdiction or seeing the bill language, and not all AVR implementations use identical mechanisms. Because the claim asserts a specific requirement and a universal practice across 'all other states,' it overstates what can be confirmed.

claim: After Fahrenheit 9/11 came out, "Bush's approval rating never was better, it only got worse."
rationale: George W. Bush's approval rating fluctuated after the June 2004 release of Fahrenheit 9/11; it did not only decline permanently from that point. There were temporary upticks (for example around his November 2004 re-election and in early 2005) before larger declines later in his presidency, so the blanket claim that it "never was better, it only got worse" is inaccurate.

claim: "Midtown crime is up by 30 percent the last quarter."
rationale: The claim is unverifiable as written because it fails to specify which 'Midtown', which types of crime, and which calendar quarter or year. Crime-statistic changes are location- and category-specific and must be backed by an official data source; without that, the blanket 30% increase cannot be confirmed. Given the missing context and common variability in reporting, the claim should be treated as unsupported.

claim: "Seventy four thousand... That’s how many mail-in ballots were recently found in Arizona that have NO clear record of being sent in."
rationale: The 74,000 figure is a misleading interpretation of ballot-tracking data. It came from counting records that lacked an "outgoing mail" flag in a specific database or audit spreadsheet, not proof that 74,000 ballots were cast without being requested or mailed; many of those records reflect in-person returns, drop-box returns, duplicate entries, provisional/military ballots, or data-sync issues. Election officials and independent fact-checkers reviewed the data and found no evidence that 74,000 illegal mail-in ballots were discovered.

claim: "President Trump just saved Christmas for 13 million retirees."
rationale: The claim is vague and unsubstantiated — there is no specific, verifiable action by President Trump documented that unambiguously "saved Christmas for 13 million retirees." Major policy changes affecting that many retirees (Social Security, Medicare, large stimulus payments) require legislation or clear executive orders with documented beneficiaries; I can find no authoritative evidence tying a single Trump action to rescuing exactly 13 million retirees. The statement reads like partisan rhetoric rather than a factual, verifiable event.

claim: Says our national debt is greater than our gross domestic product.
rationale: The claim omits which country and which year; debt-to-GDP ratios vary by country and over time. While some nations (for example Japan and in recent years the United States) have national debt exceeding their GDP, many others do not, so the blanket statement as presented is not verifiably true.

claim: "As chair of the Senate Education Committee, I led the charge to restore most of the education cuts from last session."
rationale: The statement is not verifiable as presented because it lacks essential context—no speaker identity, jurisdiction (which senate), or session/year—so there is no public record to confirm that this person, as committee chair, led efforts that restored 'most' of prior education cuts. Claims about leading legislative action and restoring budget cuts require specific evidence of bills, votes, amendments, and budget figures. Without those, the claim cannot be substantiated and should be treated as unproven.

claim: "Before the pandemic, just over 40,000 were on continuing UI claims. Now, there are well over 100,000 on state or federal UI benefits."
rationale: The statement is not verifiable as written because it gives no jurisdiction or specific dates; UI caseloads differ widely by state and over time. National and state continuing-claim counts are published weekly and depend on whether federal pandemic programs are included, so a blanket before/now comparison claiming specific round numbers is unsubstantiated without context or a source.

claim: Says Rick Scott "cut $700 million from water management."
rationale: The claim oversimplifies and misstates budget actions. Fact-checks of Rick Scott’s record as Florida governor show no single, documented action in which he outright "cut $700 million from water management" — budget changes were spread across years, different programs and agencies, included vetoes, restorations, and reallocated funds, and various totals have been aggregated or conflated to reach that number.

claim: "Disneyland estates have been used for MK-ULTRA mind control, human trafficking, occult rituals, and parading sexual deviants."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Disneyland properties were used for CIA MK‑ULTRA experiments, organized human trafficking, occult rituals, or public displays of sexual deviance. MK‑ULTRA was a documented Cold War–era CIA program conducted in research and institutional settings, and reputable news reporting and law enforcement records do not corroborate these specific allegations about Disneyland. The claim appears to be a mix of conspiracy theory and urban legend rather than fact.

claim: "The U.S. spends more money on its military than the 16 biggest military budgets in the world" combined.
rationale: Public defense-spending datasets (e.g., SIPRI) show the U.S. spends more than the next several largest military budgets combined, but not more than the next 16. In recent years the U.S. has exceeded the combined total of roughly the next 10–12 largest spenders, while summing the next 16 largest national budgets produces a figure larger than the U.S. budget.

claim: State Rep. Elena Parent "supported Governor Nathan Deal’s plan to slash the HOPE scholarship."
rationale: There is no reliable evidence that Elena Parent, a Democratic Georgia legislator, endorsed Governor Nathan Deal’s proposal to cut the HOPE scholarship; Democrats in the legislature broadly opposed Deal’s HOPE reductions and Parent’s public record does not show support for slashing the program. Without a documented vote or statement indicating she backed the plan, the claim is unsupported.

claim: Wisconsin bill "grants drug companies and medical device manufacturers immunity from injuries and deaths caused by their products."
rationale: A blanket statement that a Wisconsin bill "grants drug companies and medical device manufacturers immunity from injuries and deaths caused by their products" is incorrect. While some proposals or laws can create limited liability protections in specific contexts (for example for government-authorized products, state procurement, or during declared public-health emergencies), they do not generally eliminate all legal liability for manufacturers for injuries or wrongful deaths under state product-liability and negligence law. Determination depends on the exact bill text and scope, and most legislation imposes narrow immunities rather than broad, absolute shields.

claim: "Senator Robert Hurt voted for a bill that’s raised your electric rates seven times."
rationale: The claim is unsubstantiated and ambiguous: there is no clear evidence that a person named 'Senator Robert Hurt' cast a vote on a specific bill that directly 'raised your electric rates seven times.' Robert Hurt is better known as a former U.S. Representative (and earlier a state legislator), not a current U.S. Senator, and no authoritative record ties him to a single bill that caused seven discrete rate increases. Without identification of the bill, jurisdiction, and timeline, the assertion cannot be verified.

claim: "In 2017, we had more marijuana possession arrests in our country than all other violent crimes combined."
rationale: The claim is unlikely for a typical country (such as the United States in 2017): marijuana possession arrests numbered in the low hundreds of thousands, while arrests for violent crimes (homicide, robbery, aggravated assault, rape) in aggregate were higher. Therefore it is incorrect to say marijuana possession arrests exceeded all violent-crime arrests combined for that year.

claim: "The first so-called second hand information ‘Whistleblower’ got my phone conversation almost completely wrong."
rationale: This is a specific factual assertion about the accuracy of a particular whistleblower’s summary of a phone call, but no corroborating evidence (transcript, audio, or other independent accounts) is provided to confirm the claim. Without primary-source verification, the assertion cannot be confirmed and should be treated as unverified; per instructions, I default to FALSE when uncertain.

claim: "Republicans want to restore #gunrights to felons"
rationale: The claim is an overgeneralization. While many Republican politicians and some Republican-led states support Second Amendment rights and have backed measures to restore firearm rights to certain categories of felons (for example nonviolent offenders, or after expungement/pardons), the party does not uniformly advocate restoring gun rights to all felons and individual Republicans hold differing positions.

claim: Says "Congressman Eric Cantor wants to eliminate Social Security."
rationale: This is misleading: Eric Cantor advocated changes and reforms to Social Security (such as raising the retirement age, adjusting benefits, and supporting private-account options) but did not call for outright elimination of the program. His public statements and legislative positions focused on restructuring rather than abolishing Social Security.

claim: "Part of the increase in the cost (of higher education) has been because state support has dropped. We now spend, under Governor Walker, more on corrections than we do on higher education."
rationale: While it is true that reductions in state support have contributed to rising tuition, the specific claim that Wisconsin under Governor Scott Walker spent more on corrections than on higher education is not supported by typical budget data. State appropriations for higher education, even after cuts, generally remained larger than corrections spending in the years of Walker’s administration. The statement conflates related trends (cuts to higher ed and rising corrections costs) into an inaccurate absolute comparison.

claim: The Paul Ryan budget proposal would "privatize Medicare."
rationale: Paul Ryan’s budget proposals convert Medicare for future enrollees from a traditional defined‑benefit program into a premium‑support (voucher) system that would fund private plans and encourage beneficiaries to obtain coverage through competing private insurers. Nonpartisan analyses, including CBO commentary, concluded this would shift future beneficiaries into private coverage — an outcome commonly described as privatization.

claim: "They're saying that 40 percent of the traffic that goes over [the Sakonnet River Bridge is from] out of state."
rationale: I cannot verify a reliable source or recent traffic study that supports the specific claim that 40% of Sakonnet River Bridge traffic is from out of state. While some out-of-state vehicles (e.g., from neighboring Massachusetts) undoubtedly use the bridge, the exact percentage is unsubstantiated here and likely varies seasonally and by study methodology.

claim: The last private rocket launch "cost $80 million. If the government did it, the same thing would have cost probably 40 or 50 times that amount of money. I mean, literally."
rationale: This is an exaggerated and unsupported comparison. Typical private medium/heavy lift launches (e.g., Falcon 9) cost on the order of tens of millions of dollars, while government-run launches vary widely but are generally at most a few hundred million to a few billion dollars — not uniformly 40–50 times more than an $80M private launch. The claim’s blanket 40–50x multiplier is inconsistent with known launch prices and depends entirely on which government vehicle, accounting method, and amortization are used.

claim: "No Bridge to Nowhere could occur."
rationale: The claim is false because projects popularly labeled a “Bridge to Nowhere” have occurred or nearly occurred; political and budgeting processes can produce low‑value, high‑visibility infrastructure projects. For example, the proposed Gravina Island Bridge in Alaska received federal earmark attention before being cancelled, showing such outcomes are possible.

claim: Says when New York "implemented a program" to tax the wealthy at higher rates it saw a revenue shortfall "because of the outward migration of their top earners."
rationale: The claim asserts a clear causal link that a New York tax increase produced a revenue shortfall because top earners moved out. Empirical analyses of New York’s revenue fluctuations point to capital gains volatility and broader economic cycles (recessions, market swings) as the primary drivers of shortfalls; while some high‑income outmigration has occurred, studies and tax data show it was too small to account for major revenue declines on its own.

claim: Two federal government buses "stopped in front of a Mexican restaurant in the very small town of Green Cove Springs Florida… The passengers were illegal immigrants, straight from the southern border."
rationale: There is no reliable evidence or official confirmation that two federal government buses stopped in Green Cove Springs carrying 'illegal immigrants straight from the southern border.' Social media posts making this claim provided photos and anecdotes but lacked verifiable documentation (federal markings, manifests, or statements from federal or local authorities) tying the buses or passengers to a border transfer.

claim: "Our (Texas) graduation rate ranks 43rd out of 50 states."
rationale: The statement gives no year or data source and state graduation-rate rankings change yearly. Federal and state adjusted-cohort graduation-rate data do not consistently place Texas as 43rd — Texas typically falls nearer to the middle or higher depending on the year and metric. Without a specific year/source the categorical claim that Texas “ranks 43rd out of 50” is unsupported.

claim: Because of union rules, cooks helpers moved into DMV jobs they were not trained for
rationale: The statement is a specific causal claim presented without any jurisdiction, time frame, or evidence; there is no general rule that union provisions universally move kitchen/cook helpers into DMV positions for which they lack training. In most places unions and civil-service systems have job classifications, bidding/seniority rules, and agencies have qualification and training requirements for DMV roles, so the claim is unsupported as a blanket fact.

claim: "One of the reasons that Social Security is in so much trouble is that the only funding stream comes from people who get a wage. The people who get wages is declining dramatically."
rationale: The claim is inaccurate on both counts. Social Security’s primary funding is payroll taxes on wages and self-employment earnings, but it also receives interest on its trust funds and revenue from taxation of benefits — so payroll taxes are not the only source. Also, while the worker-to-beneficiary ratio has fallen as the population ages, the absolute number of wage earners in the U.S. has not been falling dramatically; the problem is slower worker growth relative to retirees, not a sharp drop in wage earners.

claim: "I investigated Abramoff and people ended up in jail."
rationale: The Jack Abramoff lobbying scandal did lead to convictions and prison sentences for Abramoff and several associates, but the claim asserts the speaker personally investigated Abramoff. Without knowing who 'I' refers to, that personal-actor claim cannot be verified. Therefore the statement as phrased is not supported.

claim: "We have over 300,000,000 weapons, firearms in this country. That’s almost as big as the population."
rationale: Reliable estimates place civilian-held firearms in the United States well above 300 million (Small Arms Survey and other analyses estimate roughly 350–400+ million in recent years). The U.S. population is about 330 million, so the number of firearms is indeed roughly comparable to the population. Thus the claim is accurate in broad terms.

claim: "Kids coming from an affluent background" are "taking advantage of all these student loan programs and grants" while many middle-class families with no connection to college are picking up the tab.
rationale: The statement is an overbroad characterization. In the U.S., need‑based grants (e.g., Pell Grants) are targeted to low‑ and moderate‑income students, while federal student loans are widely available but not exclusively captured by the affluent; many affluent families pay tuition out of pocket and do not rely on grants or loans. Whether middle‑class taxpayers ‘pick up the tab’ depends on which programs and tax subsidies are meant, so the blanket claim is misleading.

claim: Facebook users can avoid "problems with your Facebook going against community standards" by changing your settings.
rationale: Facebook enforces its community standards based on the content and behavior users post, not on individual account settings. While privacy or audience settings can limit who sees a post and some controls can reduce tagging or recommendations, they do not exempt content from review, removal, or other penalties if it violates the platform’s policies.

claim: Says Republican lawmakers delayed COVID-19 testing
rationale: The claim is a blanket assertion without specifying which lawmakers, which jurisdiction, or what time period; responsibility for early COVID-19 testing delays is primarily attributed to CDC test problems, regulatory constraints, and executive-administration decisions rather than any single party uniformly obstructing testing. Evidence shows a mix of actions by individual Republican lawmakers—some criticized delays and some opposed specific legislative approaches—but not clear proof that Republican lawmakers as a whole deliberately delayed testing nationwide.

claim: "No one has died of cancer or heart disease since the COVID-19 thing started."
rationale: This claim is false — cancer and heart disease continued to cause large numbers of deaths after the start of the COVID-19 pandemic and in many places remained the leading causes of mortality. National and international vital statistics from health agencies report thousands to millions of deaths from these conditions during pandemic years.

claim: Says she introduced a ban on "dirty dancing."
rationale: The claim as stated is vague and provides no named person, date, or jurisdiction; there is no well-documented instance of a prominent politician publicly saying she introduced a ban explicitly called 'dirty dancing.' While some local laws regulate 'lewd' or sexually explicit dancing, that is not the same as a named ban on 'dirty dancing.'

claim: Under H.R. 1, the Federal Election Commission "for the first time ever, instead of being an equal number of Republicans and Democrats (would be) three of one side and two of the other."
rationale: H.R.1 (the For the People Act) would restructure the Federal Election Commission from six members to five, with no more than three commissioners from the same political party. That change would institutionalize a 3-to-2 partisan majority rather than the prior statutory six-member structure that produced an equal possible split (three and three).

claim: Florida’s coastal and stormwater infrastructure are "two of the most critical areas during a storm, and received D-plus and D ratings, respectively, by the American Society of Civil Engineers in 2016."
rationale: The 2016 ASCE Florida Report Card identified coastal infrastructure and stormwater systems as among the most critical for storm resilience and assigned grades of D+ for coastal infrastructure and D for stormwater infrastructure. Both systems are widely recognized as crucial during storms because they protect shorelines and manage runoff and flooding.

claim: Says Ted Cruz "said I was in favor in Libya. I never discussed that subject."
rationale: The claim presents a specific quoted statement attributed to Ted Cruz but there is no well‑documented public record of him saying the exact line 'I was in favor in Libya. I never discussed that subject.' The phrasing is ambiguous and appears to be a likely misquote or out‑of‑context paraphrase rather than a verifiable direct quote.

claim: "While (Chris Christie) talks about job creation, we don't see jobs being created in this state."
rationale: The statement is a sweeping, time‑unspecified claim that jobs were not being created in ‘this state’ while Christie talked about job creation; as presented it lacks the specific timeframe and metrics needed to verify. Employment trends are measured by official payroll and unemployment data and varied during Christie’s tenure, so the blanket assertion cannot be confirmed. Because it is vague and not demonstrably true as stated, I mark it FALSE.

claim: "Drone technology now allows an individual to be recorded in their homes by drones as small as birds and immediately uploaded to the internet."
rationale: Compact consumer drones and research prototypes roughly the size of small birds exist and many carry onboard cameras plus wireless transmitters that can stream or upload footage in real time. That makes it technically possible for such a drone to enter a home, record a person, and immediately send the video to the internet, though exact capability depends on the model and operating conditions.

claim: Paul Ryan would "outlaw in vitro fertilization."
rationale: There is no clear record of Paul Ryan proposing or endorsing a policy to criminalize or outright outlaw in vitro fertilization. While Ryan is a consistent pro‑life politician who has supported restrictions on embryonic research and other measures to protect embryos, he has not advocated an explicit ban on IVF and public reporting and his voting record do not show sponsorship of legislation to outlaw IVF.

claim: "70 percent of the income tax that the state collects happens to come from Westchester, Nassau, Suffolk and New York City"
rationale: The claim gives a precise 70% figure without specifying year or tax type. Public fiscal data for New York show that New York City together with nearby downstate counties (Nassau, Suffolk, Westchester) account for a large majority of state personal income tax receipts, but published shares typically range around the mid-60s percent and vary by year and by whether one counts only PIT or broader tax categories, so the blanket 70% claim is not reliably supported as stated.

claim: "Politicians and their corporate lobbyists are trying to take away my right to spend my paycheck how I want."
rationale: The statement is a broad, generalized claim that lacks specifics and therefore is not uniformly true. While some politicians and industry lobbyists do push for particular laws or regulations (taxes, bans, age limits, licensing, product restrictions) that limit specific purchases, there is no universal, coordinated effort to strip people of the general right to spend their earnings as they choose; most consumer spending remains lawful and protected by existing legal and market frameworks.

claim: "Overdoses in Virginia (are) up 35%."
rationale: The claim as stated is too vague to verify — it gives no timeframe, metric (fatal overdoses, nonfatal overdoses, or ED visits), or source. Different reports for Virginia show varying percentage changes across years and measures, and no single authoritative figure of "up 35%" statewide can be confirmed without context.

claim: "Taxpayers earning $1 million pay an effective tax rate that is about four times what taxpayers earning $100,000 pay."
rationale: This overstates the gap. Recent U.S. IRS and tax-policy analyses show taxpayers with roughly $1 million in income generally face effective federal tax rates about two times (often in the 1.5–2.5x range) those of taxpayers earning about $100,000, not about four times. The claim likely confuses statutory marginal rates or selective cases with typical effective tax rates.

claim: U.S. Rep. Phil Gingrey wants public schools to teach women to "stay in their place."
rationale: There is no credible evidence or widespread reporting that Rep. Phil Gingrey explicitly called for public schools to teach women to "stay in their place." Such a striking directive would have been widely documented; public records show Gingrey has made conservative comments on gender and social issues but not this literal instruction to schools.

claim: On extreme-risk guns laws, "This idea has passed Republican legislatures in other states and has been signed by Republican governors."
rationale: The statement overstates the prevalence of extreme-risk (red flag/ERPO) laws passed by Republican-controlled legislatures and signed by Republican governors. While there are a small number of high-profile exceptions (for example, Florida’s 2018 law was enacted by a Republican legislature and signed by Republican Governor Rick Scott), most ERPO laws have been enacted in states with Democratic legislative control or Democratic governors; instances in reliably Republican legislatures are uncommon rather than widespread.

claim: President Obama’s health care law says "when you sell your house now you have to pay a 3.8 percent tax."
rationale: This is incorrect as stated. The Affordable Care Act created a 3.8% Net Investment Income Tax that can apply to capital gains for high-income taxpayers, but it does not require everyone who sells a house to pay 3.8%. Gains on a primary residence are often excluded up to $250,000/$500,000 under the tax code and the NIIT only applies when modified adjusted gross income exceeds statutory thresholds.

claim: Says "President Obama’s proposed oil tax would cost consumers 24 cents a gallon."
rationale: The 24 cents-per-gallon number was an industry/critic estimate that assumed full and immediate pass-through; independent analyses of Obama-era proposals and general economic modeling showed much smaller likely pump-price effects (only a few cents) and outcomes depend on the specific tax design and market conditions. Therefore the blanket claim that his proposed oil tax "would cost consumers 24 cents a gallon" is misleading and not reliably supported.

claim: Says President Barack Obama initially said the national health-care mandate isn't a tax, but his administration now says it is a tax.
rationale: President Obama and administration officials at times described the individual mandate/penalty as not a tax in public statements, but in defending the Affordable Care Act before the Supreme Court the administration argued the payment functions as a tax and can be upheld under Congress’s taxing power. The Roberts Court ultimately treated the payment as a tax for constitutional purposes in its decision.

claim: Says he can’t release his internal affairs record because there are Attorney General guidelines in place protecting it.
rationale: The claim is presented as a blanket justification but cannot be assumed true without jurisdiction-specific evidence. Attorney General guidelines vary widely and typically do not universally prohibit release of internal affairs records — some guidelines may advise temporary confidentiality during active investigations, while many public records laws require disclosure once investigations conclude.

claim: Says John F. Kennedy said, "If a Supreme Court Justice died one day before the election, it would be more Constitutional to indefinitely postpone the election than postpone the confirmation a single day."
rationale: There is no credible record or primary-source citation that John F. Kennedy ever made this statement, and the wording and substance do not match his documented speeches or writings. The claim appears to be a modern fabrication or misattribution and is inconsistent with constitutional practice and JFK's known rhetoric.

claim: People carrying guns can’t wear face masks to protect against the coronavirus because it’s a "class 4 felony."
rationale: This claim is false as a blanket statement: there is no general law making wearing a face mask while carrying a gun automatically a "class 4 felony." Anti-mask or "no disguise" statutes in some jurisdictions prohibit wearing masks to conceal identity during criminal activity, but they typically require criminal intent and many places exempt medical or public-health face coverings. Laws and felony classifications vary by state, so a universal claim that masks plus guns equals a class 4 felony is incorrect.

claim: Says Barack Obama "put in place a board that can tell people ultimately what treatments they're going to receive."
rationale: There was no board created by President Obama that has authority to order what specific medical treatments individual patients receive. The Affordable Care Act created the Independent Payment Advisory Board (IPAB) to make Medicare cost‑containment recommendations for policy, not to direct individual patient care, and widely circulated “death panel” claims conflated or mischaracterized unrelated provisions.

claim: Says Nevada Gov. Steve Sisolak "has banned the use of an anti-malaria drug that might help cure coronavirus."
rationale: There is no evidence that Nevada Gov. Steve Sisolak issued a blanket ban on the anti-malarial drug hydroxychloroquine for COVID-19; state and federal actions instead focused on prescribing guidance, supply protections, and the FDA later revoked its emergency use authorization. Governors generally did not 'ban' the drug outright, though some hospitals and health systems implemented their own prescribing restrictions.

claim: "Terry (McAuliffe) calls in his friend Joe Biden to actually put the DOJ on Virginia parents."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Terry McAuliffe personally phoned President Biden to order the Department of Justice to target Virginia parents. While the Biden administration and DOJ did announce attention to threats and harassment at school board meetings and prosecutors pursued related complaints, that was based on reported threats and agency priorities, not a documented private directive from McAuliffe to Biden.

claim: Says CNN reported Ben Carson was "taking a break from campaigning" and the Cruz campaign "forwarded that news to our volunteers."
rationale: I cannot verify that CNN used the exact phrase 'taking a break from campaigning' about Ben Carson nor that the Cruz campaign 'forwarded that news to our volunteers.' The claim is presented without a date, link, or additional context, and my available knowledge does not recall a verified instance combining those specific quoted phrases. Absent corroborating contemporaneous reporting or primary evidence, the assertion is unproven and should be treated as false.

claim: Says "we know" Erika Harold would "discriminate against a loving gay couple who want to adopt a child, favoring an abusive straight couple instead."
rationale: The statement presents a definitive assertion about Erika Harold's actions and intent without citing direct evidence. I am not aware of any public record—such as a quote, policy statement, or official action—in which Harold explicitly says she would favor an abusive straight couple over a loving gay couple for adoption, so the claim is unsubstantiated as presented.

claim: "This year, a majority of states are seeing premiums and costs double" under Obamacare.
rationale: Available analyses of marketplace premiums and insurer filings do not show that a majority of U.S. states experienced a doubling of premiums or overall consumer costs in any recent single year. While some states and specific plans saw very large increases, most states had smaller rate changes and many saw modest increases or even decreases.

claim: "Look at what’s happening last night in Sweden. Sweden, who would believe this? Sweden. They took in large numbers. They’re having problems like they never thought possible."
rationale: The statement implies a specific major incident occurred “last night in Sweden” because the country “took in large numbers.” Independent reporting and Swedish authorities found no such single overnight event matching that claim; it appears to conflate broader immigration and integration issues with a nonexistent immediate incident. While Sweden accepted a high per-capita number of refugees in 2015–2016 and faces long-term integration challenges, the specific ‘‘last night’’ claim is inaccurate and misleading.

claim: Says "If Oregon’s Legislature simply authorizes $450 million for the CRC, it will … leave Oregon holding the bag for a great deal more cost responsibility."
rationale: This is a speculative claim about future fiscal responsibility that depends on the specific legal terms, matching requirements, and intergovernmental agreements attached to any $450 million authorization. Without the exact authorization language and commitments from Washington and federal partners, one cannot conclude as a fact that Oregon would automatically be left with 'a great deal more' cost responsibility. Historical CRC negotiations involved cost-overrun risks and shifting liabilities, but that history does not by itself prove this specific outcome.

claim: "You had (4,925) out-of-state voters… in Georgia."
rationale: The claim is ambiguous (no election year or source and use of “you” is undefined) and there is no credible, verified evidence showing 4,925 out-of-state voters cast ballots in Georgia. Official Georgia election audits, recounts, and investigations around recent elections did not corroborate a systemic influx of thousands of nonresident voters. Without a clear time period or supporting documentation, the assertion is unsubstantiated.

claim: "Under Rick Scott, homeowners are paying higher (home insurance) premiums for less coverage."
rationale: The statement overstates and simplifies complex market changes. While homeowners' premiums in Florida rose during Rick Scott's governorship, those increases were driven by multiple factors (major hurricane losses, reinsurance costs, and insurer market exits), and reforms Scott supported targeted litigation and assignment-of-benefit practices rather than uniformly reducing mandated coverage levels. Available evidence does not support a clear, singular causal claim that 'under Rick Scott' homeowners paid higher premiums for less coverage as a direct, statewide policy outcome.

claim: Says Marsha Blackburn "voted against the Reauthorization of the Violence Against Women Act, which attempts to protect women from domestic violence, stalking, and date rape."
rationale: Marsha Blackburn, while serving in the U.S. House, voted against the 2013 reauthorization of the Violence Against Women Act, which is designed to protect women from domestic violence, stalking, and sexual assault. Her roll-call 'no' vote is documented in congressional voting records and was noted in contemporary news coverage.

claim: Says a study indicates up to $8.5 billion in lost GDP and up to 185,000 lost jobs if Texas lawmakers approve a measure limiting transgender bathroom choices.
rationale: I cannot verify a reputable study that specifically states 'up to $8.5 billion in lost GDP and up to 185,000 lost jobs' if Texas lawmakers approve a measure limiting transgender bathroom choices. While economic analyses of discriminatory laws have produced substantial and varying estimates, this exact figure and attribution appear unverified or misattributed without a cited source and clear timeframe/methodology.

claim: "Parents in Vail, Arizona just took over the school board — all according to the rules. Voted in a whole new board, and immediately removed the mask mandate."
rationale: The claim is misleading: while parent-backed candidates did win some Vail Unified School District seats in recent local elections, they did not 'vote in a whole new board' in a single instant, and mask-policy changes were governed by district procedures and county/state public-health rules rather than an immediate unilateral board action. Reports indicate only some seats flipped and any policy reversal followed meetings and legal/administrative constraints rather than an instant takeover and immediate removal.

claim: "The public option is not funded with public money. It's funded with private insurance premiums."
rationale: Whether a public option is funded by public money or by premiums depends on the specific legislative design. Some public-option proposals are intended to be financed by enrollee premiums and operate without direct taxpayer subsidies, but others include government seed funding, appropriations, or subsidies; therefore the absolute statement is incorrect.

claim: "99 percent of all new income today (is) going to the top 1 percent."
rationale: The claim is an overbroad assertion not supported as a general, current fact. While some studies of U.S. income distribution (e.g., work by Piketty, Saez and others) show that in particular short periods a very large share of post-recession income gains went to the top 1% (figures like ~95% have been reported for specific multi-year windows), saying '99 percent of all new income today' is unsubstantiated without a precise timeframe, country, and definition of 'new income.'

claim: "Collusion is not illegal."
rationale: The blanket statement is false: many forms of collusion—such as price‑fixing, bid‑rigging, and market allocation among competitors—are illegal under antitrust and competition laws in most jurisdictions. Whether a particular cooperative behavior is lawful depends on the specific conduct and legal context.

claim: Says Wisconsin’s 2011-13 state budget contains "no fee increases"
rationale: The enacted 2011–13 Wisconsin state budget included increases in multiple state fees (for example, certain licensing, user and natural-resource fees), so the assertion that it contained "no fee increases" is incorrect. While supporters framed some changes as shifts or offsets rather than broad tax hikes, the budget did raise specific fees in statute and administrative schedules.

claim: "Last year, (Bill McCollum) spent more than $2.2 million dollars to produce and air campaign-style TV ads where you were featured in almost every frame."
rationale: The statement is not verifiable as written because it omits the specific year and who “you” refers to, and I find no corroborating, attributable record tying Bill McCollum to more than $2.2 million in TV ads featuring the unnamed person. Claims about campaign ad spending and content are typically confirmed via campaign/PAC disclosures and media-buy tracking; without those specifics this assertion cannot be substantiated.

claim: "Half the kids coming out of college this year … can't find a job, or a job that's consistent with a college degree."
rationale: This claim overstates the situation. Official labor statistics and surveys show unemployment among recent college graduates is far below 50%, and although underemployment (working in jobs that don’t require a degree) affects a meaningful share of graduates, typical estimates do not support that half of new grads "can't find a job or a job consistent with a college degree."

claim: The federal government is sending refugees to states with governors who are "Republicans, not to the Democrats."
rationale: There is no evidence that the federal government directs refugees only to Republican-governed states; the federal refugee resettlement system places refugees across the country in communities served by resettlement agencies, including states and cities led by Democrats. High-profile moves of migrants by Republican governors to Democratic cities are state actions and not federal policy, so the claim that the federal government is sending refugees only to Republican states is false.

claim: Regarding the surgery that saved Jimmy Kimmel's son, "Medicaid has stopped providing this kind of service."
rationale: This claim is false. Federal Medicaid (and the Children’s Health Insurance Program) continue to cover medically necessary pediatric services, and the Medicaid EPSDT benefit requires states to provide diagnostic and treatment services for children under 21 — which includes surgeries for serious congenital conditions. There has been no nationwide policy that categorically "stopped" covering such surgeries, though access can be affected by state rules, reimbursement levels, and whether particular providers accept Medicaid.

claim: "North Carolina spends $855 less per student than it did before the Great Recession, and we have one of the lowest per pupil spending levels in the nation."
rationale: The claim presents a specific dollar decline and an absolute ranking but fails to specify the year or whether figures are inflation-adjusted; depending on the chosen baseline year and adjustment method, the change per pupil differs and can be larger or smaller than $855. While North Carolina did cut education funding during the Great Recession and has frequently ranked below the national average in per-pupil spending, the precise $855 figure and the categorical "one of the lowest" ranking cannot be confirmed without a defined time frame and data source.

claim: Says that "18 children died while in custody of Border Patrol" during the Obama administration.
rationale: There is no credible evidence or government record showing that 18 children died while in Border Patrol custody during the Obama administration. Fact-checks and official detainee-death records indicate a much smaller number of immigration-related child deaths across multiple agencies and different circumstances, but not 18 deaths specifically in Border Patrol custody under Obama.

claim: "No one visiting Disney can get in" because of protest.
rationale: The statement is an absolute claim that all visitors are prevented from entering Disney due to a protest. While protests have occurred at Disney parks and sometimes caused temporary delays, localized closures, or enhanced security, there is no general evidence that any protest has universally prevented everyone from entering all Disney properties. Park operations and local authorities typically manage demonstrations to allow continued access or only temporarily close specific entrances.

claim: "99% of NJ voters do NOT support hunting."
rationale: The claim is implausible and there is no known credible poll showing 99% of New Jersey voters oppose hunting. While relatively few people hunt, surveys and hunting-license data indicate that opposition to hunting is far below 99% and public opinion on hunting and hunting rights is mixed rather than nearly unanimous. Without a cited source, the extreme figure should be treated as false.

claim: "In the last two years, super PACs raised more than $180 million -- with roughly half of it coming from fewer than 200 super-rich people and roughly 20 percent from corporations."
rationale: The claim gives precise totals and percentages but omits a clear timeframe or source; campaign-finance data show super PAC fundraising totals and the donor-concentration share vary substantially by cycle and source. In many reported election cycles super PACs raised well more than $180 million over two years and the shares attributed to the top ~200 donors and to corporations differ by dataset and period, so the specific figures as stated are not reliably verifiable.

claim: After Britain’s vote to leave the European Union, "within 24 hours, Americans lost $100 billion from our 401(k)s."
rationale: The statement is misleading and not a verifiable, precise fact. While U.S. markets plunged after the Brexit vote and retirement account values fell temporarily, the specific claim that Americans lost exactly $100 billion from 401(k)s within 24 hours is an unverified rounding and oversimplification — estimates of short‑term paper losses varied and such losses are unrealized and depend on individual account allocations. Fact‑checkers treated similar blanket dollar claims as misleading.

claim: "The governor’s cuts would kick over 8,000 people out of their homes."
rationale: The claim is unverified as presented because it gives no specifics (which governor, which budget cuts, which program or time period) and provides no source for the 8,000 figure. Without documentary evidence (policy text, program caseloads, or independent impact analysis) linking the proposed cuts to actual evictions or loss of housing for that number, the statement cannot be confirmed and is potentially misleading.

claim: Pepsi admitted an employee contaminated its products with AIDS.
rationale: This is a long-running urban legend; PepsiCo has denied making any such admission and there is no credible evidence an employee contaminated Pepsi products with HIV/AIDS. Public-health authorities and fact-checkers also note HIV is not transmitted by beverages and no linked infections were reported.

claim: "Two-thirds of Americans disapprove of Donald Trump not wearing a face mask in public."
rationale: The exact claim that "two-thirds" of Americans disapproved is not consistently supported by available national polls. While many 2020-era surveys showed a majority disapproved of Trump not wearing a mask, results varied by pollster, timing, and question wording and do not unequivocally substantiate a two-thirds figure without a cited source.

claim: Bing Energy said it decided to move to Florida because of Gov. Rick Scott’s "plan to eliminate the corporate tax."
rationale: There is no public evidence that Bing Energy explicitly said it moved to Florida because of Gov. Rick Scott’s plan to eliminate the corporate tax. Contemporary news reports and the company’s statements attributed the relocation to local incentives, business climate and logistical considerations rather than a direct endorsement of Scott’s specific tax-elimination proposal.

claim: "South Florida ranks No. 1 in the gap between wages and housing."
rationale: The claim is too broad and there is no single, consistent authoritative dataset showing ‘South Florida’ universally ranks No. 1 on a wages-vs-housing gap. Rankings depend heavily on the exact metric, geographic definition, and time period; other U.S. metros (e.g., San Francisco Bay Area, New York City, Los Angeles) frequently top affordability or wage-to-housing-gap lists in many studies. Without a specific source and metric, the assertion that South Florida is unequivocally No. 1 is not supported.

claim: Says David Rivera "allowed House Republican leaders to strip key provisions from the STOCK Act" that would crack down on insider trading by members of Congress.
rationale: Contemporary reporting and legislative records attribute the removal of certain provisions from early STOCK Act drafts to House leadership and committee maneuvers, not to any specific action by Rep. David Rivera. There is no credible evidence that Rivera personally 'allowed' or directed leaders to strip key provisions of the bill.

claim: "If you became a Medicaid recipient through the Obamacare expansion, you are grandfathered in."
rationale: There is no universal federal rule that permanently ‘grandfathers’ people who joined Medicaid under the ACA expansion. Medicaid eligibility is means-tested and administered by states within federal rules, so coverage can change with income, state policy changes, or if a state alters its expansion program. Some states or temporary federal policies (e.g., COVID continuous coverage) have provided protections for certain enrollees, but that is not the same as an automatic permanent grandfathering for all expansion recipients.

claim: Rick Perry is "taking money away from hurricane victims" and diverting it to "remodel the Governor's Mansion."
rationale: There is no clear evidence that Rick Perry 'took money away from hurricane victims' and redirected it to remodel the Governor's Mansion. Disaster relief funds (especially federal FEMA grants) are subject to specific rules and oversight and were not simply reallocated to mansion renovations; reporting at the time noted the mansion work was funded through separate state/private appropriations rather than by cutting hurricane aid. While critics questioned budget choices, the specific claim of direct diversion is not supported by available records.

claim: "Biden wants to end Shareholder Capitalism.. that's your 401k..your pensions.. your retirement.. are you voting for that???"
rationale: There is no policy or proposal from President Biden to 'end shareholder capitalism' or to abolish 401(k)s, pensions, or retirements. Biden's administration has proposed regulations and tax changes aimed at corporate governance, worker protections, and climate goals, but these do not equate to eliminating shareholder-based investing or retirement accounts.

claim: Insurance companies "have made a fortune with Obamacare."
rationale: This is an overbroad generalization. While some large insurers did report substantial profits in certain years after the Affordable Care Act, many companies experienced losses at various times and the law includes constraints (like medical-loss ratio rules) and heavy reliance on federal subsidies—so profitability varied by insurer and year.

claim: On financial reform, there is "a million dollars being spent, per congressman, in lobbying expenses on this issue. (The) industry has four lobbyists per member of the House and Senate working on this."
rationale: The claim overstates what independently reported data support. Financial firms and industry groups do spend hundreds of millions annually on lobbying and advocacy around financial reform, but publicly available tallies for relevant years are generally below the level that would equal $1,000,000 per member when divided across all 535 members of Congress, and counts of registered lobbyists vary by definition and do not reliably equal four dedicated lobbyists per member for this single issue.

claim: "In 2021, 65 people in Milwaukee have lost their lives due to reckless driving accidents, and more than 9,000 cars have been stolen, double the amount in 2020."
rationale: The claim bundles two specific statistics that are not corroborated by readily available official sources. Public reporting and agency data for Milwaukee in 2021 show increases in vehicle thefts and traffic fatalities, but the precise figures (“65 people” killed specifically from “reckless driving” and “more than 9,000 cars” being stolen, exactly double 2020) are not clearly supported and likely conflate categories (city vs county, traffic fatalities vs reckless-driving convictions).

claim: Says Gov. Evers "has refused to identify or discipline the staff member who secretly taped" a conversation with GOP leaders.
rationale: There is no clear, corroborated public record that Gov. Tony Evers explicitly 'refused' to identify or discipline a staffer who secretly taped a conversation with GOP leaders. Coverage of the incident indicates Evers' office declined to publicly name personnel for privacy reasons and noted legal and investigative considerations, not an outright, public refusal to discipline. The claim overstates and frames routine privacy and legal responses as an explicit refusal.

claim: Children born today will carry a $30,000 share of the national debt.
rationale: The claim is misleading: national debt is a government obligation, not a legally assigned per-child bill, and any “share” per child depends on how one divides current/future debt among the population or cohorts. Per-capita or per-child calculations vary widely with the country, current debt level, population, and future economic factors (growth, inflation, policy), so a fixed $30,000 figure for every child born today is not a reliable fact.

claim: Says Texas high school "graduation rates are at an all-time high—the third-highest in the nation—which represents a significant turnaround from just a few short years ago."
rationale: While Texas has reported rising and record graduation rates in recent years, national data and state-by-state rankings do not consistently place Texas as the third-highest in the nation. The statement bundles an unqualified national ranking with an unspecified ‘‘all-time high’’ claim, which is not supported by available comparative data.

claim: "One man (New Castle, Del., County Executive, Chris Coons) thought property taxes should be hiked almost 50 percent."
rationale: There is no well‑documented evidence that New Castle County Executive Chris Coons publicly proposed hiking property taxes by nearly 50%. While Coons served as county executive and dealt with budgets and taxes, claims of an almost 50% proposed increase appear to be a mischaracterization or taken out of context rather than an accurate record of his policy proposals.

claim: "Of the top five cities for staged automobile accidents, three are in Florida. … We rank No. 1 in the country in staged auto accidents."
rationale: There is no single authoritative, consistent national ranking confirming that three of the top five cities for staged auto accidents are in Florida or that Florida ranks No. 1. Reports and lists claiming such rankings typically come from specific insurers or local news stories with varying methodology and timeframes, so the blanket claim is unverified and likely misleading without a cited source.

claim: The IAEA, or the International Atomic Energy Agency, "last month said the Iranians are not currently living up to their obligations."
rationale: I cannot confirm this specific, time-relative claim because it lacks a concrete date and IAEA issues frequent statements about Iran. Without a verifiable date and source (a specific IAEA report or press release), the assertion that the agency 'last month said the Iranians are not currently living up to their obligations' cannot be validated here, so I mark it false due to insufficient evidence.

claim: "Donald Trump praises Colonel Sanders for his service in the Civil War."
rationale: Harland 'Colonel' Sanders was born in 1890, 25 years after the U.S. Civil War ended in 1865, so he could not have served in that war. The 'Colonel' title in his case is an honorary Kentucky colonel rank, not a Civil War military commission, and there is no credible record of Donald Trump praising him for Civil War service.

claim: The White House "created a fake set for (President Joe) Biden to get his booster shot. The entire Biden presidency is one giant charade."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that the White House 'created a fake set' for President Biden's booster; contemporaneous official photos, video, and multiple news reports document him receiving the shot from medical staff in the White House medical unit. The broader claim that 'the entire Biden presidency is one giant charade' is a sweeping, subjective conspiracy assertion that is not supported by verifiable facts.

claim: "The toxicity of COVID-Omicron is 5 times higher than that of the delta variant, and the mortality rate is also higher than that of Delta."
rationale: Multiple peer-reviewed studies and public-health surveillance from the Omicron wave showed that Omicron (early BA.1/BA.2) was generally less intrinsically severe than Delta, with lower rates of hospitalization and death, not five times more toxic or more deadly. Differences in observed outcomes are strongly influenced by higher population immunity (vaccination and prior infection) and by variation among subvariants, but no robust evidence supports a 5× increase in toxicity or higher overall mortality for Omicron compared with Delta.

claim: "Nationally, the unemployment rate for veterans is far greater than the national unemployment rate," and Wisconsin is "one of those rare examples where unemployment is actually lower for veterans than it is for the population as a whole and certainly lower than it is nationally."
rationale: The claim is overstated. U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics data show veteran unemployment has at times been similar to or lower than the overall civilian unemployment rate rather than being "far greater" nationally, and whether Wisconsin’s veteran rate is lower depends on the specific year and measure — it is not reliably a rare exception without a date. The statement therefore mischaracterizes national trends and omits the time frame needed to support the Wisconsin assertion.

claim: "Most of the people that work in finance make $70,000, $80,000 a year."
rationale: The finance workforce spans many occupations with a wide pay range: entry-level or back-office roles often earn well below $70k while senior bankers, traders, and asset managers frequently earn far more. Because of this skewed distribution and variation by role, experience, and country, it is incorrect to claim that most people in finance earn $70–80k.

claim: Says Ted Cruz’s father "was with Lee Harvey Oswald" before the assassination of President John F. Kennedy.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Rafael (Ted) Cruz’s father was with Lee Harvey Oswald before JFK’s assassination. The allegation stems from misinterpretations and social-media rumors; Cruz and multiple independent fact-checkers have found no contemporaneous records or reliable testimony placing him with Oswald.

claim: The census "for years and years and years, decades, has asked, ‘Are you a citizen of the United States of America?’"
rationale: The decennial census short form has not asked a citizenship question since 1950, so it is incorrect to say the main census questionnaire has asked "Are you a citizen..." for decades. However, the Census Bureau has collected citizenship information for many years via the long-form sample and, later, the American Community Survey.

claim: Sherrod Brown "sent billions of our tax dollars to foreign countries."
rationale: No individual senator 'sends' tax dollars abroad; appropriations and foreign aid are enacted by Congress as a whole and signed by the president. While Senator Sherrod Brown has at times voted for budget or aid bills that included foreign assistance, the claim that he personally 'sent billions' is a misleading attribution of congressional spending decisions to one person.

claim: Obamacare is a "massive, massive income redistribution" with "$250 billion a year in Medicaid expansion (and) in the subsidy structure that's basically being paid for by people on Medicare, through Medicare cuts, and a lot of tax increases."
rationale: The claim mixes accurate elements with exaggeration. The Affordable Care Act did expand Medicaid and provide large premium subsidies, and it included Medicare payment reductions and several tax increases, but the specific figure of "$250 billion a year" for Medicaid expansion is much higher than official estimates and funding came from a mix of general revenues, employer/household costs, and targeted revenue/offsets rather than being "basically paid for by people on Medicare." Describing the law as a straightforward "massive income redistribution" oversimplifies the mix of spending increases, savings, and revenue changes.

claim: "Fifty percent of the Ottawa police force have all turned in their resignation."
rationale: There are no credible reports or official statements indicating that half of the Ottawa Police Service submitted resignations; such a large, sudden exodus would have been widely documented by major news outlets and city authorities. The claim as stated is implausible given typical police staffing and reporting practices.

claim: Says Alex Sink "failed Florida homeowners by using predatory lending practices."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Alex Sink herself engaged in or implemented predatory lending practices that 'failed Florida homeowners.' Claims tying her to such practices were made as campaign rhetoric linking her to banks during the mortgage crisis, but independent fact-checking and public records do not show she personally ran predatory-lending programs.

claim: Wisconsin’s middle class is the "most diminished" in the United States.
rationale: The statement is an unsupported superlative: there is no consistent, authoritative evidence that Wisconsin’s middle class is unequivocally the "most diminished" in the United States. Different analyses (by year, metric, and definition of “middle class” or “diminished”) identify different states as having the largest declines, so the claim overgeneralizes and lacks a single accepted basis.

claim: Kelly Ayotte "voted for a budget that had $90 billion of cuts to Pell Grants."
rationale: The claim is misleading. There is no clear record that Ayotte cast a vote to enact an actual $90 billion cut to Pell Grants; the $90 billion figure was associated with projected changes in some GOP budget proposals and campaign rhetoric. Budget resolutions are nonbinding policy blueprints and do not themselves cut programs, and the cited number conflates proposed savings estimates with enacted law.

claim: Says BLM activist Sasha Johnson tweeted, "The white man will not be our equal but our slave."
rationale: Multiple reputable fact-checkers investigated this claim and found the screenshot was fabricated and there is no evidence the quoted tweet appeared on Sasha Johnson’s verified account. No archived copies or credible sources corroborate that she posted that message, and the image appears to be a doctored attribution.

claim: Says Nelson Mandela "was a communist."
rationale: Nelson Mandela was not widely documented as a formal member of a Communist party; he led the ANC, described himself as a democratic socialist, and worked closely with the South African Communist Party and other leftist groups. While he accepted support and shared some goals with communists, Mandela repeatedly denied being a communist and his primary affiliation was with the ANC rather than formal communist membership.

claim: Says Sen. Kay Hagan "has missed half of the (Senate Armed Services) Committee's hearings in 2014."
rationale: There is no reliable public evidence that Sen. Kay Hagan missed half of the Senate Armed Services Committee hearings in 2014. Such assertions have appeared in partisan ads and fact-checks indicate they rely on selective counting or ambiguous definitions of which sessions qualify as 'hearings,' rather than an official attendance tally showing a 50% absence rate.

claim: "Kyle Rittenhouse used his COVID-19 stimulus check to purchase the AR-15 he used in the fatal Kenosha shooting."
rationale: Multiple reputable fact-checks and reporting concluded there is no evidence Rittenhouse used a COVID-19 stimulus payment to buy the rifle. Timelines and reporting indicate the firearm purchase preceded the stimulus payments and/or involved other parties, and Rittenhouse was a minor at the time which would have complicated a direct purchase from a dealer.

claim: "324,000 pregnant people experience domestic violence during their pregnancy."
rationale: The statement gives a precise number but no timeframe or location; I could not verify 324,000 as a current, nationally representative figure. Prevalence estimates for domestic/intimate partner violence during pregnancy vary by country and study, and such a specific number typically requires a cited source to be credible.

claim: Cuts in local government and school funding in John Kasich’s budget caused "many communities to seek school levies, local tax increases, layoffs."
rationale: Kasich’s budgets as governor included reductions to state aid streams (including cuts to the Local Government Fund and changes to school funding and taxes) that reduced revenue available to counties, municipalities and many school districts. Contemporary reporting and fiscal analyses from Ohio documented a wave of school levy campaigns, local tax increases and district staff reductions as districts and local governments sought to replace lost state dollars. While local choices and other factors also played a role, the budget cuts were a clear driver of those fiscal responses in many communities.

claim: Says Donald Trump "wants to kick thousands of kids off of BadgerCare."
rationale: There is no clear public policy or statement from Donald Trump explicitly proposing to "kick thousands of kids off of BadgerCare." The Trump administration did promote broader Medicaid changes (work requirements, waivers, and funding limits) that critics said could reduce Medicaid enrollment, but those proposals did not specifically target children on Wisconsin’s BadgerCare by name.

claim: Says Texas has so few gas-pump inspectors in the field, "the HEBs of this state, the Brookshires of this state, they're calibrating their own gas pumps. The (Texas Department of Agriculture) just sends them the stickers and they calibrate them."
rationale: This statement is an exaggeration. Texas law requires official oversight of commercial measuring devices: the Texas Department of Agriculture (Weights & Measures) inspects and certifies fuel pumps and requires licensed service agents for adjustments; regulators do not simply mail stickers and let retailers self-certify without inspection. While retailers may hire licensed technicians or service companies to perform routine maintenance, official seals and enforcement remain the responsibility of the agency and its authorized designees, not unilateral self-calibration by stores.

claim: "On average, women make 77 cents for every dollar men make."
rationale: The "77 cents" figure is an outdated and oversimplified statistic often quoted for a specific year and measurement in the U.S.; the gender pay gap varies by country, year, and how earnings are measured (median annual, weekly, full-time vs all workers). Recent U.S. median estimates for full-time workers are closer to about 82–83 cents on the dollar, and analyses that adjust for occupation, hours, and experience show smaller gaps. Therefore the blanket statement as written is misleading.

claim: "There are only about 10 people in the United States Senate who have any real business experience."
rationale: This claim is false. Far more than about ten U.S. senators have substantive private‑sector or business experience — many are former CEOs, founders, executives, investors, farmers, or small‑business owners (for example, Mitt Romney, Rick Scott, Mark Warner), and dozens of others list business occupations in public biographies. The exact count depends on how one defines “real business experience,” but it is well above ten.

claim: "Big pharmaceuticals pay off — they literally pay off — generics to keep the prices and the competition off the market."
rationale: There is a documented practice known as "pay-for-delay" or reverse-payment settlements in which brand drug makers have paid generic manufacturers to delay entering the market, which can keep competition and lower prices off the market. U.S. regulators and courts (including the Supreme Court) and the FTC have litigated and reported on these arrangements as potentially anticompetitive. While not every large drug company uses this tactic, it has occurred repeatedly and is a recognized phenomenon in pharmaceutical markets.

claim: "This is the slowest job recovery since Hoover."
rationale: The statement is too vague and misleading: comparisons of modern job recoveries typically benchmark against the post–World War II period, and analysts generally describe the 2009–2010 recovery as the slowest since WWII rather than specifically since Herbert Hoover. Moreover, labor statistics from the 1930s are not directly comparable to modern series (different measures, massive structural collapse), so claiming 'slowest since Hoover' is not supportable without precise measures and timeframe.

claim: "Jeb Bush recently noted, Reagan himself would have been too moderate, too reasonable for today's GOP."
rationale: There are no reliable reports or verifiable direct quotes up to mid-2024 showing Jeb Bush recently said that Reagan "would have been too moderate, too reasonable for today's GOP." The attribution appears to be a paraphrase or misattribution; while commentators and some politicians have suggested Reagan might not fit the modern GOP, that specific recent claim by Jeb Bush is not supported by known public statements.

claim: "The KKK was formed by the Democratic Party."
