While the law was later central to public and legal debate because it affects self‑defense claims and immunity/charging decisions, causal attribution of the death to the statute itself cannot be established from the available facts.

claim: "68% error rate in Michigan Voting Machines. Should be, by law, a tiny percentage of one percent."
rationale: There is no credible evidence or official audit showing a 68% error rate in Michigan voting machines; post-election audits, recounts, and certification processes have not found statewide error rates anywhere near that magnitude. While election equipment is subject to testing, certification, and post‑election audits that aim for very low error rates, the claim’s numeric figure is unsupported and the legal phrase quoted is vague and not an accurate citation of a single statutory error threshold.

claim: "Illegal immigration costs state taxpayers over $3 billion every year."
rationale: The claim is too vague and not verifiable as stated: estimates of the fiscal impact of unauthorized immigrants vary widely by methodology, time period, and whether federal as well as state costs and taxes are counted. Some studies show net costs in the tens of billions, others show a small net fiscal burden or even net contribution; without specifying the country, year, or what costs are included, the blanket statement that 'illegal immigration costs state taxpayers over $3 billion every year' is unsupported and misleading.

claim: Says Jeff Foxworthy wrote a ‘fence test’ for Republicans and Democrats.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that comedian Jeff Foxworthy authored a partisan ‘fence test’ comparing Republicans and Democrats. Foxworthy is known for his 'You might be a redneck' comedy bits and related books, and viral lists claiming he wrote political tests have been repeatedly circulated without reliable attribution.

claim: If women seeking an abortion see their ultrasound, "the odds are pretty high they're going to keep the baby."
rationale: Multiple peer-reviewed studies and evaluations of state 'viewing' or mandatory ultrasound laws find that most women have already decided to have an abortion before the ultrasound and only a small minority change their decision after seeing the image. Overall, mandatory ultrasound/viewing policies have not produced large reductions in abortion rates, so the claim that the odds are 'pretty high' women will keep the baby after viewing an ultrasound overstates the evidence.

claim: Wisconsin is "clearly seeing a decline in COVID infections"
rationale: The claim provides no date or data source and is time-sensitive; COVID-19 case trends in Wisconsin have fluctuated over time and cannot be labeled as "clearly declining" without current surveillance metrics. Verifying such a statement requires up-to-date case counts, test positivity, and hospitalization data from official public-health sources.

claim: Royalties for oil and other energy sources are the "second-largest revenue source to the federal government after the IRS."
rationale: Federal receipts are overwhelmingly dominated by income and payroll taxes collected by the IRS; energy royalties are a relatively small component (billions) compared with total federal revenues (trillions). Therefore royalties for oil and other energy sources are not the second-largest source of federal revenue.

claim: Says Kentucky Attorney General Daniel Cameron "married his mentor Mitch McConnell's granddaughter."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Kentucky AG Daniel Cameron married Mitch McConnell’s granddaughter. Public reporting and marriage records identify his spouse and do not show any familial relationship to McConnell; this appears to be a rumor conflating political association with family ties.

claim: "Texas now has the second-highest high school graduation rate in the country. And it has the highest graduation rate for African Americans and Hispanics."
rationale: The statement is misleading because it gives no year or data source; national graduation-rate rankings change by year and by the metric used (on-time adjusted cohort vs extended-year). While Texas has made substantial improvements and posts relatively high graduation rates for Black and Hispanic students compared with many large states, recent federal and state datasets do not consistently place Texas second-highest overall nationwide or clearly first for both African American and Hispanic subgroup rates across comparable data years.

claim: "The Border Patrol has 20,000 agents – more than twice as many as there were in 2004."
rationale: While U.S. Border Patrol staffing is around 20,000 in recent years, that figure is not more than twice the size of the force in 2004. Historical staffing records show roughly 10,000–11,000 Border Patrol agents in the mid-2000s, so 20,000 is about double but not 'more than twice.'

claim: Says each of the past three years "has been the hottest on record."
rationale: Global temperature records from major agencies do not support a blanket statement that each of the past three years was the hottest on record. While some recent years (for example 2016, 2019/2020 tied, and 2023) have been record-setting or among the warmest, other recent years (such as 2021 and 2022) were very warm but did not each individually set a new all-time annual record.

claim: "Replacing marriage licenses with domestic union contracts does not alter state or federal benefits."
rationale: A blanket replacement of marriage licenses with 'domestic union' contracts would likely change legal recognition and therefore benefits. Many state and federal programs explicitly tie rights and benefits (tax filing status, Social Security spousal benefits, immigration sponsorship, veterans and federal employee benefits) to the legal status of 'marriage' as defined by statute and case law, and differently labeled or structured contracts may not be accepted as equivalent.

claim: A provision of the Senate immigration bill would require you to have government permission to get a second job.
rationale: No major Senate immigration bill contains a provision that would require the general public (U.S. citizens or lawful permanent residents) to obtain government permission to take a second job. Existing immigration and visa rules already require certain nonimmigrant visa holders (e.g., H‑1B, some guestworker categories) to have employer-specific authorization, but that is different from a universal new requirement for everyone to get permission for a second job.

claim: Says a photo shows Adam Schiff and Jeffrey Epstein.
rationale: There is no verified, credible photograph showing Rep. Adam Schiff with Jeffrey Epstein; images circulated online purporting to show them together have been debunked as altered or misattributed. Reporting and public records do not document any confirmed meeting or authentic photo of the two together.

claim: Says "Ron Johnson calls Social Security a Ponzi scheme and wants to privatize the program."
rationale: The claim bundles two assertions; while Ron Johnson has criticized Social Security and promoted reforms including private-account ideas, there is not clear, consistent evidence that he repeatedly and explicitly labeled Social Security a "Ponzi scheme" or that he has advocated outright full privatization of the entire program. His public statements more commonly call for reforms, fiscal fixes, or options like private accounts rather than a blanket privatization.

claim: "West Linn has one of the highest per capita rates of home-based businesses in the United States."
rationale: There is no well‑known or authoritative national data identifying West Linn, Oregon, as having one of the highest per capita rates of home‑based businesses. Rankings of this type would require specific Census/ACS or business‑registry analysis, and no such widely cited study singles out West Linn. The claim appears unsubstantiated and likely stems from local promotion rather than verified national comparison.

claim: Heroin and prescription opioids are "the number one cause of accidental or preventable death in Wisconsin."
rationale: State-level cause-of-death rankings change over time and depend on definitions; while opioid-related overdoses (including heroin and illicit fentanyl) have driven large increases in unintentional deaths, it is not clearly established that heroin plus prescription opioids together are the single top cause of all accidental or preventable deaths in Wisconsin. Other causes such as motor vehicle crashes and falls have historically been major contributors, and overdose categories often include non-prescription synthetic opioids and polysubstance deaths.

claim: Says Rick Perry's proposal on driver licenses and high school dropouts has been state law since 1989.
rationale: The claim that Rick Perry’s proposal (to restrict driver’s licenses for high-school dropouts) has been state law since 1989 is inaccurate. While Texas has long had compulsory-attendance rules and some truancy-related sanctions, the specific policy Perry proposed was not a statewide driver-license restriction in place in 1989; media and legislative histories show the linkage of licenses to school attendance evolved later and varied by statute and enforcement. Therefore the blanket statement that his proposal had been state law since 1989 is false.

claim: U.S. Rep. Matt Gaetz was the lone vote in the House against an anti-human trafficking bill.
rationale: The claim is ambiguous and no clear roll-call or major news report documents Rep. Matt Gaetz as the sole House 'no' on a broadly described “anti-human trafficking” bill. While Gaetz has at times opposed or voted 'present' on certain trafficking-related measures, House roll-call records for high-profile anti-trafficking bills show bipartisan overwhelming majorities rather than a single dissenting vote by Gaetz.

claim: The FBI lost Hunter Biden’s laptop.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that the FBI 'lost' Hunter Biden’s laptop. Reporting and public statements indicate the repair-shop owner provided the device or a copy to the FBI and that copies of its data circulated, but claims that the Bureau misplaced the laptop are unsubstantiated.

claim: "Bill Gates says you don't have a choice to be vaccinated or not."
rationale: There is no reliable record of Bill Gates saying the categorical statement 'you don't have a choice to be vaccinated or not.' Gates has publicly promoted vaccines and global immunization programs, but the claim appears to be a misquote or out-of-context distortion of his pro-vaccine advocacy rather than a documented assertion that vaccination will be forcibly universal by his decree.

claim: "We have the highest corporate tax rate in the world. It’s 35 percent."
rationale: The United States’ federal corporate tax rate was 35% before the 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act, but it was cut to 21% beginning in 2018. Even when the U.S. rate was 35%, that was not the single highest corporate tax rate globally because some countries had statutory or combined (national plus regional) rates above 35%, and international comparisons depend on whether subnational taxes are included.

claim: Extending current tax rates would "average more than $100,000 a year to millionaires and even billionaires."
rationale: The claim is too vague and lacks essential context (which country, which tax rates, time period, and which population of 'millionaires' and 'billionaires'), so it cannot be verified as stated. Whether an extension of particular tax provisions would average more than $100,000 per year for people with million- or billion-dollar wealth depends on the specific provision, the measurement (per taxpayer vs. per household), and official revenue or distributional estimates. Without those details, the blanket statement is unsupported.

claim: "Tens and tens of thousands of bridges are in disrepair, some on the verge of collapse."
rationale: In many countries (notably the United States) official inspections and industry reports have identified tens of thousands of bridges rated as structurally deficient or in poor condition. While “on the verge of collapse” is a subjective phrase, inspection findings and occasional bridge failures show that some aging bridges can pose an imminent safety risk if not repaired or replaced.

claim: "I've been outspent by my opponents every time I've run for U.S. Senate."
rationale: This claim cannot be verified as stated because it omits who "I" is and which Senate campaigns and cycles are meant. Whether a candidate was outspent depends on specific election years and whether one counts only campaign committee expenditures or also outside/independent spending and self-funding. Without those details and examination of FEC and independent-expenditure records for each race, the blanket statement is unprovable.

claim: "The Earth is not warming."
rationale: Multiple independent datasets and scientific assessments show a clear long-term increase in global average temperatures over the past century, with accelerated warming in recent decades. Observed indicators — rising land and ocean temperatures, shrinking glaciers and Arctic sea ice, increasing ocean heat content and sea level rise — are inconsistent with the claim that the Earth is not warming.
